While the empirical scope could be broader and the analysis does not cover conditional/model-based estimators or multi-judge ensembles in depth, the authors are careful about assumptions and discuss plausible escape routes. Overall, the paper makes a substantive, rigorous contribution that will help anchor expectations and methodologies in the fast-moving evaluation literature. I recommend acceptance.

papers.title: DEPT: Decoupled Embeddings for Pre-training Language Models

reviews.summary: This paper proposes DEPT, a communication-efficient pre-training framework that decouples token and positional embeddings from the transformer body to better handle heterogeneous data sources (domains and languages). DEPT comprises three variants—GLOB (local-SGD/FedAvg with shared embeddings), TRIM (per-silo trimmed embeddings projected back to a global vocabulary), and SPEC (fully silo-specialized embeddings and positional encodings)—and aims to reduce negative interference, memory/communication costs, and vocabulary dilution while improving generalization and plasticity. Experiments on multi-domain (The Pile) and multilingual (mC4) mixtures with decoder-only models up to ~1.3B parameters show sizable perplexity and downstream gains, along with large reductions in communication and embedding memory, and demonstrate feasibility of vocabulary-agnostic federated pre-training at billion-parameter scale.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The core idea—to explicitly decouple (or partially decouple) embeddings from the shared transformer body across heterogeneous sources—is simple yet non-trivial, with clear architectural implications and practical benefits.

SPEC’s fully decoupled setup that supports per-silo vocabularies and positional embeddings without shared tokenization is novel in federated/heterogeneous pre-training contexts and addresses vocabulary dilution and tokenization mismatch head-on.
The TRIM variant’s projection mechanism with zero-padding and per-token aggregation is a neat, lightweight way to reduce memory/communication while maintaining a global vocabulary.
Experimental rigor and validation

The paper evaluates across both multi-domain (16 The Pile subsets) and multilingual (8 mC4 languages, with OOD languages) scenarios, reporting perplexity, OOD performance, plasticity, and downstream NLU tasks.
Comparisons include multiple sampling baselines (STD at τ=0, 0.3, 1), and an active forgetting baseline (ACT) adapted to the setting.
The “continued pre-training” stage with random embedding initialization is a thoughtful diagnostic that isolates transformer body quality.
Results are shown at multiple model scales (125M–1.3B), and the authors discuss stability (activation/parameter norms), communicating training robustness.
Clarity of presentation
The motivation—capacity contention, vocabulary dilution, and suboptimal tokenization under heterogeneity—is well articulated and connects to prior empirical findings.
The three variants are clearly contrasted in terms of communication/memory trade-offs and assumptions (shared vs. specialized vocabularies/positions).
The TRIM aggregation is formalized with indicator matrices; the communication/memory table succinctly conveys scaling implications.
Significance of contributions

Communication and memory savings are practically important for cross-silo and low-bandwidth pre-training; enabling vocabulary-agnostic federated pre-training at billion-parameter scale is a meaningful milestone.

The consistent generalization/plasticity gains suggest DEPT can be a useful first-stage pre-training recipe that complements data-centric strategies (e.g., filtering, mixture engineering) highlighted in recent literature.
Findings are relevant to multilingual and multi-domain LLM pre-training, where scalability, stability, and fairness to low-resource sources matter.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

SPEC requires a post-hoc “continued pre-training” stage to build a usable global embedding; this dependency can add 15–19% extra steps and potentially alter comparisons to baselines that do not intrinsically need a second stage.

TRIM changes the training objective by restricting the output space locally during pre-training (given tied input-output embeddings), which may introduce subtle comparability concerns to STD that predicts over the full vocabulary at all times.
The algorithm pseudocode interleaves the three variants in a single loop and is confusing in its current form (lines 4–7 read as executed in sequence rather than mutually exclusive paths).
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Many headline improvements rely on the “randomly reinitialized embeddings” evaluation to isolate transformer body quality; while justified, this setup downplays the role of embeddings in real deployments. The “pre-trained embedding” comparison for GLOB/TRIM shows smaller or mixed gains, indicating sensitivity to the continued pre-training mixture and sampling.

The multilingual suite is limited to eight languages (with three OOD languages); claims about alleviating the curse of multilinguality would be stronger with larger language coverage (e.g., 30–100+ as in recent studies).

Comparisons to other low-communication/distributed pre-training approaches (e.g., DiLoCo, DisTrO, Local SGD baselines beyond FedAvg, or MoE-style decoupling of capacity) are discussed but not empirically benchmarked.

Compute/wall-clock accounting and cost-equivalence across methods are under-specified; communication byte counts are helpful, but end-to-end training time and throughput are crucial for practical claims.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some tables (e.g., Table 2) mix memory/comms units and relative factors in ways that are hard to parse at a glance; consistent units and a clearer definition of “per-step comms” versus “per-round” would help.
The OOD perplexity numbers are extremely large for some languages, suggesting substantial tokenization mismatch; framing and normalization could be improved to ease interpretation.
Missing related work or comparisons

The paper could better position DEPT relative to strong, recent multilingual findings that attribute “curse” effects more to data quality and absolute token counts than to language count per se (e.g., 2510.25947): DEPT’s gains appear complementary but this nuance is not fully explored.

More direct connections to monolingual tokenizer advantages (Goldfish; 2408.10441) and massively multilingual continual pre-training (EMMA-500; 2409.17892) would clarify how DEPT bridges monolingual tokenization benefits with a shared body.
Empirical comparison to other vocabulary/embedding transfer approaches (e.g., trans-tokenization/vocabulary transfer, Remy et al., 2024) would strengthen the SPEC story.
reviews.questions:
1. How are TRIM’s per-token updates weighted during aggregation across silos to avoid overweighting frequent tokens or sources? Do you normalize by token counts or client data size?
2. Can you provide wall-clock time and throughput comparisons (end-to-end, including the continued pre-training phase for SPEC) to substantiate the practical efficiency claims, not just communication bytes?
3. How sensitive are the results to Nlocal (local steps) and client participation rate? Is there a stability or accuracy trade-off as Nlocal grows (as in Local SGD literature)?
4. Could you include an empirical comparison with DiLoCo/DisTrO-style low-communication training or a MoE baseline, to better position DEPT against state-of-practice communication-efficient or capacity-partitioning alternatives?
5. For SPEC, how critical is specializing positional embeddings versus only token embeddings? An ablation (SPEC without positional specialization) would clarify the incremental benefit.
6. The continued pre-training stage adds 15–19% extra steps: how do results change if this budget is reduced/increased? Is there a minimal budget at which SPEC/GLOB/TRIM maintain their advantage?
7. Multilingual experiments cover 8 languages (plus 3 OOD). Do your conclusions persist with 30–50+ languages (e.g., mC4 or FineWeb-2 subsets)? Any preliminary results or insights?
8. Can you release code/tokenizers and, if possible, trained checkpoints for at least the 125M/350M settings to aid reproducibility?
reviews.assessment: This paper tackles a timely and practically important challenge in multilingual and multi-domain pre-training: how to prevent embedding-level interference, reduce communication/memory costs, and improve robustness when training on heterogeneous corpora. The central idea—decoupling or partially decoupling embeddings from a shared transformer body—is simple yet promising, and the SPEC/TRIM design choices are well-motivated. Empirically, the authors present a convincing body of evidence that DEPT produces transformer bodies with better generalization and plasticity and can drastically reduce communication. The work is not without caveats: the strongest gains are measured in a “random-embedding” continued pre-training setup that emphasizes transformer-body quality rather than end-to-end readiness; SPEC requires a follow-up stage; and comparisons to alternative low-communication or capacity-partitioning methods are limited. Nonetheless, the contribution is significant and likely to be of interest to the ICLR community working on scalable, multilingual, and federated LLM pre-training. With additional clarifications (aggregation weighting, wall-clock reporting), expanded multilingual coverage, and a couple of stronger baselines, this paper would be a solid accept. As it stands, I lean toward acceptance due to the novelty, technical soundness, and compelling empirical findings.

papers.title: Homomorphism Expressivity of Spectral Invariant Graph Neural Networks

reviews.summary: The paper studies the expressive power of spectral invariant graph neural networks (GNNs) through the lens of homomorphism expressivity. Its central result (Theorem 3.3) shows that d-iteration spectral invariant GNNs are exactly characterized by the ability to distinguish graphs via homomorphism counts of a new “parallel trees” family with parallel-tree depth at most d, and proves maximality. This yields a quantitative hierarchy among spectral invariants, clarifies the impact of iterations (strictly increasing power with depth, disproving a prior conjecture), extends to higher-order spectral invariant GNNs, and provides precise subgraph counting guarantees (e.g., cycles up to length 7), with supporting experiments.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces a new and elegant homomorphism characterization (parallel trees) for spectral invariant GNNs, establishing existence and maximality of their homomorphism expressivity.

Bridges two previously separate strands—spectral invariants (including projections) and homomorphism indistinguishability—via walk-encoding equivalences and tailored pebble games adapted to spectral refinement.
Resolves open questions from prior work (e.g., strictly increasing power with iterations; precise role of projections vs eigenvalues; bounding symmetric power by Local 2k-GNN).
Provides extensions to higher-order spectral invariant GNNs through a parallel strong nested ear decomposition concept.
Experimental rigor and validation
Uses homomorphism counting benchmarks, cycle counting tasks, and a standard molecular dataset (ZINC) to qualitatively validate theoretical predictions and the proposed hierarchy.
Compares against strong baselines (MPNN, Subgraph GNN, Local 2-GNN) aligned with the theoretical framework.
Clarity of presentation
Core concepts—parallel edges/trees, parallel-tree depth, and the connection to walk-encoding—are well-motivated and intuitive, aiding the reader.
Clear articulation of implications: hierarchy vs 1-WL/2-FWL, the role of iterations, and subgraph counting capabilities.
Significance of contributions
Offers a quantitative, fine-grained, and maximally tight characterization that complements and substantially extends WL-style analyses.
Establishes a reusable methodology (walk equivalence + spectral pebble game + Fürer-graph reduction) that is likely applicable to analyzing other global positional/spectral augmentations in GNNs.
Clarifies practical capabilities (e.g., which subgraphs can be counted and how many iterations suffice), informing design choices in spectral GNNs.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The main spectral-encoding equivalence leverages exact spectral projection information (or equivalently all walk counts up to n−1), which is computationally heavy and only approximated in practice; the gap between idealized theory and practical approximations is not discussed.

Some key steps (e.g., maximality via the spectral pebble game and Fürer-graph construction, and the higher-order “parallel strong NED” formalism) are deferred to the appendix, limiting verifiability in the main text.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Experiments validate trends but are relatively light given the breadth of claims; e.g., iteration-depth ablations are limited, and there is no explicit test showing success on C7 but failure on C8 as predicted by the theory.
Table formatting is hard to parse; the cycle-counting section focuses on 3–6 cycles though the theory highlights 7-cycles as a boundary case.
No ablation isolating eigenvalues vs. projections vs. refinement iterations to empirically substantiate the incremental gains each provides.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some notation and figure references have minor inconsistencies or artifacts (likely due to extraction), and several crucial counterexamples are referenced but not fully visible/legible in the main body.
The higher-order section is only “informal” in the main text; readers must consult the appendix for essential definitions and proofs.
Missing related work or comparisons

While the coverage is strong, a brief discussion of computational costs and stability in extracting spectral projections (and the implications for training/inference) would strengthen the connection to practical spectral GNN implementations.
Additional context on recent positional encodings/graph transformers that approximate global spectral structure could help position the results’ practical relevance.
reviews.questions:
1. How sensitive are your empirical results to approximations of projections (e.g., truncated eigenspaces, randomized SVD, top-K eigenpairs)? Can your theory be partially extended to these approximations?
2. Could you include an explicit empirical test for subgraph counting on C7 vs C8 to directly validate Corollary 3.15 and the stated iteration requirements?
3. Beyond constant initialization, how do node/edge features interact with your expressivity results? Do the characterizations extend when features are present?
4. Can you provide more details or intuition on why parallel trees (specifically) match the spectral-walk refinement dynamics and why depth corresponds to parallel-tree depth?
5. In practice, what is the computational complexity of one spectral invariant GNN layer under your formulation, and how do you recommend implementing it efficiently for medium/large graphs?
6. For the higher-order extension: could you move a concise formal definition of “parallel k-order strong NED” into the main text and give a minimal illustrative example?
7. Are there natural graph classes where spectral invariant GNNs achieve the 2-FWL bound (i.e., become equivalent), or can you prove a strict gap persists over all graph families?
reviews.assessment: This is a strong and timely theoretical paper that provides a clean, maximal homomorphism-expressivity characterization for spectral invariant GNNs and leverages it to answer several open questions, establish a clear hierarchy against other architectures, and derive concrete subgraph counting capabilities with iteration bounds. The technical approach—equating spectral projections with walk features, devising a spectral pebble game, and reducing maximality to Fürer-type constructions—is nontrivial and insightful. While experiments are supportive, they are relatively light and could better illustrate key boundaries (e.g., C7 vs C8) and the role of approximation in practice. Some essential formal details reside in the appendix, and a brief treatment of computational considerations would improve practical relevance. Overall, the contributions are original, well-motivated, and significant for the ICLR community interested in GNN expressivity; I recommend acceptance after addressing the empirical and presentation clarifications.

papers.title: Kinetix: Investigating the Training of General Agents through Open-Ended Physics-Based Control Tasks

reviews.summary: This paper introduces Kinetix, an open-ended suite of 2D physics-based reinforcement learning environments built on a new JAX-native engine, Jax2D. The authors procedurally generate tens of millions of diverse control tasks under a unified, simple reward (make green touch blue without touching red) and train a permutation-invariant transformer policy with PPO for billions of steps using a UED method (SFL). The resulting agent exhibits emergent physical reasoning, zero-shot solves a large fraction of small hand-designed environments, and shows substantial gains from fine-tuning—often outperforming tabula rasa training and solving some deceptive tasks that PPO-from-scratch fails to learn.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

A JAX-native 2D rigid-body physics engine (Jax2D) with dynamically specified scenes enabling vmap across heterogeneous morphologies is a meaningful systems contribution distinct from static-graph simulators (e.g., Brax) and appears to unlock efficient multi-task parallelism.

Kinetix unifies a wide variety of 2D physics tasks (robotics-style locomotion/manipulation, classic control, game-like pinball) under a single reward and observation interface, enabling generalist agent training and evaluation.

The policy architecture leverages permutation-invariant entity representations, masked multi-head attention keyed to physical structure (joints, collisions, n-step neighborhoods), and message-passing, which is well-motivated for physics.
Experimental rigor and validation
Scale: 5B environment interactions, 5 seeds, periodic evaluation on 74 hand-designed holdouts, plus focused analyses (goal-conditioned locomotion, deceptive task Car-Ramp).
UED via SFL provides an automatic filter against degenerate and unsolvable levels; comparisons to PLR/ACCEL are reported (albeit in the appendix).
Evidence of transfer: fine-tuning consistently improves learning efficiency and unlocks capabilities that failed for from-scratch baselines on several challenging tasks.
Clarity of presentation
The paper is generally clear, with a coherent motivation for 2D physics as a broad yet tractable open-ended domain and a careful description of the architecture, generator, and evaluation protocol.
The unified reward and entity-based observation simplify cross-task reasoning and are well explained.
Significance of contributions
An open-source, fast simulator and a large, diverse environment suite should be valuable infrastructure for the community to study open-endedness, UED, and large-scale online pretraining.
The results support the feasibility of pretraining general agents online on mixed-quality procedurally generated tasks, a topic of high current interest.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns
Generalization on larger, more complex holdouts remains modest (near ~0.1 solve rate), suggesting limited emergent breadth despite strong scale.
SFL’s prerequisites (binary reward, determinism) constrain the generality of the UED approach; it’s unclear how robust the pipeline is if the environment departs from those assumptions.
The approach depends on very large compute budgets (billions of steps); guidance on scaling efficiency and trade-offs is limited.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Limited ablations on the architecture: it’s unclear how much each component (masked attention heads, joint/thruster message passing, gating, lack of positional embeddings) contributes.
Minimal in-text baseline comparisons for level selection (DR vs. SFL) and limited discussion of their relative benefits in the main paper; the reader must rely on appendices.
No comparisons to vision-based observations or to continuous action variants, despite Kinetix supporting them.
Lack of a systematic study of training distributions (single-size vs. mixed-size curricula), scaling laws (model capacity vs. performance), or the effect of auxiliary dense reward coefficient.
Clarity or presentation issues
Key performance numbers (e.g., Jax2D vs. Box2D speedups, fraction of rejected degenerate/unsolvable levels) are relegated to appendices and could be highlighted more prominently.
The Large evaluation non-monotonic trends warrant deeper analysis in the main text (e.g., unsolvable rate estimates, curriculum effects).
Missing related work or comparisons
While XLand is discussed, the paper could more explicitly connect to other generalist control frameworks and foundation-agent paradigms with online RL or environment generators.
More discussion of differentiable vs. impulse-based engines (and implications for learning) would be useful, as well as positioning versus MJX and Isaac Gym beyond the 2D/3D distinction.
reviews.questions:
1. Can you provide ablations quantifying the contribution of (a) masked attention heads, (b) joint/thruster message passing, and (c) gating to zero-shot and fine-tuning performance?
2. How sensitive are results to the dense reward coefficient κ and to the termination rules (e.g., early termination on touching red)? Do different κ values materially change zero-shot vs. fine-tuning trade-offs?
3. What is the parameter count of the policy/value networks, and how does performance scale with model size and training steps, especially on the Large holdouts?
4. Could you report, per size (S/M/L), the percentages of sampled levels rejected as trivial (no-op solves), as well as estimates of unsolvable levels filtered by SFL (e.g., levels with empirically near-zero success despite exploration)?
5. How does training on mixed-size distributions (e.g., curriculum from S→M→L or interleaved S/M/L) affect zero-shot and fine-tuning outcomes compared to single-size training?
6. Have you evaluated continuous action spaces and/or pixel observations in Kinetix? If so, how do they compare to multi-discrete symbolic observations for zero-shot and fine-tuning?
7. Can you bring more of the Jax2D vs. Box2D benchmarking (raw engine and end-to-end RL) into the main text, including hardware specs and wall-clock times for 5B steps?
reviews.assessment: This paper makes a strong systems-and-benchmark contribution by releasing Jax2D and Kinetix, demonstrating that large-scale online RL on a procedurally generated, heterogeneous distribution can produce nontrivial zero-shot capabilities and substantial fine-tuning gains. The technical choices are well-justified, and the results are encouraging—especially the emergence of physically grounded behaviors and the ability to solve deceptive tasks after pretraining. The main limitations are moderate zero-shot performance on the most complex tasks, a heavy reliance on large compute, and limited ablations and baseline comparisons in the main text. Nonetheless, the open-source infrastructure and the demonstrated feasibility of online pretraining for control are timely and valuable for the community. With additional ablations and a more thorough analysis of scaling and curriculum effects, this work could become a go-to platform for open-ended RL research. I recommend acceptance.

papers.title: OptionZero: Planning with Learned Options

reviews.summary: The paper proposes OptionZero, an extension of MuZero that learns and plans with temporally extended actions (“options”) discovered autonomously via self-play, without human-provided options or demonstrations. The key ideas are (i) an option head that predicts a “dominant option” per state through a sequence of distributions with a stop token, and (ii) a modified dynamics model that can advance multiple steps and return aggregated discounted rewards for composite actions, enabling deeper search under a fixed number of unrolls. On 26 Atari games, the authors report substantial gains over their MuZero baseline and provide analyses of learned option usage patterns.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The integration of an option head into MuZero’s prediction network and corresponding modifications to MCTS that handle both primitive and option edges within the same tree are interesting and practically motivated.
The idea of a “dominant option” that avoids combinatorial explosion without enumerating all action sequences presents a pragmatic approach to temporal abstraction in model-based planning.
Modifying the dynamics model to predict multi-step transitions and aggregated rewards for composite actions is a nontrivial and useful extension for model-based planning.
Experimental rigor and validation
The paper evaluates on a reasonably broad set of 26 Atari games and reports improvements for the majority of them.
The behavior analysis is thoughtful, including statistics of option utilization, option length distributions, and repeated vs. non-repeated action compositions, along with qualitative examples.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level method and motivation are generally clear, with helpful figures explaining the option head and the modified MCTS phases.
The paper provides a code link and claims to include appendices with implementation and training details.
Significance of contributions

If validated, learning and planning with automatically discovered options within MuZero is an impactful direction that could inspire further work on hierarchical, model-based planning in visually rich domains.
The reported aggregate gains over a strong MuZero-like baseline suggest practical value in long-horizon control.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The definition and training of the “dominant option” are ad hoc. The fixed 0.5 cumulative-product threshold and the training rule that depends on whether the predicted option matches the executed composite action raise concerns about stability, stationarity, and potential degenerate solutions (e.g., overproducing stop).

The MCTS modifications (e.g., subtracting option contributions from primitive statistics and non-negativity clamping of priors) are heuristic; potential edge cases (e.g., N(s,a)=N(s,o) leading to division by zero) and their handling are not clearly addressed.

The multi-step dynamics model faces known challenges with compounding model error for longer horizons. The paper does not quantify model accuracy, uncertainty, or sensitivity of performance to option length/model rollout error.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Compute fairness is unclear. Table 3 mentions different “simulation budgets” across settings (50, 150, 300), suggesting that longer-option variants may use substantially more search per move than the baseline. This undermines the central claim that OptionZero searches deeper “under the same simulation constraints.”

Missing baselines: No comparisons to strong non-hierarchical or hierarchical “action repetition” variants (e.g., Learning to Repeat, Dynamic Action Repetition), or to planning with macro-actions without a specialized option head. This makes it difficult to attribute gains to the proposed option learning vs. simpler repetition mechanisms.
Statistical robustness is not discussed: number of seeds, confidence intervals, and sensitivity to hyperparameters (including the 0.5 threshold) are not reported.
Clarity or presentation issues

The training target for the option head is defined via a conditional rule that depends on the model’s own current prediction (“if o equals O then learn actions, else learn stop”), which is unusual and may confuse readers; a clearer rationale and ablations are needed.
Notation around states s^k (hidden), s_k (environment), and indices can be hard to follow in places; some formulae read as fragile with implementation details deferred to appendices.
Missing related work or comparisons

While option-critic and macro-action works are cited, the experimental comparison omits direct quantitative baselines that learn/plan with action repetitions or macro-actions on Atari. Prior work that learns repetition rates or uses simple macro-operators would be a natural reference point.

There is limited discussion of related hierarchical model-based approaches that roll out abstractions (e.g., Dreamer variants) or prior MCTS-with-options integrations in pixel-based Atari with learned models.
reviews.questions:
1. How are simulation budgets matched across l1, l3, and l6? Table 3 suggests different maximum depths (50, 150, 300). Can you provide results with equalized compute (e.g., same simulations per move and total network calls) to validate the “deeper search under the same constraints” claim?
2. How many random seeds were used for each game, and what are the mean ± standard deviation (or confidence intervals)? Please also specify evaluation details (sticky actions, no-op starts) and training steps.
3. Can you provide ablations against learned action repetition baselines (e.g., Sharma et al., Lakshminarayanan et al.) integrated into MuZero, and an ablation where options are used in MCTS but the dynamics model still rolls one step per action?
4. The option head training target depends on whether the predicted option equals the executed composite action, otherwise labeling stop. Why does this learning scheme converge to the intended “cumulative-product” semantics rather than collapsing to frequent stop predictions? Any diagnostics showing ω_i(a*) ≈ ∏j≤i p(aj*)?
5. How sensitive are results to the 0.5 threshold for defining the dominant option? Have you tried different thresholds or adaptive criteria?
6. In Eq. (4), how do you handle cases where N(s,a)=N(s,o) (division by zero) and negative values after subtracting P(s,o) from P(s,a)? Are there safeguards to ensure numerical stability and unbiased selection?
7. What is the representation of a composite action for the dynamics model input? Is it encoded as a length plus a sequence, or summarized (e.g., repeated-action token)? Any analysis of model error vs. option length?
reviews.assessment: OptionZero tackles an important problem—temporal abstraction for model-based planning—and proposes a practical integration of options into MuZero through a “dominant option” head and multi-step dynamics. The empirical results on 26 Atari games are encouraging, and the behavior analyses are informative. However, the paper currently has critical methodological ambiguities that limit confidence in the central claims: compute fairness across variants is unclear, the dominant-option learning procedure is heuristic and insufficiently justified, and key ablations and statistical robustness are missing. Moreover, comparisons to natural macro-action or action-repetition baselines are absent, making it difficult to attribute performance gains to the proposed components rather than to simpler mechanisms or increased compute. With stronger controls (equalized compute), comprehensive ablations, multiple-seed reporting, and clearer exposition of the option-target learning dynamics, this work could become a valuable contribution. As it stands, I lean toward rejection, but I view the direction as promising and potentially impactful with a more rigorous empirical and methodological treatment.

papers.title: Instant Policy: In-Context Imitation Learning via Graph Diffusion

reviews.summary: The paper proposes Instant Policy, an in-context imitation learning (ICIL) framework that produces closed-loop visuomotor policies instantly from 1–2 demonstrations without weight updates. The core ideas are (i) a heterogeneous graph representation that unifies context demonstrations, current point cloud observations, and future actions, and (ii) a graph diffusion model that denoises action-node positions to sample future SE(3) end-effector motions and gripper states. A key practical contribution is training purely from procedurally generated pseudo-demonstrations in simulation, providing an effectively unlimited data source. Extensive simulated (RLBench) and real-world evaluations demonstrate strong success rates, favorable scaling trends, and promising emergent generalization to novel object geometries, with initial results on cross-embodiment transfer and language-conditioned zero-shot execution.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Frames ICIL as a graph generation problem and applies diffusion over heterogeneous graphs to generate future action subgraphs conditioned on demo and observation subgraphs.
Introduces a well-motivated action denoising scheme that decouples translational and rotational flows in Cartesian space, followed by SVD-based SE(3) extraction, improving stability.
Proposes training exclusively on simulated pseudo-demonstrations (“arbitrary but semantically consistent” trajectories), decoupling training from real-world data scarcity and enabling scaling.
Designs a structured, bottlenecked architecture with staged message passing (σ, φ, ψ) and heterogeneous attention to enforce efficient information aggregation from context to action nodes.
Experimental rigor and validation
Comprehensive RLBench evaluation across 24 tasks (100 rollouts each), with both PD-only and PD++ (with a small amount of task demos) regimes, plus ablative analyses and scaling curves.
Real-world evaluation on 16 everyday tasks (10 rollouts each), outperforming multiple in-context baselines adapted to the same point cloud encoders.
Generalization experiments to novel object geometries by varying demos across different object instances of the same category, showing improved success with more diverse context.
Clarity of presentation
Clear problem setup, graph construction, and diffusion training/deployment descriptions with equations and intuitive figures.
Ablation table succinctly isolates critical design choices (action parameterization, diffusion mode, horizon) and inference-time parameters (K, N, L).
Limitations and assumptions are candidly discussed.
Significance of contributions
Demonstrates a practical path to ICIL without massive robot datasets via pseudo-demonstrations, with encouraging scaling behavior.
The graph-diffusion formulation and staged attention may influence future ICIL and structure-aware visuomotor policy designs.
Emergent cross-embodiment and language conditioning suggest potential as a reusable foundation model interface.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns
Strong reliance on segmented point clouds and object tracking (SAM + XMem++ seeding), which can be brittle; robustness to segmentation errors is only lightly addressed via limited co-finetuning.
The pseudo-demonstration generation ignores kinematic/physics feasibility; the claim that sufficient randomization yields a convex hull covering test-time tasks is speculative and unvalidated.
No explicit collision avoidance or joint-space feasibility; method outputs task-space deltas and depends on low-level controllers, which may limit precision/contact-rich tasks.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Runtime and computational overhead at inference are not reported (K steps, graph size vs. latency), making it hard to judge real-time feasibility on modest hardware.
Cross-embodiment results rely on handcrafted mappings with qualitative anecdotes; quantitative comparisons and robustness analyses are missing.
Zero-shot language conditioning is qualitative only; lacks rigorous metrics or comparisons to established VLA baselines.

Baseline parity could be further substantiated: extensive hyperparameter tuning details, ablations with stronger non-language baselines (e.g., Perceiver-Actor), and inclusion of recent object-trajectory diffusion baselines (e.g., SPOT) would strengthen claims.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some training details are deferred to appendices (e.g., occupancy pretraining, graph memory footprint), hindering reproducibility from the main text.
Occasional notation overload (multiple graph symbols/functions) increases cognitive load; a consolidated notation table would help.
Missing related work or comparisons

Limited discussion and empirical comparison to object-centric diffusion policies (e.g., SPOT/SE(3)-trajectory approaches) that also facilitate cross-embodiment and geometry generalization through SE(3) abstraction.
Interaction with recent diffusion guidance for feasibility (e.g., optimization-guided denoising) is not explored and could address some noted limitations.
reviews.questions:
1. What is the per-step inference latency (ms) and throughput as a function of K, N, L, M, and T on your deployment hardware? How do you tune K at test time to balance performance vs. latency?
2. How sensitive is performance to segmentation/tracking errors? Can you quantify robustness by injecting segmentation noise or evaluating with automated segmentation only (no manual seeding)?
3. Could you report an ablation on the occupancy-network encoder vs. simpler point features (e.g., FPFH or PointNet++ without occupancy pretraining), and on the high-frequency edge embeddings?
4. How does Instant Policy compare to object-centric baselines like SPOT on a subset of RLBench/real tasks, especially those requiring constraint compliance (e.g., maintaining pose of liquid containers)?
5. Can you incorporate feasibility guidance during denoising (e.g., collision penalties or IK reachability) without retraining, and if so, does it improve real-world robustness?
6. For cross-embodiment transfer, can you provide quantitative results across several tasks and embodiments, and analyze failures of the handcrafted mapping?
7. How large is the memory footprint of the graph at test time for typical settings (N=2, L=10, T=8, M per point cloud)? Any batching/tiling strategies to keep memory linear as claimed?
reviews.assessment: This paper tackles an important problem—true in-context imitation learning for manipulation—through a technically elegant and experimentally compelling approach. Modeling ICIL as graph diffusion over a unified demo–observation–action graph is novel and well-justified; the decoupled flow parameterization and SVD-based SE(3) extraction are pragmatic and effective. The pseudo-demonstration training pipeline is a strong practical contribution that shows encouraging scaling behavior, with solid simulation and real-world results, and emergent generalization to unseen object geometries. The work is not without limitations: reliance on segmentation, lack of explicit feasibility constraints, missing runtime reports, and some comparisons (e.g., to object-centric diffusion) could be strengthened. Nonetheless, the contribution is substantial and timely, and the empirical evidence largely supports the central claims. I recommend acceptance, with suggestions to add runtime metrics, more robustness analyses to segmentation noise, and, if possible, a comparison or discussion bridging to object-centric diffusion policies and feasibility-guided denoising.

papers.title: What should a neuron aim for? Designing local objective functions based on information theory

reviews.summary: This paper proposes “infomorphic neurons,” units trained by local, per-neuron objective functions expressed as linear combinations of Partial Information Decomposition (PID) atoms. Moving beyond earlier bivariate formulations, the authors introduce trivariate infomorphic neurons that separately aggregate feedforward (F), contextual/feedback (C), and lateral (L) inputs, enabling neurons to target specific unique, redundant, and synergistic information contributions to their outputs. On supervised classification (MNIST, with some CIFAR-10 results), they show that properly chosen or hyperparameter-optimized PID goals allow a single-hidden-layer network to approach backpropagation performance while yielding per-neuron interpretability of local information processing.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Extends prior “infomorphic” local-learning work to trivariate PID with three input classes (F, C, L), significantly expanding the space of interpretable local objectives beyond bivariate settings.

Leverages the differentiable shared-exclusion PID measure (I∩sx) to construct per-neuron goal functions and demonstrates that combining atoms (e.g., redundancy between F and C that is unique w.r.t. L) enables self-organization and division of labor via lateral inputs.
Proposes hyperparameter optimization over PID-atom weights to both improve performance and reveal interpretable task-relevant information-processing goals.
Experimental rigor and validation
Evaluates on MNIST with multiple architectures and lateral-connectivity regimes (dense and sparse), and provides a feedback-instead-of-label configuration to suggest stackability across layers.
Compares to bivariate (two-input) variants and random-projection baselines; includes ablation analyses that highlight a small subset of PID terms as most critical.

Tests transfer of optimized goals to larger hidden layers and to CIFAR-10 with a separate optimization run, and explores an alternate linear activation to demonstrate some robustness to forward-modeling choices.
Clarity of presentation
Clear motivation for moving to three input classes and for interpreting local neuron goals via PID atoms.
Intuitive figures and explanations of redundancy/uniqueness/synergy; helpful pseudocode and code availability.
Good use of ablation to connect hyperparameters back to interpretable computational roles.
Significance of contributions
Provides a principled, interpretable per-neuron objective framework grounded in modern information theory, offering a bridge between normative local learning and practical neural network training.
The interpretability angle—identifying which information atoms are most important per task—could inform future local-learning design and analysis.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Gradients are computed by treating the empirical p(f, c, l) as fixed, differentiating only through p(y|f, c, l). This approximation is nontrivial; its implications for bias/stability are not analyzed theoretically and only ex post justified.

Reliance on discretization (20 bins) for PID with a plug-in estimator invites bias/variance issues, especially at small batch sizes; sensitivity to binning schemes, batch size, and smoothing is not systematically studied.

The lateral recurrence is handled by iterating the same input twice; convergence properties and stability are only briefly discussed and appear to degrade as layer size increases without sparse laterals.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Empirical comparisons to other local/biologically motivated training methods (e.g., feedback alignment, predictive coding, leader–follower, local greedy/contrastive objectives) are missing; the primary comparisons are to backprop and to internal bivariate/trivariate variants.
Evaluation is largely on MNIST with fully connected layers; CIFAR-10 results are low and limited (non-convolutional), and scalability to modern architectures/datasets remains unclear.
Computational cost is not reported. Per-neuron PID estimation on discretized joint distributions each batch may be significant; runtime/memory comparisons vs. backprop would be valuable.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some notation in the trivariate section is terse (e.g., repeated γFCL in Eq. 3 likely a typesetting artifact); a compact table listing the 18 atoms and their interpretations would help.

The setup where hidden-layer neurons directly receive labels as context is useful but not “local” in a strict sense; while the paper includes a feedback alternative, the distinction and implications deserve more prominent discussion in the main text.
Missing related work or comparisons

While the related work section is broad and fair, the absence of empirical baselines against strong local-learning contenders (e.g., DFA/Weighted DFA, predictive coding variants, recent BP-free methods) weakens the case for competitiveness as a general local-learning alternative.
reviews.questions:
1. How sensitive is training to the choice of discretization (number of bins, binning strategy) and batch size for the PID estimation? Can you provide ablations varying these, or smoothing strategies, and their effect on accuracy and stability?
2. Can you quantify the computational overhead (time/memory) relative to backprop for the reported settings, and how this scales with number of neurons and lateral connections?
3. The gradient approximation treats p(f, c, l) as fixed. Did you observe failure modes traceable to this approximation? Are there practical ways to partially account for the dependence of p(f, c, l) on weights (e.g., REINFORCE-like corrections, stop-gradient ablations)?
4. In the backprop baseline, is the architecture strictly matched (including lateral connections/recurrence), or is it a standard feedforward MLP? Please clarify to ensure fairness.
5. Can you report comparisons against at least one recent BP-free/local baseline (e.g., DFA/Weighted DFA, predictive coding, LFNN-ℓ) on MNIST and the non-convolutional CIFAR-10 setting to contextualize performance?
6. For setup 3 (feedback as context), have you explored deeper stacks (two or more hidden layers) in the main text with the same goals, and can you share quantitative results beyond the appendix?
7. Did any optimized goals over-emphasize residual entropy (γres) or pathological atom combinations? Are there constraints/regularizers on γ you recommend to avoid degenerate objectives?
reviews.assessment:
This is a thoughtful and well-executed extension of infomorphic (PID-based) local learning from two to three input classes, demonstrating that suitably constructed per-neuron information-theoretic goals can drive self-organization and approach backprop performance on MNIST, with interpretable insights into local computation. The central idea—using trivariate PID atoms to jointly target task-relevant redundancy and lateral uniqueness—is original and compelling, and the ablations nicely translate optimized hyperparameters into understandable computational roles.

However, the experimental scope is still modest (primarily MNIST with fully connected layers; limited CIFAR-10), and key methodological aspects merit deeper evaluation: the discretization dependence, the gradient approximation (fixed p(f, c, l)), runtime/memory costs, and comparisons with other strong local-learning baselines. The “label-as-context” setup for hidden layers is a useful stepping stone but weakens the strictly local learning narrative; the feedback alternative is promising and should be more fully developed in the main results. Overall, I find the conceptual contribution strong and the initial empirical validation convincing enough to warrant interest, especially for the interpretability of local objectives. With additional comparisons and methodological analyses, this work could make a valuable contribution to the ICLR community.

papers.title: Cross-Entropy Is All You Need To Invert the Data Generating Process

reviews.summary: This paper develops an identifiability theory for cross-entropy-based learning under a cluster-centric data generating process (DGP). Starting from a von Mises-Fisher (vMF) latent model with class “cluster vectors,” the authors prove that parametric instance discrimination (DIET) recovers latent variables and cluster vectors up to a linear (orthogonal/affine) transform, and then extend the result to standard supervised classification with cross-entropy. Empirical studies on synthetic data (matching assumptions), disentanglement benchmarks (DisLib), and ImageNet-X show that features learned with cross-entropy permit strong linear decoding of latent/proxy factors.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Extends nonlinear ICA-style identifiability to a parametric instance discrimination (PID) setup with an explicit, cluster-centric vMF DGP, including both normalized and unnormalized representations.

Bridges identifiability results in SSL (GCL/TCL/InfoNCE) to supervised learning by proving that cross-entropy classification can recover ground-truth factors up to a linear transform under the proposed DGP; the genealogy framing is conceptually unifying.
Identifies conditions under which the classifier head rows collapse to class cluster vectors, and links the encoder’s latent variables to ground truth via a shared orthogonal/affine map.
Experimental rigor and validation
Synthetic experiments closely match theoretical assumptions and provide near-perfect linear recovery (R² ≈ 1) across a range of dimensions, numbers of clusters, dataset sizes, and concentrations.
Stress tests with misspecified conditionals (Laplace/Normal) still show high linear recoverability, suggesting empirical robustness of the identifiability phenomenon beyond the vMF assumption.
DisLib experiments and ImageNet-X linear probing demonstrate that cross-entropy-trained representations linearly encode salient factors in controlled and naturalistic settings.
Clarity of presentation
Clear statement of DIET objective and the DGP; helpful intuition for why rows of W align with cluster vectors and why embeddings align with latent z.
The genealogy figure/treatment effectively situates the contribution relative to GCL/TCL/InfoNCE and clarifies how supervised learning emerges as a special case.
Significance of contributions
Offers a plausible formal explanation for widely observed phenomena (linear decodability, transfer with linear probes, convergence of representations/superposition).

If accepted, could influence how the community reasons about when and why supervised cross-entropy yields linearly structured, interpretable features, bridging SSL identifiability and practical supervised pipelines.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The identifiability guarantees rely on a strong and specific DGP (vMF on a hypersphere with sufficiently “large and spread out” cluster vectors; injective generator; global minimization), and some assumptions are informal (e.g., what “sufficiently large and spread out” entails).

The supervised learning result (Theorem 2) is stated concisely and somewhat unusually (“h = f ∘ g is a linear map from S^(d-1) to R^d”); the precise assumptions (Assumption 3) and proof mechanics need more transparency for readers to assess generality and edge cases.

The transition from instance-level heads (N rows) to class-level heads (|C| rows) is nontrivial; the paper asserts equality of rows for the same class at optimum, but the conditions ensuring this collapse are not fully spelled out.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

DisLib and ImageNet-X results show linear decodability, not full identifiability up to a linear transform; a direct linear alignment test (e.g., Procrustes) between learned features and known factors would strengthen the empirical claim.
Missing comparisons to strong SSL baselines (InfoNCE/SimCLR/MoCo) trained under similar regimes to test the “cross-entropy is sufficient” claim against alternatives.

Real-data results are modest in effect size for many factors (ImageNet-X accuracies often ~0.60), and proxy labels complicate causal interpretation as true latents; broader benchmarking or ablations (e.g., label noise, data imbalance) would contextualize robustness.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some assumptions and theorem statements are given in “simplified” form; key technical conditions (e.g., exact distributional separations, capacity/regularization requirements, optimization landscape) should be specified in the main text, not only appendices.
The supervised theorem’s conclusion of linearity on the sphere may be counterintuitive; more intuition or an outline of the proof is needed to avoid overinterpretation.
Missing related work or comparisons
Limited discussion of supervised identifiability or theory beyond ICA (e.g., connections to information geometry, Bayes-optimal linearity under specific priors, margin/separability analyses).
Empirical comparisons to identifiable disentanglement methods (e.g., β-VAE/FactorVAE variants; weakly supervised disentanglement) are absent, despite conceptual overlap.
reviews.questions:
1. Theorem 2 states that h = f ∘ g is a linear map from S^(d-1) to R^d. Could you restate the full assumptions (Assumption 3) and provide a proof sketch in the main text? In particular, is the linearity global (i.e., extends to a linear operator on R^d), and how does it reconcile with nonlinearity off the sphere?
2. What are the precise, checkable conditions behind “the system {v_c} is sufficiently large and spread out”? Can you quantify required angular separations, cluster count relative to d, or concentration κ for the identifiability to hold?
3. Under what conditions do the DIET rows collapse to identical vectors for samples of the same class (w_i = w_j if C(i)=C(j))? Is additional regularization (e.g., row normalization, temperature β, weight decay) required, or does the result hold for any global minimizer?
4. How sensitive are the supervised results to label noise or class imbalance? Since cross-entropy is known to be robust up to a point, does identifiability degrade gracefully with controlled noise (e.g., symmetric/asymmetric flips)?
5. Can you provide a direct alignment analysis on DisLib (e.g., Procrustes to match learned subspaces with true continuous factors, including permutation/scale ambiguities) to more tightly mirror the identifiability claim rather than only reporting correlations?
6. Could you include a direct comparison to an InfoNCE baseline (with and without projector discard) and a standard β-VAE/FactorVAE on DisLib to contextualize performance and linear identifiability?
7. For non-Euclidean factors (e.g., rotations), do you expect identifiable subspaces (e.g., 2D sin/cos planes) under the proposed DGP? If not, what minimal extensions to the DGP/theory would accommodate group-structured latent manifolds?
8. Does your theory imply anything about the geometry of class prototypes learned in practice (e.g., approximate vMF structure on the penultimate layer)? Could you test this on ImageNet by fitting vMFs per class?
reviews.assessment: This paper presents a compelling and timely attempt to unify identifiability results across SSL and supervised learning by proving that cross-entropy minimization in a cluster-centric vMF DGP yields linearly identifiable representations. The DIET analysis is technically interesting and well-supported by synthetic experiments; the extension to supervised classification is particularly impactful if the assumptions and consequences (linearity of h on the sphere) are made more explicit and convincing. The empirical evidence on DisLib and ImageNet-X supports the central narrative of linear decodability, although it falls short of an exhaustive validation of identifiability in natural data. I view the work as a meaningful conceptual advance that will interest the ICLR community, with room to strengthen clarity (assumptions and proofs in the main text), add baselines, and tighten empirical alignment with the theoretical claims. I lean toward acceptance, contingent on clarifications around Theorem 2 and expanded empirical comparisons.

papers.title: Unlocking State-Tracking in Linear RNNs Through Negative Eigenvalues

reviews.summary: This paper studies the state-tracking limitations of Linear Recurrent Neural Networks (LRNNs) and shows that constraining state-transition eigenvalues to be nonnegative fundamentally impedes learning even simple regular languages like parity. The authors generalize prior diagonal results to non-diagonal LRNNs (including DeltaNet), prove that non-triangular transitions (and, in some cases, complex/negative eigenvalues) are necessary for counting modulo m, and show that products of generalized Householder (GH) matrices with eigenvalues in [-1,1] can implement any regular language with bounded-norm transitions. They demonstrate that a simple, training-stable modification to Mamba and DeltaNet enabling negative eigenvalues unlocks strong empirical state-tracking on synthetic tasks and yields competitive large-scale language modeling, with notable gains on coding/math perplexity for modified DeltaNet.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Extends impossibility results for parity from diagonal LRNNs to general LRNNs with nonnegative real eigenvalues, and establishes a new necessity result for counting modulo m that requires non-triangular structure (and imaginary eigenvalues for certain cases).

Provides constructive positive results: products of GH matrices with eigenvalues in [-1,1] can represent bounded-norm transitions broadly (via Cartan–Dieudonné), enabling one-layer realizations for group-transition FSAs (including Zm via rotations / reflections) and multi-layer constructions for all regular languages via Krohn–Rhodes.

Proposes a minimal architectural change (expanding eigenvalue range to [-1,1]) that preserves stability (spectral norm ≤ 1), has no additional compute overhead, and unlocks state-tracking expressivity.
Experimental rigor and validation
Synthetic tasks from the Chomsky hierarchy: clean recoveries of parity and substantial gains on modular arithmetic, particularly with non-diagonal DeltaNet variants.
Group word problems (S5 and restricted variants) validate theoretical predictions about when swaps are representable and when deeper compositions are needed.
Large-scale pretraining (340M–1.3B) on FineWeb-100B shows stable training and task-dependent improvements (code/math perplexity) for DeltaNet [-1,1], supporting real-world viability.
Clarity of presentation
Clear statement of limitations (Theorems 1–2) and positive results (Proposition 1, Theorems 3–4), with helpful intuition (e.g., alternating dynamics for parity).
Good linkage from theory to architecture design (diagonal vs GH; products of GH) and to experimental design (tasks mapping to cyclic and symmetric groups).
Significance of contributions
Addresses a central bottleneck in LRNNs—failure to track finite-state computations—and provides both necessary conditions and practically implementable remedies.
Suggests a compelling, low-cost direction to improve state-tracking in scalable sequence models, with immediate relevance to code/math and other structured reasoning domains.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Theorem 4’s construction for arbitrary regular languages may be width- and depth-inefficient (authors note potential exponential blowup in worst case), making the positive expressivity result more of a theoretical guarantee than a practical recipe.

Conditions in Theorem 2 (need for complex/imaginary eigenvalues or non-triangularity) are necessary but not shown to be tight for practical finite precision and finite depth; more fine-grained lower bounds or constructive minimality would strengthen the claims.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Main-table synthetic results report best-of-3 rather than median; while medians appear in the appendix, emphasizing best-of-3 in the main table may overstate robustness.

S5 experiments stop short of solving the full problem at long lengths; improvements are strongest under simplified setups (swaps-only, multi-token encodings). This is consistent with the theory but leaves open practical success on standard S5 with the proposed changes alone.

The Mamba variants often degrade on language modeling; the paper does not deeply analyze why diagonal LRNNs benefit less (or are harmed) by negative eigenvalues, limiting practical guidance for that class.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some notation and assumptions (finite precision model, layerwise dependencies in Theorem 2) could be more explicitly stated in the main text rather than deferred to the appendix.
Occasional formatting artifacts (from PDF extraction) make parts of tables/equations harder to parse.
Missing related work or comparisons

Limited discussion of orthogonal/unitary RNNs and stable recurrent parametrizations (e.g., unitary/orthogonal RNNs, gated orthogonal architectures), which are relevant to the theme of eigen-structure and stability in state tracking.
Empirical comparisons with other recent non-diagonal LRNNs or hybrid designs (e.g., RWKV variants, Gated DeltaNet follow-ups) are discussed but could be expanded for breadth.
reviews.questions:
1. Do trained models indeed learn substantially negative eigenvalues in practice? Could you report the empirical distribution of learned eigenvalues (or the GH coefficient φ) over layers/timesteps, and how it correlates with task success?
2. For Theorem 2, can you comment on tightness? Are there architectures with minimal deviations from triangularity (e.g., almost triangular with small off-diagonals) that can still count modulo m reliably at finite precision?
3. Mamba shows degraded performance on several language modeling tasks under [-1,1]. Do you have diagnostics (e.g., gradient noise, gating saturation, variance of activations) that explain why diagonal LRNNs are more fragile under this change?
4. How sensitive are results to initialization and normalization choices? For example, does initially biasing s(x) or φ(x) toward 0 or 1 materially affect training stability or convergence speed on state-tracking tasks?
5. Could you provide compute/throughput numbers confirming “no additional cost,” and discuss any numerical stability differences (e.g., compatibility issues with log-space cumulative products) in more depth for Mamba2/GLA/mLSTM-like variants?
6. In the S5 experiments, have you tried stacking enough GH factors explicitly (k > 1 per layer) rather than across layers, or mixing diagonal and GH matrices as suggested in your discussion, to push beyond sequence lengths where accuracy drops?
7. For Theorem 4, are there practical heuristics for constructing efficient layer cascades for common automata (e.g., bracketed math) that reduce the worst-case layer/width blowup?
reviews.assessment: This paper makes a clear, principled, and practically impactful contribution: it identifies a fundamental spectral limitation underlying LRNNs’ failure at state-tracking, proves new necessity results for modular counting, and proposes a minimal architecture change—allowing negative eigenvalues via diagonal or GH parametrizations—that both resolves parity and significantly improves broader state-tracking tasks. The theoretical results are well-motivated and connect elegantly to classical linear algebra and automata theory; the experiments validate the claims from small synthetic problems to billion-parameter pretraining, with the strongest gains for non-diagonal LRNNs (DeltaNet) on code/math. While some constructions in the positive results are not computationally optimal, and Mamba’s mixed performance deserves further analysis, the central message is both novel and useful: spectral flexibility (including negative/complex behavior) is key to unlocking finite-state computation in efficient LRNNs. I recommend acceptance.

papers.title: Attention as a Hypernetwork

reviews.summary: The paper proposes a new perspective on multi-head attention (MHA) by showing it is mathematically equivalent to a hypernetwork: head-specific attention scores act as a low-dimensional latent code that linearly combines head parameters to generate a key–query-specific value network. Building on this view, the authors introduce HYLA, a drop-in modification of linear attention that increases the expressiveness of the implicit value network via a nonlinearity and applies RMS normalization across heads per key–query pair. They validate the perspective and modification on two controlled compositional reasoning settings (a fuzzy-logic function task and a new symbolic Raven’s Progressive Matrices benchmark, SRAVEN) and provide initial language modeling experiments, showing improved out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization with structured latent codes predictive of the sub-operations being performed.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The hypernetwork reformulation of MHA along the head dimension is clean and yields an interpretable latent code (the per-(q,k) vector of head scores) that configures a key–query-specific value network.

HYLA is a simple, parameter-free architectural tweak (nonlinear value network plus RMS head-normalization) that directly operationalizes the hypernetwork perspective and empirically strengthens compositional generalization.
Experimental rigor and validation

Demonstrations span two carefully controlled synthetic/compositional tasks and a language-modeling setup, including ablations (e.g., number of heads) and latent structure analyses (tSNE, linear decoders).
Scaling studies on SRAVEN (data, width, depth) probe when OOD compositional performance emerges and quantify the sensitivity to the number of heads (i.e., latent dimensionality).
Clarity of presentation
The core derivation (Eqs. 2–5) is concise and persuasive; figures are informative and align well with the main claims (e.g., structured clusters in latent codes by task terms/rules).
The SRAVEN task is specified with an explicit generative process, controllable difficulty, and a principled compositional split.
Significance of contributions
The perspective helps relate attention, hypernetworks, and compositional generalization, offering a unifying lens that could inform analysis and design of transformer variants.
SRAVEN fills a gap among Raven-inspired benchmarks by isolating “finding correspondences” via feature permutations, while remaining symbolic and scalable.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The equivalence result, while neat, is largely a linear-algebraic rearrangement and conceptually close to prior “fast weight programmer” and hypernetwork views; the degree of conceptual novelty is moderate.

HYLA’s benefits may partly stem from the specific normalization choice (RMS across heads) rather than the nonlinearity per se; although the appendix ablations are said to disentangle this, fuller causal evidence in the main text is limited.

The paper sometimes refers to “linear attention” as σ = Id without discussing kernelized linear-time attention; this may confuse readers familiar with “linear attention” as efficiency-oriented methods.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Limited causal mechanistic tests: while latent codes are decodable and structured, there is no intervention (e.g., head or score patching/ablation per rule) to establish necessity/sufficiency of the discovered codes for function.
Missing or minimal variance reporting (seeds, error bars) in several plots; robustness across random initializations is not always clear.

The language modeling experiment uses a small model trained on a very large token budget; it is unclear how sensitive results are to scale, kernels, and sequence lengths where softmax advantages are typically more pronounced.
Clarity or presentation issues
The “linear attention” terminology (σ = Id) without clarifying computational complexity may mislead; in these experiments it remains O(T^2), unlike typical linear-time attention.
Some notation/section labeling (e.g., Section 2.1 header vs content) is slightly inconsistent.
Missing related work or comparisons

There is limited engagement with closely related recent work that inserts an explicit latent bottleneck/hypernetwork head to recover compositional generalization (e.g., hypernetwork transformer bottlenecks), which bolsters the central hypothesis.
Comparisons on established Raven-style benchmarks (PGM, RAVEN, I-RAVEN) are not provided, making it harder to position SRAVEN difficulty and the reported accuracies relative to prior art.
Metrics like homomorphism error (HE) that quantify representational compositionality could complement the probing and strengthen claims.
reviews.questions:
1. What precisely do you mean by “linear attention” in your experiments—σ = Id with standard O(T^2) complexity, or kernelized linear-time attention? If the former, could you clarify terminology and discuss whether HYLA is compatible with efficient kernelizations?
2. Can you report variance across multiple seeds (with error bars) for the key OOD curves (fuzzy logic, SRAVEN, language modeling)? How stable are the latent-code decoders across seeds?
3. Beyond head-count ablations, can you provide causal interventions on the latent code (e.g., head patching, targeted head dropout, editing a_{h,qk}) to demonstrate that specific code directions are necessary/sufficient for particular rules?
4. How do HYLA’s two ingredients (head-wise RMS normalization, nonlinearity) contribute individually versus jointly on SRAVEN and fuzzy logic, and are the effects robust across other normalizations (e.g., L2, LayerNorm over heads)?
5. Could you compare on established Raven-style benchmarks (PGM, RAVEN, I-RAVEN) to calibrate SRAVEN’s difficulty and the gains from HYLA against prior baselines?
6. In the language modeling setup, does HYLA help on tasks known to stress binding/associative recall? Can you provide retrieval or long-range association probes to support the claim that strengthening the hypernetwork mechanism helps there?
7. Have you explored decoupling the two generated matrices in HYLA (e.g., separate parameter sets for W and W′ or per-head nonlinearities) to test whether additional expressivity further helps, and at what cost?
reviews.assessment: This paper offers a clear and useful reframing of multi-head attention as an intrinsic hypernetwork and provides empirical evidence that the resulting low-dimensional latent code is functionally structured and reused under compositional OOD conditions. The proposed HYLA modification is simple, parameter-free, and yields consistent OOD gains on two controlled reasoning tasks, with preliminary signs of benefit in language modeling. While the conceptual novelty is moderate—building on fast-weight and hypernetwork perspectives—the articulation along the head dimension is crisp and explanatory. The main limitations lie in the absence of stronger causal analyses, limited variance reporting, and incomplete comparisons to established Raven-based benchmarks and closely related hypernetwork-bottleneck transformers. Nonetheless, the work is well-executed, the insights are valuable, and SRAVEN is a timely addition to the compositional reasoning toolkit. I lean toward acceptance, contingent on clarifying the “linear attention” terminology, adding robustness statistics, and situating the contribution more fully relative to adjacent hypernetwork-transformer work.

papers.title: Transformers Provably Solve Parity Efficiently with Chain of Thought

reviews.summary: The paper studies how training transformers to generate chain-of-thought (CoT) style intermediate states enables efficient learning of the k-parity problem, a canonical hard task for gradient-based methods. The authors prove (i) hardness of learning parity from end-to-end labels with any finite-precision, iterative gradient-based algorithm in a finite-sample setting; (ii) a sharp positive result showing a one-layer transformer trained with intermediate supervision via teacher forcing learns any parity in one gradient step; and (iii) an end-to-end CoT training regime (without teacher forcing) that learns parity in O(log k) steps by augmenting data for internal consistency checks and using a simple weight quantization scheme. Targeted simulations on synthetic parity corroborate the theoretical claims.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Extends known impossibility results for parity to a finite-sample setting with approximate gradient oracles, closing a gap between population-level hardness and practical regimes.

Provides the first (to my knowledge) optimization analysis showing that a one-layer transformer trained to generate CoT-like intermediate states can learn k-parity efficiently with teacher forcing, and further gives a provably efficient scheme without teacher forcing via self-consistency checks and quantization.
The careful reparameterization and causal masking make the training dynamics tractable while preserving an autoregressive CoT mechanism, yielding clean gradient signal separation arguments.
Experimental rigor and validation

Although modest in scope, the simulations cleanly demonstrate qualitative behaviors predicted by the theory: failure of direct end-to-end supervision; success of CoT with teacher forcing; staged convergence under self-consistency filtering.
The ablations across four training regimes (direct, CoT end-to-end, CoT+forcing, CoT+self-consistency) directly map to the theoretical settings and illuminate error propagation and filtering effects.
Clarity of presentation

The paper is generally well-organized with a clear problem setup, model description, and statements of main theorems. Visualizations of the decomposition tree, causal masks, and staged learning behavior aid understanding.
Technical sketches explain how gradient signals concentrate on the correct edges in the decomposition tree, connecting intuitively to the formal results.
Significance of contributions

Offers a constructive, optimization-based account of how CoT-style task decomposition can emerge in transformers, complementing the literature that focuses primarily on expressivity or in-context learning analyses.
The finite-sample hardness result and the separations established under CoT training provide principled insight into why process supervision and internal verification methods can matter in practice.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The architecture and link function are specialized: the feedforward nonlinearity φ is crafted to map averages of ±1 inputs to their parity with derivatives vanishing at key points, and the attention is position-only with a value matrix that simply copies inputs. This raises questions about robustness to more standard transformer parameterizations and nonlinearities.
The causal masks and training objectives assume knowledge of the decomposition tree and hierarchy; this is strong prior structure not available in general reasoning tasks.

The end-to-end (no teacher forcing) result additionally relies on integer quantization of weights and a filtering scheme triggered by augmented unlabeled inputs; both are nonstandard and may be brittle to design choices.
The hardness and positive results hinge on approximate gradient oracles with specific precision/scaling; while standard in theory, this may limit practical interpretability.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Experiments are limited to synthetic parity with d=64 and do not probe scaling trends (e.g., across d, k, n), robustness to noise or different φ, or sensitivity to the filtering threshold and quantization (which is not used in the experiments).
No variance estimates or multiple random seeds are reported; the number of runs and variability are unclear.
The self-consistency experiments omit quantization, which is required in the theory, leaving a gap between the theoretical and empirical setups.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some assumptions (e.g., exact properties of φ, filter thresholds, and oracle precision) could be foregrounded earlier with discussion of their necessity and practical realizability.
A succinct summary table contrasting assumptions and guarantees across the three regimes would help readers track what is required for each theorem.
Missing related work or comparisons

While the related work is broad and mostly complete, additional discussion of how the crafted inductive bias compares to other theoretical accounts of step-by-step reasoning or algorithmic task decomposition (e.g., neural algorithmic reasoning, scratchpads with learned verification) would help situate the contribution.
Empirical comparisons to simple RNN baselines (as in Wies et al.) or to shallow MLPs with intermediate supervision could strengthen the experimental narrative.
reviews.questions:
1. How sensitive are your guarantees and empirical results to the exact choice of φ? Can a small two-layer ReLU MLP approximate φ sufficiently to preserve the theoretical separations, and do simulations with a standard MLP recover the same behavior?
2. The causal mask encodes the decomposition tree. Can the model discover this structure from data (e.g., with a learnable or regularized attention pattern) and still achieve similar guarantees?
3. For the end-to-end regime, is integer quantization theoretically necessary, or could similar stability be obtained via projection/regularization (e.g., weight decay, clipping) or margin arguments? Empirically, what changes when quantization is included?
4. The filtering rule uses augmented unlabeled data and a threshold ε0. How should ε0 scale with d and n'? Can you provide sensitivity plots or theoretical guidance on setting it?
5. Can you relax the position-only attention and identity value assumptions while retaining the main results (e.g., standard QKV with learned token features)? What are the main technical obstacles?
6. How do the required sample sizes (n = Ω(d^{2+ε})) and gradient oracle accuracies compare with practical regimes (SGD noise)? Could your hardness and positive results be reformulated under stochastic gradient noise models?
7. Beyond parity, do you foresee generalization to other compositional tasks (e.g., majority, modular arithmetic, Dyck languages) where CoT can be laid out as hierarchical subproblems? What ingredients of the analysis would transfer?
reviews.assessment: This paper makes a solid theoretical contribution to our understanding of how CoT training can enable task decomposition in transformers. By extending parity hardness to finite samples and proving sharp positive results under teacher forcing and an end-to-end self-consistency scheme, the authors establish clear separations between end-to-end supervision and CoT-style training. The assumptions required to obtain these results—specialized nonlinearity, position-only attention, known hierarchy via masks, and (for end-to-end) quantization and filtering—limit immediate generality. The experiments, while limited to synthetic parity, nevertheless align well with the theory and illustrate key phenomena such as staged learning and error propagation. On balance, I view this as a meaningful and timely step toward a principled account of CoT optimization in transformers. I recommend acceptance, with the caveat that clarifying the robustness of the results to more standard modeling choices and broadening the empirical study would further strengthen the paper.

papers.title: Oscillatory State-Space Models

reviews.summary: The paper introduces Linear Oscillatory State-Space models (LinOSS), a new family of state-space models derived from discretizations of forced harmonic oscillators. Two discretization schemes are developed: a fully implicit (dissipative) scheme and a symplectic implicit–explicit (IMEX, volume-preserving) scheme, both implemented efficiently via associative parallel scans. The authors provide theoretical analysis showing stability (requiring only nonnegative diagonal A), explicit eigenvalue characterizations, and a universality result for approximating continuous, causal operators; extensive experiments on long- and very-long-range sequence tasks demonstrate consistent gains over strong SSM baselines (e.g., Mamba, LRU, S5/S6) and controlled ablations illuminate design choices.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
