reviews.assessment: This paper presents a compelling and practical approach to GNN explainability grounded in graphlet orbits as human-interpretable concepts, and it unifies global and local explanations through a coherent decomposition framework. Empirically, the method is strong on synthetic tasks with known ground truths and delivers competitive fidelity and clean, connected subgraphs on real datasets, which is valuable for practitioners. The main concerns center on missing algorithmic details for the coefficient solver, an underplayed preprocessing cost in the main text, lack of ablations around key modeling choices (nonnegativity, solver, stability), and limited demonstration of the claimed user-defined unit generality. With clarifications and the suggested ablations (particularly on solving S, runtime including preprocessing, and sensitivity/stability), I believe this work could make a meaningful contribution at ICLR due to its clear interpretability benefits and unified perspective. As it stands, I lean toward a weak accept, contingent on strengthening the methodological clarity and scalability analysis.

papers.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly: Watermarks, Transferable Attacks and Adversarial Defenses

reviews.summary: The paper formalizes backdoor-based watermarks and adversarial defenses as interactive protocols, and introduces a third notion—transferable attacks—capturing indistinguishable, distributional queries that fool all efficient defenders. The main theorem (via a zero-sum game argument) asserts that for any efficiently learnable task, at least one of: a watermark, an adversarial defense, or a transferable attack must exist. The authors further (i) construct a transferable attack using fully homomorphic encryption on a mixed “clear/encrypted” distribution and (ii) show that the existence of transferable attacks implies EFID pairs (and hence standard cryptographic primitives), while also providing instantiations of defenses and watermarks for hypothesis classes of bounded VC-dimension.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Unifies watermarking and adversarial robustness under a common interactive-protocol lens and identifies a trichotomy (watermark/defense/transferable attack).
Establishes an intriguing link between transferable attacks and cryptography, with both a construction (via FHE) and an implication (transferable attacks ⇒ EFID pairs ⇒ PRGs).
Adapts large zero-sum game techniques (Lipton–Young) to argue the existence of one of the three mechanisms, a nontrivial idea that conceptually bridges two previously separate literatures.
Provides new existence results for bounded VC-dimension tasks: robust defenses against arbitrary (even unbounded) attackers and an example watermark against very fast adversaries.
Experimental rigor and validation
The work is theoretical; theorems, reductions, and constructions are the right tools here. Within that scope, the claims are structured with formal statements (albeit much deferred to the appendix).
Clarity of presentation
The high-level motivations and the interplay between the three notions are explained clearly and intuitively, with helpful figures and concrete narratives (Alice/Bob).
The cryptographic construction is motivated step-by-step, starting from a familiar geometric learning task.
Significance of contributions

Provides a principled map of possibilities for adversarial testing vs. watermark detection, with practical takeaways for AI safety: either watermarking or detectable defenses should prevail under broad conditions, unless the task hides cryptographic hardness.
The cryptographic equivalence result clarifies when “undetectable” adversarial testing can be expected in practice.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The main trichotomy result appears largely non-constructive and rests on game-theoretic existence coupled with small-support equilibrium arguments; algorithmic efficiency and how the time exponents (e.g., T1/√log T, O(T)) concretely arise need clearer justification in the main text.
The FHE-based transferable attack is built on a contrived distribution that mixes clear and encrypted samples—a powerful proof-of-existence, but arguably far from most ML practice.

Several core definitions (watermark “uniqueness,” “unremovability,” indistinguishability thresholds) are only informally specified in the main body, making it hard to audit edge cases without the appendices.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

No empirical case studies or toy simulations demonstrating how the proposed defense/watermark protocols behave on natural tasks; while not required for a theory paper, even small-scale illustrations could strengthen intuition and relevance.
Clarity or presentation issues

The “almost every task” phrasing is potentially misleading—Theorem 1 actually quantifies over all efficiently learnable tasks; the caveat seems to be about excluding tasks without efficient learners or those with cryptographic structure. This should be reconciled explicitly.

The watermark “verifiability” discussion acknowledges needing an external oracle or stronger gaps; this is important, but the current exposition leaves the practical detection criterion somewhat underspecified.
Some repetition and inconsistencies in the related work section (e.g., duplicated text about attacker control of the distribution).
Missing related work or comparisons

The comparison to Christiano et al. (2024) is promising but remains informal; a more formal side-by-side of assumptions (who chooses the distribution/trigger), resources, and guarantees would benefit readers.
Additional discussion of impossibility/possibility frontiers in watermarking for generative models and their relationship to the current discriminative setting would add useful context.
reviews.questions:
1. Can you provide a more explicit, constructive description (in the main text) of how BNASH is found/represented and how BDEFENSE simulates it efficiently to achieve the claimed time bounds (especially the T and T1/√log T terms)?
2. How sensitive is Theorem 1 to the exact definitions of indistinguishability and the advantage thresholds? Can you state the quantitative dependence on ε, q, and advantage δ in the main theorem?
3. The FHE-based transferable attack relies on a mixed clear/encrypted distribution. Is there a variant that avoids mixing modes (e.g., entirely clear data) under weaker cryptographic assumptions, or can you argue a lower bound ruling that out?
4. The watermark “uniqueness” property hinges on resource gaps (TB < TA). In realistic settings where independent developers have TA-like resources, how would your verifiability test avoid false accusations? Can you formalize the “third-party oracle” assumption further?
5. For Lemma 1, could you sketch the concrete algorithm in your no-rejection, indistinguishability-required setting, and provide explicit sample/time complexity, highlighting differences from Goldwasser et al. (2020)?
6. The “almost every task” phrasing seems stronger than Theorem 1 (which quantifies over efficiently learnable tasks). Could you clarify this wording, and precisely delineate the set of excluded tasks?
reviews.assessment:
This is an ambitious and thought-provoking theory paper that unifies watermarking and adversarial defenses and adds a third, cryptography-linked pillar—transferable attacks—leading to a clean trichotomy. The connection to EFID/PRGs is elegant and conceptually valuable, and the bounded VC-dimension instantiations help ground the framework. That said, the main theorem is largely non-constructive and relies on game-theoretic existence with delicate time-parameter claims that deserve clearer exposition in the main text. The cryptographic construction, while insightful, uses an artificial mixed distribution that limits immediate practical resonance. Definitions and verification criteria (especially for watermark “uniqueness” and defense detectability) would benefit from more precise, quantitative statements up front, and the comparison to closely related work could be tightened.

On balance, I find the conceptual contribution meaningful for ICLR’s theory and safety communities. If the authors can strengthen the main-text proofs/algorithms for time bounds, clarify definitions and verifiability, and sharpen the comparison to Christiano et al. (2024) and robust learning works, this would be a valuable addition. I lean toward a weak accept for its unifying perspective and cryptographic boundary insights.

papers.title: Common Feature Learning for Zero-shot Image Recognition

reviews.summary: The paper proposes CF-ZIR, a two-stage embedding framework for zero-shot image recognition that aims to capture fine-grained, image-level visual–semantic relationships via coupled dictionary learning. In stage one (visual–attribute embedding), a “common visual feature” dictionary is constrained by attribute features to produce per-image semantic vectors; in stage two (visual–semantic embedding), a second coupled dictionary aligns image features with these image-level semantic vectors, aided by a discriminative loss. Experiments on aPY, AwA1, and AwA2 show competitive conventional ZSL accuracy, with ablations indicating contributions from the discriminative term and the visual–semantic alignment.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The idea of explicitly producing image-level semantic vectors via a common visual feature dictionary that is guided by attribute features is a thoughtful attempt to address intra-class variability that class-level semantic prototypes cannot capture.

The two-stage, dual-layer embedding (visual–attribute, then visual–semantic) is a coherent architectural decomposition that could, in principle, strengthen alignment by progressively refining supervision signals.
Experimental rigor and validation
Ablation experiments, though limited, do demonstrate that both the discriminative loss and the visual–semantic alignment contribute to gains, especially on AwA2.
Clarity of presentation

The high-level motivation and pipeline (as conveyed by the framework figure and staged description) are accessible and intuitive: extract common features guided by attributes, then align those to the semantic space for recognition.
Significance of contributions
Zero-shot recognition remains a challenging, impactful problem, and lightweight, embedding-based methods that avoid heavy generative training can be valuable for efficiency and interpretability.
If rigorously validated, image-level semantic vector construction could be broadly beneficial beyond the specific dictionary-learning instantiation.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Inconsistencies and potential issues in the formulation: the text refers to “sparsity coefficients,” but the losses (Eq. 1, Eq. 4) do not include any sparsity-inducing penalties (e.g., ℓ1) or constraints. This undermines both the interpretability claim and the expected behavior of dictionary coding.

Notation and dimensional errors suggest gaps in technical soundness: e.g., Eq. (2) lists D_A ∈ R^(M_v × K) instead of R^(M_a × K); X_r is K×K without justification; several variables are updated against the wrong objective in Algorithm 1 (e.g., line 10 says “Update X_r via Eq. (6)” where X_e is intended).

The optimization protocol is under-specified: no mention of norm constraints on dictionary atoms, no convergence criteria beyond “maximum iteration,” and no details on joint vs alternating updates and their stability.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Evaluation is limited to conventional ZSL on three largely legacy datasets (aPY, AwA1, AwA2). Key, widely used modern benchmarks and settings (CUB, SUN, generalized ZSL with U/S/H metrics) are missing, making it hard to assess real-world competitiveness.

Baselines are incomplete or mismatched. Several recent strong CLIP-based or transformer-based embedding baselines and state-of-the-art generative models are absent or inconsistently categorized. The claims of “best” or “second-best” among embedding methods are therefore not convincing.
It is unclear which of the three proposed recognition spaces (visual/embedding/semantic) underlies the reported main results; no comparison across these inference protocols is provided.
Clarity or presentation issues
Numerous typos, inconsistent symbols, and incorrect cross-references (e.g., Lus vs L_vs; D_s^image vs D_x; updates in Algorithm 1) significantly impede understanding and confidence in correctness.
TEFN (text encoder) and the attribute feature extraction pipeline are under-described (which encoder? preprocessing? attribute phrase construction? dimensionalities?).
The paper states “four datasets” in Section 4.1 but lists three; aPY statistics differ from some standard reports; formatting artifacts compound ambiguity.
Missing related work or comparisons

The method is closely related to prior coupled dictionary learning approaches for ZSL (e.g., CDL, hierarchical coupled discriminative dictionary learning), but the differentiation is not articulated in depth, especially regarding per-image semantic vector estimation and how it exceeds prior image-level alignments (e.g., part-based, attribute-classifier, or attention-based embeddings).

Recent CLIP-aligned or prompt-based methods and strong GZSL studies (e.g., CoOp/CoCoOp variants, robust causal/alignment methods, and modern generative backbones with improved embeddings) are not adequately compared or analyzed.
reviews.questions:
1. How do you enforce sparsity or interpretability of X^s and X_e? If no explicit sparsity is used, why do you refer to “sparsity coefficients,” and how do you prevent degenerate solutions?
2. Please clarify dimensionalities and correct typos: what are the exact shapes of D_A, D_F, F, A, X_r, D_y, D_x, and X_e? Why is X_r ∈ R^{K×K}? Is K equal to the number of attributes?
3. What text encoder constitutes TEFN? How are attribute phrases formed and embedded? Please provide dimensionalities and preprocessing details.
4. Which recognition space (visual/embedding/semantic) was used to produce the main results in Table 2? How do the three choices compare empirically?
5. How are dictionaries and codes optimized in practice (alternating minimization steps, constraints on dictionary atom norms, learning rates, stopping criteria)? Are you using ℓ2-only losses? Any regularization on D and F?
6. Could you report results on standard GZSL (U/S/H) and include CUB and SUN, with comparisons to strong CLIP-based/prompt-based and recent state-of-the-art generative methods under the PS protocol?
7. Please include ablations removing L_cf (no visual–attribute coupling), varying K and L, and sensitivity to the attribute encoder choice. Also discuss runtime/compute relative to generative baselines.
reviews.assessment: The paper addresses a timely and important problem and puts forward a conceptually appealing idea: derive image-level semantic vectors by attribute-guided common feature extraction and then align them to the visual space using coupled dictionaries. This direction could provide a lightweight alternative to generative ZSL while better handling intra-class variability. However, the current submission has substantial issues that preclude publication at a top-tier venue: technical inconsistencies (notation, dimensions, algorithmic steps), missing or unclear modeling details (true sparsity/regularization, optimization procedure, encoder specifics), and a limited and outdated evaluation protocol without GZSL or modern baselines. The gains reported are modest and not contextualized against recent strong methods. With thorough corrections, stronger theoretical/optimization grounding (including proper sparsity/constraints), and comprehensive experiments on standard benchmarks and protocols (including CUB, SUN, and GZSL with strong baselines), the work could become a valuable contribution. In its current form, I recommend rejection.

papers.title: Learning Fused State Representations for Control from Multi-View Observations

reviews.summary: The paper introduces MFSC, a representation learning module for multi-view visual reinforcement learning that fuses information from multiple camera views into a compact, task-relevant latent state. MFSC combines a Transformer encoder with a learnable [CLS]-like fusion token, bisimulation metric learning to align latent distances with reward and transition similarity, and a mask-based latent reconstruction auxiliary task to encourage cross-view consistency and handle missing views. Experiments on Meta-World manipulation and PyBullet Ant (with/without color cues), ablations, and attention visualizations show improved performance over several multi-view baselines and robustness to missing views.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Integrates a [CLS]-style fusion token with bisimulation-guided metric learning for multi-view aggregation, an appealing combination of ideas from Transformers and RL state abstraction.
Proposes mask-based latent reconstruction across views (inspired by SimSiam-style predictions) to reduce redundancy, promote cross-view consistency, and enable missing-view handling via mask tokens.
Presents a theoretically motivated view of multi-view abstraction via bisimulation metrics, connecting the learned aggregator to a summarized MDP.
Experimental rigor and validation
Evaluates on six Meta-World tasks and a challenging PyBullet Ant locomotion setting, including a “no color” variant that removes helpful cues to test task-relevance in representation learning.
Includes ablations dissecting the impact of bisimulation constraints and reconstruction loss, showing both contribute to gains.
Provides qualitative attention/Grad-CAM analyses to probe what the model attends to within and across views.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level architecture and training objectives (fusion loss, reconstruction loss) are fairly clear, with intuitive explanations for the role of each component.
The overall pipeline and how MFSC can be plugged into standard RL algorithms are communicated reasonably well.
Significance of contributions

Addresses an important and recurring challenge in multi-view RL—fusing complementary and redundant information into compact, task-relevant states—potentially benefiting a broad set of control problems.
Demonstrates robustness to missing views, a practically relevant scenario for embodied agents with partial sensor failures or occlusions.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The bisimulation objective relies on a learned latent dynamics model and reward scaling, but training details, stability considerations, and potential biases/errors from this model are largely deferred to the appendix, limiting understanding of reliability.

The self-attention fusion complexity is claimed to be favorable compared to pairwise cross-attention, but both scale quadratically in the number of views; a more careful complexity/efficiency analysis is missing.

Some theoretical elements are thin or underspecified (e.g., constants like c, distance terms, and clustering assumptions) and largely restate known bisimulation bounds without strongly tying them to the proposed implementation.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Inconsistency between using PPO for control and references to a replay buffer and SAC-style notation for the bisimulation/critic training; it is unclear whether representation learning is off-policy or on-policy and how rollouts/data are shared.

Missing-view experiments do not compare to other methods explicitly adapted for missing views (e.g., information-theoretic MVRL with missing-view handling, or MV masked world models); thus robustness claims are not contextualized against strong baselines.
Limited diversity of tasks and camera setups: only three cameras, mostly simulated domains; no stress tests varying the number/placement/calibration of cameras or severe occlusions.
No runtime or memory analysis; it is unclear what the overhead of the Transformer fusion and dual-branch masking is compared to simpler concatenation or cross-attention encoders.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some notation and equation formatting are inconsistent, and a few symbols/constants (e.g., c in bounds, g, and d variants) are insufficiently defined in the main text.
The training pipeline for the latent dynamics model used in the bisimulation target (Eq. 8) is not clearly explained in the main body; essential details are relegated to appendices.
Missing related work or comparisons

Empirical comparisons to recent world-model baselines (e.g., Dreamer/Masked-World-Model variants beyond those cited) and bisimulation-based representation methods adapted to multi-view settings are limited.

No comparison to simple alternatives like averaging/MLP-fusion of per-view embeddings or concatenation plus projection heads with strong regularization, which would help quantify the specific benefit of the [CLS]-fusion plus bisimulation.
reviews.questions:
1. How exactly is the latent dynamics model trained for the bisimulation target, and is it off-policy? If the control algorithm is PPO (on-policy), what data are used for training the dynamics and the bisimulation loss (replay buffer vs. PPO minibatches)? Please clarify the data flow and update schedules.
2. What is the computational overhead (training time, FLOPs/memory) of MFSC relative to (i) concatenation-based fusion and (ii) LookCloser’s cross-attention? How does this scale with the number of views?
3. How sensitive is MFSC to the mask ratio, the number of attention layers/heads, and reward scaling in the bisimulation loss? Could you provide sensitivity curves or at least ablation tables?
4. In the missing-view setting, which specific view(s) were dropped at test time? Could you report results by dropping each view individually and at different probabilities to better understand view importance and robustness?
5. Did you attempt to adapt F2C or multi-view masked world models to the missing-view scenario for direct comparison? If not, what challenges prevented such a comparison?
6. Can you quantify attention distribution across views (e.g., attention entropy on the [CLS] token across heads/layers) and correlate it with which views carry more task-relevant information?
7. How does MFSC perform when camera parameters (pose, intrinsics) drift over time or are perturbed between training and testing? Does the [CLS]-fusion remain robust?
reviews.assessment: This paper tackles an important problem in multi-view visual RL and presents a well-motivated combination of techniques—Transformer-based fusion with a [CLS]-style token, bisimulation metric learning for task relevance, and mask-based latent reconstruction for cross-view consistency and robustness. The empirical results across Meta-World and PyBullet Ant are encouraging, with consistent gains over several baselines, meaningful ablations, and informative visualizations. However, there are notable gaps: the on-/off-policy inconsistency and limited details for the latent dynamics model used in the bisimulation target, missing-view comparisons against strong baselines, lack of efficiency analysis, and thin theoretical grounding beyond standard bisimulation bounds. Overall, I view MFSC as a solid, moderately novel contribution that is likely to be useful to practitioners; with clarifications and additional experiments (particularly on missing views and efficiency), it could be a strong paper. As it stands, I lean toward a weak accept.

papers.title: Flow Matching for One-Step Sampling

reviews.summary: The paper proposes a one-step sampling scheme for flow-matching generative models by constructing approximate pairings between target data points and “prototypes” drawn from the prior. The key idea is to integrate a reverse-time ODE driven by an explicit velocity field derived in prior work (Ryzhakov et al., 2024), with the field’s integrals over the unknown target density estimated via importance sampling from a buffer of target samples. A regression model is then trained on (prototype, target) pairs to learn a direct map from the prior to the data, eliminating ODE solving at inference.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Using the explicit flow-matching velocity to define target-to-prior pairings and training a direct one-step generator is an intriguing idea that connects explicit FM theory to transport map learning.
The introduction of a small regularization σ to guarantee invertibility of the conditional map and enable reverse-time integration is a thoughtful design choice and is empirically probed on toy data.
The construction with a minibatch “buffer” to approximate the velocity integrals via self-normalized importance sampling is simple and potentially adaptable to various settings.
Experimental rigor and validation
The paper shows proof-of-concept demonstrations on 2D toy datasets and MNIST, including a conditional version with labels, and a color-transfer application at the per-pixel level.
The methodology is described sufficiently to allow a motivated reader to attempt reproduction on small-scale datasets.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level pipeline—compute prototypes by integrating the explicit velocity backward, then train a one-step map—is easy to follow.
Algorithms 1 and 2 concisely convey the training workflows for unconditional and conditional settings.
Significance of contributions
Reducing inference cost via one-step sampling for flow-matching is a timely and important direction, connected to a broader trend of distillation and straightening in generative modeling.
If shown to scale and maintain sample quality, the approach could be impactful for applications where inference latency dominates.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The proposed coupling relies on approximate reverse-time ODE integration with a discretized, self-normalized importance-sampled velocity; no theoretical guarantees are provided about the accuracy of the resulting prototypes, their distribution under ρ0, or the consistency of the learned transport.

The method’s computational cost is substantial at training time: for each target sample, multiple evaluations of vσ^dis require summing over a potentially large buffer, inside an ODE solver. There is no complexity analysis or empirical profiling.
The argument that the learned map is “almost monotone” and that “segments almost never intersect” is asserted without quantification or proof.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

There are no quantitative metrics (e.g., FID/sFID on CIFAR-10, CelebA, ImageNet subsets), no comparisons to strong baselines (Rectified Flow, OT-CFM, InstaFlow/one-step distillation methods, DDIM/DPM-Solver accelerations), and no ablations on N (buffer size), σ, ODE tolerance, or the number of integration steps.
The MNIST results are purely qualitative, and the use of a large-capacity DiT on MNIST without metrics or comparison is not informative about competitiveness.

The color-transfer experiment lacks comparisons to standard baselines (e.g., histogram matching, CycleGAN, neural color transfer) and uses per-pixel MLPs without reporting objective quality or user studies.
Clarity or presentation issues

Notational inconsistencies: vθ is called a velocity network but is trained and used as a direct mapping; loss (3) applies X0(·) to a noise-perturbed target sample, which is conceptually unusual and not well justified; the use of ε around target vs. prototype is confusing.
Multiple typographical errors and formatting artifacts (e.g., section 4.1 title, figures’ captions, inconsistent symbols), and missing details about ODE step counts and tolerances per task.
Missing related work or comparisons

Limited discussion and no empirical comparison with recent and highly relevant one-step/straightened approaches such as InstaFlow (Liu et al., 2024), rectified/accelerated flow straightening, and progressive/teacher-student distillation methods for diffusion/flow models.
No connection to the broader literature on learning Monge maps/transport maps from Gaussian to data directly, or equivalences with energy-based and normalizing flow maps when couplings are provided.
reviews.questions:
1. Can you provide quantitative results (FID/sFID/IS) and wall-clock sampling times on standard benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10 32×32, CelebA-HQ 64×64) compared to Rectified Flow, OT-CFM, InstaFlow, and distilled one-step baselines?
2. What is the computational complexity per training iteration for prototype computation (ODE steps × buffer size × model calls)? Please include empirical profiling (GPU hours) versus a conventional FM baseline trained to similar perceptual quality.
3. How sensitive is the method to N (buffer size), σ, and ODE tolerances? Please include ablations and report how these hyperparameters affect prototype stability, coupling monotonicity, and final sample quality.
4. Do the computed prototypes empirically follow ρ0? Can you report MMD or KL estimates between prototypes and a Gaussian prior to validate the claim?
5. Is the self-normalized importance sampling introducing noticeable bias in practice? Have you tried alternatives (e.g., rejection sampling as mentioned) and compared performance/variance?
6. In loss (3), why do you pass x1+ε into X0(·) instead of adding noise in the prototype space (i.e., X0(x1)+ε)? Please clarify the rationale and show an ablation on this design choice.
7. How many ODE function evaluations (NFE) are needed to compute a prototype on average? Is the reverse-time integration stable for large σ and high-dimensional x?
8. Can you provide a theoretical statement (even under simplifying assumptions) about conditions under which X0(x1) computed with the exact vσ would push forward ρ1 to ρ0 and yield a valid Monge map, and discuss how approximate SIS affects this?
9. The paper mentions “almost monotone” and “segments almost never intersect.” Can you formalize and empirically test these claims (e.g., counting crossings in 2D/low-D projections)?
10. For color transfer, please compare against standard baselines (histogram matching, CycleGAN) with objective metrics (e.g., color hist similarity, LPIPS) and user studies if possible.
reviews.assessment: The paper tackles an important goal—one-step sampling for flow-matching—by leveraging an explicit FM velocity to construct target-to-prior couplings via reverse-time ODE integration, then training a direct transport map. Conceptually, this is an interesting and potentially useful bridge between explicit FM theory and practical one-step generators. However, the current submission falls short on several critical fronts: it lacks theoretical guarantees for the approximate coupling; it provides only small-scale, qualitative demonstrations without quantitative metrics or strong baselines; it omits runtime and complexity analyses; and it has clarity issues (notational inconsistencies, unexplained design choices). Given the maturity of competing one-step/few-step approaches and the central claim of accelerated sampling “while preserving performance,” more rigorous empirical validation is necessary. Overall, I recommend rejection in the current form, with the caveat that the core idea is promising and could be competitive if supported by comprehensive experiments, ablations, and clearer theory.

papers.title: Alternating Optimized Stochastic Vector Quantization in Neural Compression

reviews.summary: The paper addresses differentiable training of vector quantization (VQ) in neural compression by (i) reframing encoder/decoder learning as optimizing quantization boundaries/centers and (ii) proposing an alternating encoder–decoder training scheme to reduce train–test mismatch. It further introduces a stochastic “sphere-noise” VQ approximation for encoder updates, arguing that it yields gradients at boundaries that better reflect RD-loss differences between adjacent centers. Experiments on synthetic vector sources and Kodak images (within a factorized baseline) show improved RD trade-offs over additive uniform noise and VQ-STE-style baselines.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The encoder–decoder alternating optimization is a principled way to decouple boundary and center learning, reducing train–test mismatch for the decoder while still enabling encoder updates through a surrogate.

The interpretation that, in source-space VQ induced by neural compressors, encoder determines boundaries and decoder determines centers provides a clear conceptual lens to reason about surrogates and gradients.
The sphere-noise stochastic approximation is an interesting alternative to additive uniform noise, intended to align encoder gradients at boundaries with RD-loss differences.
Experimental rigor and validation

The paper provides a set of controlled toy-source experiments (1D Gaussian, 2D Boomerang, 8D Laplace) that are well-suited to interrogate the boundary/center behavior and visualize mappings/gradients.
Image experiments on the Kodak dataset show consistent BD-rate gains against additive uniform noise within the same factorized architecture, and the method scales to 4D latent VQs.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level motivation and the boundary/center decomposition are clearly conveyed with intuitive diagrams.
The gradient analyses for AUN and STE in the scalar/uniform case help explain well-known empirical behaviors in neural compression.
Significance of contributions

Reducing train–test mismatch while keeping useful encoder gradients is an important, recurring challenge in learned compression; improvements here can translate to better RD performance and more stable training.
If robust and extensible to richer models (e.g., hyperpriors, context models), the approach could influence training protocols for learned VQ modules.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The gradient derivation for the sphere-noise estimator assumes dỹ/dy = 1 and then invokes a surface-integral argument via a generalized Stokes/divergence theorem without fully accounting for the dependence of the noise radius on y (it is defined as the distance to the nearest codeword). In reparameterized form, ỹ = y + r(y) z with z uniform on a unit sphere implies ∂ỹ/∂y ≠ I in general; ignoring ∂r/∂y may bias gradients, especially at or near boundaries where the nearest codeword can switch discretely.

Theoretical claims that the proposed estimator better matches “RD loss difference between adjacent centers” at boundaries are plausible but not rigorously established beyond the 1D/uniform analogy; a careful proof or controlled ablation isolating this effect is missing.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Image experiments are restricted to a single-layer factorized baseline and unconditional priors; the method is stated to be “only applicable” under this setting, which severely limits practical relevance given that strong NIC models rely on hyperpriors, autoregressive/context models, and multi-stage quantization.

Comparisons do not include modern NIC baselines beyond factorized models (e.g., hyperprior, mean-scale hyperprior, or context-adaptive variants), and results are only on Kodak, which is small and prone to variance. Reporting on CLIC/Tecnick and including stronger baselines would better support claims.

Ablations are limited: alternating frequency, codebook sizes, stability across seeds, and computational/training overhead are not reported. Alternatives like “decoder-rounding with encoder-noise” two-stage schedules are mentioned but not quantitatively compared under matched settings.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some mathematical steps are hand-wavy (e.g., use of Stokes/divergence theorem, definition of integration domains), and there are typos (“finds”, “encode-decoder”), plus minor equation formatting artifacts.

The definition of the sphere radius (equal to distance to the nearest codeword) and how it is computed/stabilized during encoder updates is not precisely specified, especially around ambiguous boundary cases.
Missing related work or comparisons

Several prior strategies partially resemble the proposed alternating approach (e.g., training with noise for encoder and rounding for decoder, staged or alternating schedules), but the paper does not position its alternation frequency/scheme and practical benefits against these closely related techniques with matched architectures/training budgets.

Recent advances in learned VQ for compression (e.g., product quantization, residual vector quantization, lattice VQ with learned companding, hierarchical VQ) are mentioned sparsely; a more thorough contextualization would help.
reviews.questions:
1. The sphere-noise estimator assumes dỹ/dy = 1 while the sampling radius r(y) equals the distance to the nearest codeword. How do you justify dropping ∂r/∂y terms in the gradient, especially near boundaries where argmin switches discontinuously? Is the estimator unbiased, or can you quantify/justify the bias?
2. Could you provide a precise derivation for the surface-integral relation via Stokes/divergence theorem, including the choice of vector field and boundary terms, and conditions under which it holds when q(ỹ|y) depends on y through r(y)?
3. How is the nearest-center distance computed for determining the sphere radius during encoder updates? What happens at ties/boundaries, and how do you stabilize training in those cases?
4. What is the alternation schedule (e.g., per-step, per-epoch, ratio of encoder-to-decoder updates)? Did you tune this schedule, and how sensitive are results to it?
5. For image experiments, what are the exact codebook sizes per subvector and how do you prevent codebook under/over-utilization? Please report codebook utilization statistics.
6. Can your method be adapted to hyperprior or context models (e.g., alternating within each module or alternating across layers)? If not, what are the fundamental obstacles?
7. Please report training stability across multiple seeds and provide error bars for BD-rates. Is the observed gain consistent?
8. How does the method compare, under a matched setting, to a strong two-stage schedule (pretrain with AUN for encoder, finetune decoder with rounding) with multiple rounds of finetuning (i.e., coarse alternation)?
9. What is the computational overhead of sphere sampling and nearest-center queries versus AUN, and what are the training/inference time and memory impacts?
reviews.assessment: This paper offers a clear and useful conceptual decomposition of how encoder and decoder affect boundaries and centers in source-space VQ induced by neural compressors, and builds on it with an alternating optimization scheme and a novel sphere-noise surrogate for encoder training. The toy-source experiments convincingly illustrate known pitfalls of STE and the benefits of smoother boundary gradients. However, the core theoretical treatment of the sphere-noise estimator appears incomplete: the assumption dỹ/dy = 1 neglects the dependence of the sampling distribution on y through the radius, making the surface-integral argument questionable and potentially biasing gradients near boundaries. Experimentally, while the Kodak/factorized results are encouraging, the scope (single dataset, single architecture family) and the stated inapplicability to more realistic multi-layer/hyperprior setups limit practical impact. With a more rigorous derivation or empirical validation of unbiasedness/benefit, deeper ablations (alternation schedule, stability across seeds), and demonstrations on stronger NIC baselines, this work could make a solid contribution. In its current form, I lean toward rejection, while acknowledging the promising direction and the clarity of the boundary/center perspective.

papers.title: SEAL: Scaling to Emphasize Attention for Long-Context Retrieval

reviews.summary: This paper proposes SEAL, a lightweight, learning-based attention scaling framework to improve long-context retrieval in LLMs. The core idea is to learn small head-wise (SEAL-H) or channel-wise (SEAL-C) multiplicative scales that reweight attention head outputs using a tiny, synthetic, task-formatted dataset (≈50 examples), thereby emphasizing heads that correlate with better retrieval. Experiments on line retrieval, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and LongBench document QA show large and consistent gains across several 7B/13B models, and SEAL complements training-free context extension methods (e.g., NTK, Self-Extend), yielding strong improvements beyond original context limits with negligible additional parameters and short tuning time.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The paper articulates a simple, practical mechanism—learnable head/channel scales—that targets long-context retrieval specifically, grounded in a careful pruning-based observation that head contributions are heterogeneous and sometimes counterproductive.

SEAL’s channel-wise variant (SEAL-C) provides finer-grained control within heads and empirically outperforms head-level scaling in several regimes, offering a compelling design space between training-free tricks and heavier PEFT approaches.
The offline folding of scales into adjacent projection weights to avoid inference overhead is a nice engineering detail that increases practicality.
Experimental rigor and validation
Clear, consistent gains on line retrieval and Needle-in-a-Haystack across multiple base models and context lengths, including near-window limits where models typically degrade.
Orthogonal compatibility with training-free context extension (NTK, Self-Extend) is shown and quantitatively strong, demonstrating practical utility in extending effective context use at low cost.
The synthetic, format-aligned data generation strategy is efficient and appears robust; ablations on number of samples indicate SEAL can work with as few as 10–25 examples.
Clarity of presentation
The motivation, intuition from per-head pruning, and the escalation to head/channel scaling are well explained and visually supported.
The direct effect analysis, while limited, provides a helpful qualitative lens for how reweighting attention may shift downstream MLP contributions and final logits.
Significance of contributions
Long-context retrieval is a central bottleneck for applied LLMs; a method that is cheap, general, and easy to layer on top of existing models and even training-free extensions is highly valuable.
The parameter-efficiency and speed (single A100, <1 hour) make the method attractive to a broad set of practitioners and researchers.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The core mechanism—learnable multiplicative scales on attention—overlaps substantially with prior PEFT/gating methods (e.g., IA3) and earlier head-importance/gating works; the novelty is more in the application focus and experimental framing than in the mechanism itself.

The direct-effect analysis is anecdotal and uses a simplified variant (no normalization term); the causal link between head scaling and improved aggregation at long ranges is suggestive but not conclusively established.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Missing baselines: no comparisons against IA3 or other lightweight gating/adapter methods that specifically modulate attention/MLP channels with few parameters; LoRA/DoRA are heavier than SEAL-H and are not the closest conceptual comparators.
Limited robustness analysis: results are presented without variance, seed sweeps, or statistical testing; sensitivity to decoding parameters is not explored.

The out-of-domain results on LongBench are modest and limited to doc QA subsets; broader downstream tasks (summarization, multi-hop reasoning, structured retrieval) would strengthen generalization claims.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some implementation details are under-specified: the exact placement of scales (pre/post o_proj, constraints on sign/range), training loss/objective, decoding settings, and whether scales are layer-normed or constrained remain unclear.
A few figures/tables contain formatting artifacts; while not fatal, they occasionally slow comprehension.
Missing related work or comparisons

No discussion or empirical comparison to IA3 (multiplicative gating with few parameters) or related per-channel/per-head gating methods in PEFT or interpretability (e.g., learning head importance), which closely parallel SEAL’s mechanism.
The paper references quantization-motivated head gating (e.g., Quantizable Transformers) but does not fully position SEAL within that broader landscape of gating/factoring approaches.
reviews.questions:
1. How are the scales s initialized and constrained during training (e.g., initialized to 1.0, positivity enforced via softplus/exponential, any regularization)? Are negative scales possible and, if so, did you observe instability or degradation?
2. What exact loss/objective and decoding configurations were used for scale tuning and evaluation (e.g., supervised next-token cross-entropy on the answer string, greedy decoding vs. temperature sampling)? Please report for each experiment family.
3. Can you compare SEAL-H/C to IA3 (and, if feasible, prefix-tuning/p-tuning) under the same synthetic data and budget? This would better isolate whether SEAL’s placement of multiplicative factors at attention head outputs is the key driver versus general multiplicative gating.
4. How consistent are the learned scales across different random synthetic datasets (and seeds)? Please report variance across at least 3–5 runs to establish robustness.
5. Are the improvements concentrated in specific layers or head patterns (e.g., mid vs late layers)? A layerwise analysis of learned s and their correlation with depth/positional sensitivity would be informative.
6. For LongBench, which metrics and prompts/templates were used, and do in-domain tuned scales ever hurt tasks outside doc QA (e.g., summarization, multi-hop reasoning) at long lengths?
7. Could SEAL scales be jointly learned across multiple long-context tasks to produce a single, task-agnostic set of scales? If attempted, how did it fare relative to task-specific scales?
reviews.assessment: SEAL is a practical and effective technique that delivers notable improvements in long-context retrieval at very low cost. The empirical gains on line retrieval and NIAH are strong and consistent, and the orthogonal combination with training-free context extension is particularly useful. The main weakness is conceptual novelty: head/channel scaling is closely related to prior multiplicative gating methods (e.g., IA3), which are not discussed or compared, and the mechanistic analysis is suggestive rather than definitive. Nonetheless, the paper’s engineering value is high, the experiments are broad enough to establish utility, and the method appears robust with tiny synthetic datasets. I lean toward acceptance provided the authors (a) add IA3 and related comparisons/discussion, (b) clarify training/decoding details and scale constraints, and (c) include variance analyses to establish robustness. With these additions, SEAL would offer a solid, actionable contribution to the community’s toolkit for making long contexts more usable.

papers.title: Slashed Normal: Parameterize Normal Posterior Distributions with KL Amplitude

reviews.summary: The paper proposes Slashed Normal, a new parameterization of Gaussian posteriors for variational inference in which the KL divergence to a Gaussian prior equals the squared L2 norm of a complex “KL amplitude” ψ output by the encoder. This is achieved by introducing a stdplus activation, constructed via the Lambert W function, to map the imaginary part of ψ to the posterior standard deviation while mapping the real part to the posterior mean. The authors analyze univariate and multivariate cases (including degenerate priors), show that KL becomes ||ψ||², and demonstrate applications to direct rate control (fixed-rate VIB) and mitigating posterior collapse, with small-scale empirical results on MNIST/CIFAR-10 classification robustness and an LSTM-VAE text setting.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Introduces a principled, closed-form parameterization (via Lambert W) that makes the exact per-sample KL equal to the squared norm of the encoder output (“KL amplitude”), enabling direct, interpretable rate control.
Derives a new stdplus activation that smoothly stitches the two real branches of Lambert W, with careful analysis of differentiability and a practical numerical routine.
Extends to multivariate Gaussians (including degenerate priors) with a clean factorization; the KL equality naturally generalizes dimension-wise.
Provides a compact stationary-point relation linking ψ to locally smoothed gradients, offering a unifying perspective with SmoothGrad and IB-based attribution.
Experimental rigor and validation
Demonstrates fixed-rate VIB that improves adversarial robustness on MNIST/CIFAR-10 relative to a base model and dropout, and compares different normalization schemes for rate allocation.

Includes a posterior-collapse study in a text LSTM-VAE with standard metrics (NLL, KL, AU, MIq), baselines (warmup, cyclic anneal, BatchNorm), and ablations (batch/instance/feature normalization, learnable global rate), showing reduced collapse and interpretable trade-offs.
Clarity of presentation
Mathematical derivations for the univariate case are clear and easy to verify; the reduction to Lambert W and the transformation from (μ, σ) to (a, b) is presented coherently.
The numerical algorithm for stdplus is documented and includes attention to precision and stability.
Significance of contributions

Direct control of the KL/rate is relevant across VAEs, information bottlenecks, and compression, and can simplify or unify several heuristics (e.g., β-tuning, committed rate, free bits, batch-norm–based KL floors).
Conceptually reframes the encoder output as an information-theoretic resource (channel capacity) with straightforward knobs for per-instance/feature/batch allocations.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns
The complex-valued ψ is conceptually elegant but practically unnecessary and may complicate implementations; an equivalent 2-vector parameterization could be simpler.

Claims of improved numerical stability are asserted, but no quantitative evidence (e.g., gradient statistics, loss spike rates, overflow/underflow incidence) or wall-clock/overhead analysis is provided; stdplus itself relies on nontrivial numerics that may be slower than softplus.

The multivariate extension introduces an orthogonal matrix P, but training/parameterization details (e.g., Householder, Cayley, or Stiefel optimization) and empirical use with full covariance are not presented.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Empirical validation is limited in scope: no standard image VAE likelihood benchmarks (BPD/NLL) with strong decoders, no comparison to recent anti-collapse methods (e.g., λ-VAE, LIDVAE/IL-LIDVAE), and no generative sampling quality assessment or aggregate prior match (q(z) vs p(z)).

Fixed-rate VIB is compared primarily to base and dropout; missing comparisons to strong adversarial regularizers or alternative IB implementations (e.g., GECO, free bits, β-schedules) under matched conditions.
The posterior-collapse text results show that adding a skip connection (not specific to the proposed method) dominates others, tempering claims that the parameterization itself is the main driver.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some notation and exposition around branch selection (b’s sign → Lambert W branch) and its implications for optimization dynamics could be clearer (e.g., intuition for when σ < 1 vs σ > 1 branches are selected and whether branch-switching is ever harmful).
The multivariate degenerate-prior discussion is terse; conditions for well-defined KL in subspaces and how this interacts with training are left to appendices and citations.
Missing related work or comparisons

Limited discussion and no empirical comparison to recent principled anti-collapse methods (λ-VAE; identifiability-based decoders such as LIDVAE/IL-LIDVAE), capacity control methods (free bits, GECO), or aggregate-posterior matching approaches (InfoVAE/TCVAE), and no positioning relative to phase-transition analyses of collapse.
reviews.questions:
1. What is the computational overhead (forward/backward time, memory) of stdplus compared to softplus/exp in typical encoder architectures, and how stable is autodiff through your Newton-based routine across FP32/FP16?
2. How do you parameterize and train the orthogonal matrix P in the multivariate full-covariance version? Did you experiment with full-covariance posteriors, and if so, what are the empirical costs/benefits?
3. Is stdplus globally C1 (and is C2 needed) at the branch junction b = 0? Have you observed any training instabilities when b crosses zero frequently?
4. In fixed-rate VIB, how does your method compare to GECO, free bits, or β‑schedules tuned by validation under the same architectures and data? Can you report MI estimates to relate achieved capacity to the theoretical bound?
5. For generative VAEs, does fixing per-sample capacity increase aggregate posterior mismatch q(z) ≠ p(z)? How does this impact sample quality from the prior and IWAE test likelihood?
6. Can the ψ framework be extended to non-Gaussian variational families or combined with flows while retaining a tractable, directly controllable KL?
7. Do you have evidence that Slashed Normal reduces numerical pathologies (e.g., loss spikes) relative to softplus/exp? Gradient/loss trace plots or failure rates would help support this claim.
reviews.assessment: This paper presents a neat and principled parameterization that makes the per-sample KL divergence exactly equal to the squared norm of the encoder output via a Lambert W–based stdplus activation. The idea is elegant, easy to reason about, and potentially useful for direct and interpretable rate control in VAEs and information bottlenecks. The mathematical construction is sound and the numerical routine is thoughtfully designed. However, the empirical evaluation is too limited for a top-tier venue: there are no standard likelihood benchmarks with strong decoders, no comparisons to recent state-of-the-art anti-collapse methods, and no quantitative evidence supporting the claimed numerical stability advantages. Some of the most positive results (e.g., skip connections) are orthogonal to the main proposal. I see real promise in the contribution and would be enthusiastic with a more comprehensive empirical section (including runtime/overhead), broader baselines, and generative quality/likelihood results. As it stands, I lean toward rejection on experimental grounds, while acknowledging the conceptual contribution as original and potentially impactful.

papers.title: Defend against Jailbreak Attacks via Debate with Partially Perceptive Agents

reviews.summary: This paper proposes a training-free, black-box defense against typographic jailbreaks in vision-language models (VLMs) via a multi-agent debate framework. One “integrated” agent sees the full (potentially attacked) image, a “partial” agent sees a cropped or resampled image, and a text-only moderator coordinates message passing, critical debate, or persuasive debate. On a subset of MM-SafetyBench scenarios (8 categories, 20 examples each that initially succeed in attacking the full-vision agent), the persuasive debate variant substantially lowers the reported attack success rate (ASR), with additional analyses on model diversity (Qwen-VL-Plus vs. GPT-4o), perspective-belief priming, and different image resampling choices.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Using agents with asymmetric visual access (full vs. cropped/compressed) to exploit the fragility of typographic attacks is a neat and plausible design.
The examination of debate styles (message passing, persuasive, critical) and perspective-belief priming adds an interesting behavioral dimension beyond standard majority voting.
Text-only moderator as a lightweight coordinator avoids hard-coded safety post-processing and is consistent with a black-box setting.
Experimental rigor and validation
Includes multiple ablations: debate styles, model diversity (Qwen-VL-Plus vs GPT-4o), perspective-belief priming levels, and resampling strategies (crop/compress/noise).
Tracks refusal rates and uses a response-quality score to address helpfulness/usability concerns in addition to ASR.
Provides concrete prompts and some implementation details in the appendix.
Clarity of presentation
The overall pipeline is intelligible, with a clear intuition: clean full-view agents tend to be more persuasive; if compromised, the partial agent can pull them back.
The roles of integrated/partial/moderator agents and the debate phases are described with examples and prompt snippets.
Significance of contributions
The problem is important: typographic attacks on VLMs remain a pressing and practical safety issue.
A training-free, API-compatible defense that can be composed with existing systems could provide immediate utility if validated rigorously.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns
No evaluation against adaptive attackers who target the debate protocol (e.g., overlays that influence both crops or inject instructions anticipating the debate prompts).
Reliance on a text-only moderator and persuasive prompts raises the risk of new attack surfaces (prompt injection targeting the moderator or debate meta-instructions).
The mechanism remains heuristic; there is no analysis that the integrated agent is more/less persuadable conditional on clean/attacked inputs beyond empirical claims.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Selection bias: evaluation samples are filtered to those that initially succeed in attacking the fully observable agent, making the headline “100% to 22%” reduction potentially misleading for general usage.

Missing strong baselines: no direct “crop-only” or “compress-only” single-agent baselines on the same selection; no baseline that instructs the model to ignore overlaid text or to rely on scene content; no comparison to recent prompting defenses (e.g., AdaShield), or simple OCR-stripping/region masking pipelines.

Potential mis-implementation of SmoothVLM: the paper states “utilize 10 VLMs for majority voting,” whereas the original method votes over multiple perturbed images; mixing multiple VLMs could either be a different method or unfairly disadvantage that baseline.
ASR and quality are judged with GPT-4, but inter-rater reliability, rubric details, and calibration are not reported; no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests.
No measurement of runtime, number of queries, or cost; the multi-round debate involves many API calls and could be costly and slow in practice.
No evaluation on clean (non-attacked) data to verify preservation of normal task performance beyond refusal-rate and quality metrics on attack-selected cases.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some ambiguity about the final decision maker: at times the moderator is described as summarizer, elsewhere a “judge” appears in figures; text states “final conclusion provided by the agent that was initially attacked,” which is nonstandard and may bias outcomes.
Numerous typos and minor inconsistencies (likely due to PDF extraction, but some appear conceptual), e.g., repeated phrases and unclear metric formulas.
Missing related work or comparisons

Limited discussion and empirical comparison to: adaptive shield prompting (e.g., AdaShield), safety fine-tuning baselines (e.g., SafetyFT at almost no cost), OCR-aware defenses (text-region detection/erasure), patch defenses, or single-agent self-critiquing with targeted instructions to ignore overlaid text.
reviews.questions:
1. How exactly was SmoothVLM reproduced? Did you vote over multiple perturbed images for the same VLM (as in the original paper), or across multiple distinct VLMs as stated? Please clarify and, if needed, provide corrected results.
2. What is the performance of simple preprocessing alone (e.g., crop-only, compress-only, OCR-masking-only) without any debate on the same attacked-only subset, in terms of ASR, refusal rate, quality, and cost?
3. How many API calls and what average latency does each defense configuration incur (message passing, critical, persuasive; single- vs. dual-VLM debates; with/without moderator)? Please report approximate costs relative to SmoothVLM and MLLM-Protector.
4. How robust is the method to adaptive attackers who: (a) place adversarial text in multiple spatial locations to survive center-crop; (b) craft overlays that manipulate the debate prompts or the moderator (e.g., meta-instructions to the “judge”)? Any preliminary experiments?
5. Who produces the final answer—one of the agents or the moderator? The text mentions “final conclusion provided by the agent that was initially attacked,” while figures suggest a judge. Please clarify the aggregator’s logic.
6. How were harmfulness and quality labels obtained from GPT-4 configured? Did you randomize response order, use a rubric, or measure inter-rater reliability on a subset (e.g., human vs. GPT-4)?
7. Can you report results on an unfiltered test set (not only initially successful attacks) and on a clean dataset to assess benign utility?
8. Did you try stronger prompting-only baselines (e.g., “ignore any text that appears overlaid in the image; focus only on non-textual scene elements; adhere to safety policy X”)? How do these perform relative to your debate approach?
reviews.assessment:
The paper tackles an important and timely problem with an intuitively appealing idea: pit a full-view agent against a partial-view agent in a structured debate to blunt typographic jailbreaks while preserving semantics. Empirical results suggest persuasive debate reduces ASR substantially on a filtered subset of attacks and can lower refusal rates relative to a strong safety-prompt baseline. The exploration of debate styles, model diversity, and perspective-belief priming is interesting and could inspire follow-up work.

However, there are significant methodological concerns that limit confidence in the conclusions: likely mis-reproduction of SmoothVLM, absence of strong and fair single-agent preprocessing baselines, evaluation limited to attack-selected samples with no clean-data study, reliance on GPT-4 adjudication without reliability statistics, no cost/latency analysis, and lack of adaptive-attack evaluation. The “Level 3” belief manipulation raises additional concerns about generalization and principled safety behavior. Overall, while the direction is promising and the empirical trends are encouraging, the current evidence is not yet at the rigor expected for ICLR. I recommend rejection in the current form, with a clear path to strengthening: correct and broaden baselines, add robust and adaptive evaluations, include clean-utility and cost analyses, and clarify the final-decision and moderator roles.

papers.title: Recovering Knowledge by Hardening Language Models

reviews.summary: This paper studies how knowledge about regular languages is represented inside small generative language models (LSTM and decoder-only Transformers) trained on strings from five regular languages. The authors propose LaMFA, a post-hoc “hardening” pipeline that clusters hidden states of the neural LM on generated prefixes, estimates a probabilistic transition system, merges/denoises states, and converts the result to a DFA (and then to a regex via state elimination). On several synthetic languages, the extracted automata often match or exceed the LM’s validity on in- and out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluations, with some cases achieving 100% OOD validity.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Extends classical DFA extraction ideas from RNN recognizers to generative LMs and to transformers; proposes a simple, end-to-end clustering-to-automaton pipeline that is easy to implement.
Introduces a practical merging/denoising heuristic that operates on estimated transition/output statistics and can reduce over-fragmentation from k-means.
Experimental rigor and validation
Evaluates across five regular languages spanning local/global dependencies and AC^0/TC^0 distinctions, connecting to known theoretical separations.
Reports both in-distribution and OOD results and shows cases where the hardened automata generalize better than the original LMs.
Clarity of presentation
The pipeline is described clearly with algorithms and a helpful schematic; the mapping from neural hidden states to clustered “automaton states” is intuitive.
Figures comparing true DFA states and learned clusters aid interpretability.
Significance of contributions
Addresses an interpretable bridge from probabilistic neural modeling to symbolic automata, a direction of broad interest to the ICLR community.
Observations about the role of global vs local dependencies align with and contextualize recent theoretical work on transformer expressivity.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The method selects K and guides merging by “valid rate,” which requires access to a ground-truth membership oracle (Algorithm 2, Step 7; Section 4.2: “accuracy improvement threshold τ”). This contradicts the motivating claim of recovering an unknown regex from the model alone and constitutes strong supervision beyond the trained LM.
Heavy reliance on k-means over raw hidden states is fragile (sensitive to scaling/rotation, mode coverage, and sampling biases); there is no analysis of stability across seeds, K, or sample size N.

The pipeline may enforce correctness by using the oracle, not by faithfully decoding the model’s internal structure; this risks attributing improvements to extrinsic supervision rather than genuine model interpretability.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Missing comparisons to decades of DFA extraction and grammar inference methods (e.g., Weiss et al. 2018; Michalenko et al. 2019; classic state merging like RPNI/AALERGIA; spectral/weighted automata learning). Without baselines, it is hard to quantify progress.

Model scales are extremely small (e.g., “GPT-tiny” ~0.68K parameters, GPT-nano ~86K), limiting the relevance to contemporary LMs; no ablation on denoising temperature T, frequency threshold τ0, or subset-construction choices.

The “mdY” dataset is regular only because it is finite (1900–2023). The reported regex \d{2}/\d{2}/\d{4} does not encode calendar constraints; complexity and state-count claims for this language are thus ambiguous.

Several metrics are unclear or inconsistent: how cross-entropy is computed for the automaton-based generator; whether EOS handling aligns with language acceptance; and why some CE values increase post-hardening despite claims of improved modeling.
Clarity or presentation issues

The paper occasionally conflates recognition complexity classes (AC^0/TC^0) and generative modeling difficulty without a careful formal link; the “context dependency > circuit complexity” conclusion is plausible but largely qualitative.
Some tables/figures contain artifacts; precise definitions of “valid rate” for DFA generators (with an output matrix) would benefit from a rigorous description.
Missing related work or comparisons

Limited contextualization against formal-language benchmarks for recognizers (e.g., FLaRe) and recent theoretical results about local-vs-global attention and LTL fragments; related work is cited but not empirically connected.
No discussion of membership-query-based automata learning (e.g., Angluin-style L*) given that the method effectively uses a membership oracle (valid rate) to guide merging/model selection.
reviews.questions:
1. Does LaMFA require access to the ground-truth regex (or membership oracle) to choose K and to drive merging (Algorithm 2, Step 7)? If yes, can you provide a variant that does not use this oracle and report results to isolate what is learned purely from the LM?
2. How exactly is cross-entropy computed for LaMFA-DFA models? Is it the negative log-likelihood of evaluation strings under the PDFA defined by ω and δ? How are EOS and termination handled?
3. How sensitive are results to the number of generated samples N, the initial K, the temperature T in sharpening, and τ0? Please provide ablations and stability across random seeds.
4. Can you include baselines from prior DFA-extraction or state-merging grammar-inference methods (e.g., Weiss et al. 2018; Michalenko et al. 2019; RPNI/AALERGIA; spectral/weighted automata learning) and compare both extraction fidelity and generalization?
5. For mdY, do your “real dates” encode calendar constraints (month lengths, leap years)? If so, what is the actual minimal DFA size and why is this task classified as AC^0? If not, is the language just numeric formatting (which is trivial regular), and how should the complexity label be interpreted?
6. Several LaMFA-DFA models have more states than the minimal DFA (e.g., GPT-tiny on alter). Do these supernumerary states correspond to consistent functional distinctions (e.g., sink/refusal states), or are they clustering artifacts? Can you quantify state interpretability?
7. Could you clarify whether improvements in OOD validity (e.g., parity0 for GPT-nano to 100%) persist when oracle-guided selection is removed? Otherwise, how much of the improvement is attributable to the oracle?
reviews.assessment: The paper pursues a timely and interesting goal—bridging neural autoregressive models and symbolic automata—and presents a simple, practical pipeline that often recovers compact automata with strong OOD generalization on regular-language datasets. The qualitative insight that global dependencies pose the real challenge (more so than AC^0 vs TC^0 per se) is consistent with current theory and empirical benchmarks and is articulated clearly. However, the central methodological issue is that LaMFA appears to depend on the ground-truth regex (membership oracle) to choose hyperparameters and guide state merging, which contradicts the framing of extracting an unknown automaton purely from the trained LM and conflates interpretability with supervised grammar inference. The lack of comparisons to established DFA-extraction/state-merging/spectral baselines and the use of very small model scales further limit the strength of the empirical claims. With a truly unsupervised variant (or a precise, limited form of supervision made explicit), thorough ablations, and stronger baselines, this line of work could be impactful. In its current form, I do not recommend acceptance to ICLR.

papers.title: Leveraging Implicit Sentiments: Enhancing Reliability and Validity in Psychological Trait Evaluation of LLMs

reviews.summary: This paper proposes Core Sentiment Inventory (CSI), an IAT-inspired, bilingual (English/Chinese) instrument that implicitly measures LLMs’ sentiment tendencies by asking models to rapidly associate common, purportedly neutral words with “comedy” (positive) or “tragedy” (negative). CSI reports three aggregate metrics—Optimism, Pessimism, Neutrality—and claims to improve reliability over self-report human inventories (e.g., BFI) and to exhibit predictive validity by correlating the sentiment of model-generated stories with the proportion of positive/negative “trigger” words sampled from CSI. Experiments on six models suggest CSI reduces refusals/neutral responses and yields more consistent outcomes than BFI, while revealing cross-lingual differences in sentiment tendencies.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Extends the idea of implicit association-style evaluation from social bias to general sentiment tendencies, framing a bottom-up, LLM-native alternative to human self-report inventories.
Proposes a large-scale, bilingual inventory (5,000 items per language) intended to broaden stimulus coverage and mitigate test-fatigue issues of short questionnaires.
Attempts to avoid anthropomorphic refusal modes by reframing items as association judgments rather than self-referential personality questions.
Experimental rigor and validation
Evaluates multiple widely used models across two languages and reports consistent monotonic trends in a downstream story-generation task as the ratio of negative to positive triggers increases.
Introduces two reliability indicators (consistency and reluctance) and compares them to BFI-based evaluations across the same models.
Clarity of presentation
Motivates the need for LLM-native psychometric tools and illustrates reliability failings of naïvely administered human self-reports (e.g., refusal examples, sensitivity to prompt settings).
Provides qualitative lists of “positive” and “negative” triggers and cross-lingual analyses that make the findings interpretable to practitioners.
Significance of contributions

Addresses a timely, important gap identified by recent surveys and critiques: human psychometric instruments often lack content and construct validity when applied to LLMs; new LLM-native behavioral measures are needed.
If validated more rigorously, a robust implicit sentiment instrument could be valuable for alignment auditing, cross-lingual evaluation, and tracking drift across model versions.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The adaptation of IAT is superficial: LLMs do not have response latency, and the task is a single forced-choice labeling (“comedy/tragedy”) without IAT’s dual-class categorization or D-score computation, undermining the “implicit” claim.

Choice of “comedy vs tragedy” as valence labels is ad hoc, linguistically loaded, and potentially culture- and language-dependent; no ablation shows invariance to label synonyms (e.g., pleasant/unpleasant, positive/negative, approach/avoid).

The inventory construction contradicts its own criteria: sample lists contain many function words and pronouns (e.g., “is”, “you”, “we”, “was”), not just nouns/verbs as claimed; this calls into question the POS filtering and the assumption of “neutral headwords.”

Scoring definitions are unclear/inconsistent: Optimism/Pessimism are normalized by N = size of CSI, yet the experiments sample only 30 words per trial; it is not specified how many iterations were run, how many times each word was presented, or how unobserved items are treated. Neutrality conflates disagreement across runs with out-of-set responses (“neutral/unrelated”).
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Predictive validity is likely circular: “positive/negative” seed words are derived from the same model’s prior CSI classification, then used to elicit stories whose sentiment is scored—thus manipulating the very features previously labeled, which risks tautological confirmation rather than out-of-sample behavioral prediction.
The story sentiment is judged by a single LLM (Qwen2-72B) without human annotation, inter-rater checks, or sensitivity analyses; this threatens validity and can import model-specific biases.

The BFI baseline appears weakly instantiated. Prior work shows refusals can be largely eliminated with constrained prompts and log-prob option scoring; the paper compares CSI to an arguably naïve BFI administration where the neutral option and provider guardrails confound “reluctance.”

No statistical testing, uncertainty estimates, or robustness checks (e.g., confidence intervals, test–retest correlations, split-half reliability) are reported; temperature is fixed at 0 across studies, which inflates apparent “consistency.”

Cross-lingual comparisons may be confounded by inventory content differences rather than genuine language-conditioned behavior; no translation alignment or measurement-invariance analysis is provided.
Clarity or presentation issues

Key protocol details are missing: number of iterations, per-word exposure counts, coverage of the 5,000-item inventory, time/compute budget, and how inconsistent or out-of-option responses are reconciled across runs.
Several tables include artifacts and the narrative sometimes contradicts the design principles (e.g., nouns/verbs vs presence of pronouns/auxiliaries in top lists).
Missing related work or comparisons

The paper does not sufficiently engage with recent psychometric critiques and LLM-native pipelines showing how refusal/neutrality can be controlled in human inventories (e.g., constrained numeric response formats, log-prob scoring) and how validity should be established (e.g., 2307.00184; 2406.17675; 2502.05248; 2607.02325). This weakens the fairness of the BFI comparison and the claims of superiority.
reviews.questions:
1. How many iterations were administered per model/language, how many distinct words were actually shown, and how often was each word repeated? Please clarify how O_score/P_score/N_score are normalized if only a fraction of the 5,000 words are observed multiple times.
2. Why “comedy/tragedy” as valence labels? Did you test alternative label pairs (pleasant/unpleasant, positive/negative) and find CSI scores invariant? Please report such ablations, especially cross-lingually.
3. Your principle states nouns and verbs only, yet the top lists include pronouns and auxiliaries (“is,” “you,” “was”). Was POS filtering relaxed? If so, why, and how does including function words affect validity?
4. How is Neutral Score decomposed between (a) out-of-option responses and (b) cross-run label flips? Please provide these components separately and their reliability over runs.
5. For the story-generation validity test, are the positive/negative seeds derived from each target model’s own CSI classification (model-specific)? If so, can you provide a cross-model or predefined lexicon control to rule out circularity?
6. Why rely on a single LLM (Qwen2-72B) as the sentiment judge? Can you report inter-rater reliability against human annotations and at least one additional LLM judge, plus sensitivity to prompting of the judge?
7. How did you administer BFI? Did you try constrained numeric responses or log-prob option scoring (as in 2307.00184; 2502.05248) to mitigate refusals? If not, please add these stronger baselines to fairly assess “reluctance” and “consistency.”
8. What statistical tests and uncertainty estimates support the reported improvements (e.g., “up to 45% improvement,” “correlation > 0.85”)? Please provide per-model confidence intervals, effect sizes, and p-values.
9. For cross-lingual claims, did you evaluate measurement invariance using translation-aligned subsets of stimuli? If not, can you report whether English–Chinese differences persist on aligned word pairs?
10. Will you release the CSI word lists, code, prompts, and per-word outputs to enable replication and further validation?
reviews.assessment: This paper addresses an important and timely problem: psychometric-style evaluation of LLMs is hampered by refusals, prompt sensitivity, and weak construct validity when reusing human instruments. CSI is a promising direction—a large, bilingual, bottom-up association task that could, in principle, sidestep anthropomorphic framing and yield higher reliability. However, the current methodology and evidence are not yet sufficient for a top-tier venue. The IAT analogy is thin (no latencies or D-scores), the label choice is not justified or stress-tested, the inventory construction appears to violate its own criteria (presence of function words), the scoring protocol is under-specified relative to the claimed normalization over all 5,000 items, and the predictive validation is likely circular and judged by a single LLM without human checks. The comparison to BFI is weakened by the absence of modern constrained-response or log-prob baselines that substantially reduce refusals. Cross-lingual conclusions are potentially confounded by differences in inventory composition rather than model behavior.
