It provides general in-fill and long-span asymptotic results—consistency and a central limit theorem—for empirical estimators of expected signature coordinates under broad regularity and dependence assumptions, and introduces a simple control-variate “martingale correction” that substantially reduces estimator variance when (some components of) the latent process is a martingale. Theoretical results are complemented by examples (BM, fBm, CAR/OU, Heston) and experiments demonstrating practical gains in several signature-based learning tasks.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Provides unified L^m in-fill convergence (Theorem 2.8) for discrete expected signature estimators to their continuous-time counterparts under flexible continuity/conditional-moment conditions (Aα–Aδ), covering non-semimartingale settings (e.g., fBm with H>1/2) and irregular, sample-dependent partitions.

Establishes a long-span CLT (Theorem 2.10) under strong mixing with a clean separation of discretization and statistical error via conditions (11)–(13), and a feasible HAC-type variance estimator (Corollary 2.12).

Introduces a control-variate estimator tailored to signature coordinates that leverages martingale structure for variance reduction, with a practical estimator for the optimal coefficient c and a generalization to partial martingales.
Experimental rigor and validation

Demonstrates variance reduction and accuracy improvements in synthetic studies for option pricing under BM/Heston and in learning tasks (classification via GPES and distributional regression via SES).
Verifies assumptions on representative processes (BM, fBm, CAR/OU, Heston) and clarifies when mixing or covariance-decay conditions apply.
Clarity of presentation
Careful set-up of canonical geometric processes and signature-defining partitions, with an accessible glossary and clear decomposition of estimation error.
Good balance between main-text intuition and technical appendices (sewing-type lemmas, mixing-to-ergodicity implications, Gaussian covariance decay).
Significance of contributions

Bridges a key gap between continuous-time expected signature theory and computable discrete estimators that underpin many signature-based ML methods, offering a probabilistic interpretation and finite-sample improvements that can impact practice.
Complementary to analytical/PDE/cumulant approaches in prior work by addressing the model-free, data-driven estimation regime prevalent in ML pipelines.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Strong mixing is a relatively stringent assumption for the CLT; the paper gives a Gaussian alternative (Theorem 2.14) for consistency but not a CLT under weaker dependence (e.g., long memory), and does not treat non-mixing regimes more generally.

The martingale correction is analyzed for martingale inputs; when used as a “data transform” in non-martingale settings it introduces bias, but there is no theoretical MSE trade-off or guidance on selecting/regularizing c to control bias.
Verification of conditions (Aβ) and (Aγ) may be nontrivial outside the presented examples; more readily checkable sufficient conditions would increase applicability.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Experiments are synthetic only; no real-world datasets are reported. Some large accuracy gains (e.g., OU in GPES) lack a deeper diagnostic (bias/variance decomposition, sensitivity to partition mesh, truncation level).
The impact of estimating c (versus oracle cπ*) on asymptotics is not analyzed; finite-sample regression-based estimation can introduce additional variability and potential overfitting.
No direct comparison to analytical expected-signature computations (e.g., recent cumulant-based recursions) where available, to validate estimator bias at small mesh.
Clarity or presentation issues
A few minor typos/notation inconsistencies (e.g., hats vs. Π(N) superscripts; stray “option Checkbox”) and occasional dense passages around Assumption 2.6 and Lemma usage.
The link between truncation level, p-variation order, and practical feature computation could be stated more explicitly for practitioners.
Missing related work or comparisons

While analytical approaches (PDEs, cumulants/expected signature of semimartingales) are cited, a more explicit positioning versus log-signature/cumulant recursions (e.g., Friz–Hager–Tapia 2024) in terms of numerical estimation could help.
Recent signature-based finite-sample/block-averaging perspectives and non-asymptotic bounds are not discussed; adding a brief perspective would contextualize the asymptotic focus.
reviews.questions:
1. Can you provide theoretical MSE analyses for the martingale correction when the process is not a martingale (e.g., a bias–variance decomposition with bounds in terms of deviations from martingality), or at least a diagnostic to decide when to enable it?
2. How sensitive are your asymptotic conclusions to estimating c with the regression slope? Does √N-consistency of ĉ hold under your assumptions, and does plugging in ĉ alter the CLT for the corrected estimator?
3. Can you offer more user-friendly sufficient conditions that imply (Aβ) and (Aγ), beyond the example classes in the appendix—e.g., conditions on Markov generators or covariance kernels that practitioners can check?
4. In the pricing experiments, could you report empirical variance ratios and correlations between S^I and S_c^I to verify the predicted 1−ρ^2 variance reduction?
5. How does truncation level (and the choice of words I) affect the rates and constants in practice? Any guidance for balancing truncation error, mesh size, and sample size?
6. Could you include at least one real-data experiment (e.g., financial time series classification/regression) to illustrate robustness beyond synthetic settings?
7. For Theorem 2.14, is there a path to a CLT under covariance-decay conditions (without strong mixing), perhaps in the Gaussian case using Breuer–Major or martingale approximations tailored to signature functionals?
reviews.assessment: This paper makes a solid and timely contribution by giving a general asymptotic theory (consistency and CLT) for expected signature estimation from discrete observations, under assumptions that cover many processes of interest and realistic observation schemes. The martingale control variate is simple yet effective and, together with the asymptotics, strengthens the probabilistic footing of several signature-based ML methods. While some conditions (e.g., strong mixing) are demanding and parts of the analysis (e.g., bias control for the martingale correction in non-martingale settings) remain largely empirical, the theoretical developments are sound, the examples are representative, and the empirical section—though limited to synthetic data—demonstrates practical value. I recommend acceptance after minor revisions focused on clarifying assumption verification, analyzing the plug-in c estimator’s effect, and deepening experimental diagnostics; these would further increase the work’s impact and usability for the ICML community.

papers.title: Statistical Query Hardness of Multiclass Linear Classification with Random Classification Noise

reviews.summary: This paper studies the computational complexity of multiclass linear classification (MLC) under random classification noise (RCN) in the distribution-free PAC setting. While binary linear classification with RCN is known to admit polynomial-time SQ algorithms achieving optimal error, the authors show that for k ≥ 3 the situation changes dramatically: they prove super-polynomial Statistical Query (SQ) lower bounds for learning MLC under RCN. Concretely, they give: (i) for k = 3 and constant separation σ between diagonal and off-diagonal noise probabilities, a super-polynomial SQ lower bound for achieving opt + ε error; and (ii) for larger k and small σ, super-polynomial SQ lower bounds even for constant-factor approximation to opt or for beating the trivial random-guess baseline.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Introduces a new hardness framework for multiclass learning with RCN by coupling a carefully crafted hypothesis testing reduction with a hidden-direction distribution family that enforces moment-matching and controllable chi-squared correlation.

Key conceptual idea: exploit a row of the noise matrix being a convex combination of others to align D_y with the kth row while the conditional x|y structure encodes a hard low-correlation hidden-direction problem. This seems new in the context of multiclass RCN.
Uses and extends recent moment-matching constructions over disjoint intervals (à la G_{δ,ξ}) and adapts them to the multiclass setting to synchronize the conditional distributions across labels.
Experimental rigor and validation
Theoretical work with rigorous lower bounds via the SQ dimension framework; the reductions and bounds are well-structured and backed by clear parameters and dependencies.

Clear quantitative statements: e.g., for k = 3 with constant separation, learning to opt + ε requires d^{Ω(log^{0.98} d / ε^{1.98})} queries or very small tolerance; for larger k, hardness persists even for approximations and for beating 1 – 1/k.
Clarity of presentation

Good high-level overview and roadmap, including an intuitive explanation of how the convex combination property of H and the structure of A_i produce indistinguishability at the label marginal while hiding a direction in x.

The paper isolates the core technical steps: (i) hypothesis-testing reduction (Lemma 4.4), (ii) construction and properties of hidden-direction families (Theorem 5.3), and (iii) parameter choices for final lower bounds (Section 6).
Significance of contributions
Establishes a striking computational barrier for multiclass learning with random label noise, sharply contrasting the binary case.
Provides strong evidence that widely used SQ-compatible methods (including many gradient-descent-style and label-correction techniques) cannot efficiently solve MLC under RCN in the worst case.
Has downstream implications for the low-degree polynomial testing model, broadening the impact within theory of computation and learning.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The hardness construction critically uses that one row of H is an exact convex combination of the others. This implies the noise matrix can be singular and may be viewed as a structural restriction. It is unclear how robust the hardness is to small perturbations (approximate convex combination) or to well-conditioned, full-rank H with a lower-bounded minimum singular value.

The reduction goes through multiclass polynomial classifiers and then lifts to linear classifiers via a Veronese map; while standard, the parameter accounting between the “base” dimension and the final dimension d is intricate. The main text gives intuition but defers several details to the appendix, making it hard to verify tightness of the bounds without digging through supplements.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

As a theory paper, there are no empirical validations. While not required, a brief discussion connecting the constructions to practical regimes (e.g., typical confusion matrices in noisy multiclass data) would help contextualize the assumptions on H.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some notational inconsistencies/typos: e.g., in Theorem 6.2 the statement uses max_{i,j}(H_{ii} − H_{ij}) = ζ > 0, whereas the rest of the paper emphasizes separation via a minimum; clarifying whether min separation is bounded below would avoid confusion.
A few minor formatting artifacts and inconsistent subscripts (D_0 vs D0, D^A_{v,a} vs D_v^{A,a}), and stray text tokens (e.g., “option : [ ]”) distract from otherwise clean exposition.
Missing related work or comparisons

The discussion of prior multiclass-with-noise methods focuses on approaches that invert H; it would be useful to more explicitly articulate whether the hardness results persist, or are expected to persist, under alternative assumptions (e.g., well-conditioned H, structured D_X like isotropic log-concave marginals).
A sharper contrast with the exact binary RCN-to-realizable reduction of Kearns (1998) and why it fails for k ≥ 3 (beyond lack of known extension) could strengthen motivation.
reviews.questions:
1. How robust are your lower bounds to approximate versions of condition 1 in Definition 4.1 (i.e., if h_k is only within ℓ1 distance η of Conv(h_1, …, h_{k−1}))? Can your correlation testing reduction tolerate small deviations and still yield super-polynomial SQ lower bounds?
2. Do any of your hardness results extend to the regime where H is full-rank and well-conditioned (e.g., minimum singular value bounded below by a constant)? Or is the convex-combination dependence essential to the construction?
3. In Theorem 6.2, the statement uses max_{i,j} (H_{ii} − H_{ij}) = ζ > 0. Do you intend min separation (as elsewhere), and if so, what lower bound on min_{i≠j} (H_{ii} − H_{ij}) is guaranteed by your displayed H?
4. Could the hardness be preserved under commonly used structural assumptions on D_X (e.g., isotropic log-concave or even standard Gaussian marginals) for the original linear problem without going through polynomial lifting?
5. For k = 3 and constant separation, can you comment on whether any sub-exponential (but super-polynomial) non-SQ algorithms might circumvent your barriers, or do you expect the hardness to extend to broader models like low-degree or SoS (beyond the brief remark about low-degree)?
reviews.assessment:
This paper makes a clear and significant theoretical contribution by establishing the first super-polynomial SQ lower bounds for multiclass linear classification under random classification noise. The contrast with the tractable binary case is compelling and advances our understanding of the computational landscape of noisy multiclass learning. The construction is technically careful, leverages modern SQ techniques, and introduces a neat idea connecting the geometry of the noise matrix to indistinguishability in a hypothesis testing reduction.

The main caveat is that the hardest instances rely on a structured (indeed, row-dependent) noise matrix, raising questions about robustness to perturbations and to well-conditioned H. Clarifying these aspects and tightening some presentation points (notational consistency, separation parameter, an explicit parameter map) would further strengthen the paper. Even with these caveats, the work is novel, well-motivated, and likely to be of high interest to the ICML theory community.

papers.title: Expected Variational Inequalities

reviews.summary: This paper introduces expected variational inequalities (EVIs), a relaxation of the classical variational inequality (VI) problem in which the VI condition is required to hold in expectation under a distribution over the domain, for a family of deviation maps Φ. The authors establish general existence of approximate EVI solutions under weak regularity, pinpoint complexity barriers for rich deviation classes, and—crucially—show that when Φ is the set of linear endomorphisms, ε-approximate EVI solutions can be computed in time polynomial in the dimension and log(1/ε) via an extension of the Ellipsoid Against Hope framework. They further provide a more practical regret-minimization-based algorithm for polytopes, connect the framework to correlated equilibrium notions in games (including a refined “anonymous” variant), identify structured settings where EVIs coincide with VIs, and extend Roughgarden’s smoothness framework to derive performance guarantees for EVI solutions.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces a clean, general relaxation of VIs that unifies and extends correlated equilibrium-like notions beyond games, offering a new lever for tractability without restricting the operator class.

Leverages and extends the Ellipsoid Against Hope paradigm to the VI setting with general convex domains given by membership oracles via SEPorGER oracles, yielding poly(d, log(1/ε)) algorithms for ΦLIN.

Develops an explicit polyhedral representation of ΦLIN over polytopes (Theorem 4.3), enabling practical no-regret methods with quadratic programming updates and improving per-iteration complexity over prior work.

Proves existence of approximate EVI solutions under minimal assumptions (measurable bounded F, Lipschitz Φ), and provides structural results where EVIs coincide with VIs (e.g., quasar-concave optimization and polymatrix zero-sum settings).
Experimental rigor and validation
Rigorous theoretical development with clear complexity-theoretic lower bounds (PPAD/FIXP-hardness) delineating when EVIs remain hard, and positive algorithmic results precisely scoped to ΦLIN.
Sound use of standard tools (Brouwer, Sion, Carathéodory, LP duality) to substantiate existence, support-size bounds, and polyhedral representations.
Clarity of presentation

The paper is well-organized with a concise summary table of contributions, a self-contained overview of EAH, clear statement of oracle models, and clean formal definitions tying EVIs to game-theoretic equilibrium notions.
Intuitive interpretations of the ALCE concept and a simple illustrative figure clarifying differences with CE.
Significance of contributions
Addresses a central barrier: intractability of general VIs, by shifting the solution concept rather than restricting problem classes.
Offers practically relevant algorithms in a widely used oracle model and ties to widely influential concepts in game theory and mechanism design (CE/CCE, smoothness).
The smoothness-style guarantees for EVIs broaden the applicability of price-of-anarchy-like analyses outside standard games.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The main poly-time algorithmic advance for ΦLIN relies heavily on prior machinery (EAH and the SEPorGER framework of Daskalakis et al., 2025). While the adaptation to the VI setting is meaningful, the core algorithmic novelty is incremental.

The EAH-based algorithm, though polynomial, is known to be impractical; the proposed regret-based alternative is limited to explicitly represented polytopes and scales as O(1/ε^2) with quadratic programs that may still be heavy in large-scale settings.

The term “expected variational inequalities” risks confusion with the well-established literature on stochastic variational inequalities (SVI), where expectations are over exogenous noise rather than distributions over decision variables; this distinction is not made explicit early on.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
No empirical or computational study is provided to assess practical performance of the regret-based method or to illustrate behavior on non-game VI instances.
Limited discussion of numerical stability, conditioning, or constant factors in the poly(d, log(1/ε)) bound, which can matter greatly for EAH-based approaches.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some key ideas (e.g., the semi-separation oracle for ΦLIN with membership-only access to X) are deferred to external results; a more self-contained explanation or pseudocode sketch would improve readability.

The ALCE concept is compelling but its relationship to implementability and incentives (e.g., “spying” operations) may puzzle non-game-theory readers; the main text could benefit from a succinct formalization rather than deferring to appendices.
Missing related work or comparisons

Limited discussion of connections with ergodic/averaged-gap solution concepts widely used in VI algorithms (e.g., extragradient guarantees on averaged iterates) and how EVIs relate or differ in strength.
The relation to SVI (stochastic VI) and to “gap function minimization” paradigms is not discussed; clarifying terminological and conceptual differences would help positioning.
reviews.questions:
1. Could you explicitly contrast EVIs with the ergodic/averaged-gap guarantees commonly used in VI algorithms (e.g., extragradient), and clarify whether an ε-EVI implies bounds on the standard VI gap or Minty gap for averaged iterates?
2. The term “expected VI” may be confused with stochastic VI (SVI). Would you consider a brief positioning paragraph early on to avoid ambiguity and to compare formal problem statements?
3. For Theorem 4.1, can you provide more detail on the bit complexity and oracle call counts (in terms of d, B, R, and log(1/ε))? Are there practical preconditioning or isotropic transformations that materially reduce constants?
4. In Theorem 4.3/Corollary 4.4, what is the concrete per-iteration cost of the QP (variables/constraints counts), and how does it compare in practice to the ellipsoid-based approach on moderate-size instances?
5. Beyond games, can you provide a worked example where EVIs produce qualitatively different solutions or guarantees for a non-game VI (e.g., a simple nonmonotone operator), and discuss interpretability?
6. Does the ALCE set always form a convex set in the space of distributions? Is its marginal projection necessarily convex, and can the boundary be characterized more generally than the 2×2 example?
7. In Theorem 3.1, does the chosen δ depend on a global Lipschitz constant for all φ ∈ Φ; can the result be strengthened if Φ is compact in an appropriate function space norm?
reviews.assessment: This paper presents a compelling conceptual and technical advance: a principled relaxation of variational inequalities that retains rich expressivity while enabling polynomial-time computation for linear deviation classes over very general domains (membership-oracle access). The framework unifies and extends correlated-equilibrium-like notions beyond games, offers solid complexity delineations, and provides further structural and performance results (equivalence in structured problems, smoothness guarantees). While the core algorithmic machinery builds on prior EAH/SEPorGER work, the extension to the VI setting is nontrivial and likely to influence future research on tractable solution concepts for equilibrium and stationarity problems. The paper is clearly written and well-situated in the literature. I would recommend acceptance. Including a short empirical illustration or further elaboration on practical constants would strengthen the submission, but the theoretical contributions alone are, in my view, sufficient for ICML.

papers.title: The Role of Randomness in Stability

reviews.summary: This paper studies the intrinsic role of internal randomness in achieving strong stability guarantees in learning, specifically replicability and differential privacy (DP). The central contributions are (i) a tight weak-to-strong boosting theorem equating the number of random bits needed for better-than-1/2 replicability (certificate complexity) with the log-inverse of the best deterministic collision probability (global stability), up to a single bit; (ii) two-way reductions between differential privacy randomness complexity and global stability, including a cleaner user-level DP formulation; and (iii) an application to agnostic PAC learning showing that bounded randomness complexity is possible if and only if the Littlestone dimension is finite, with certificate complexity scaling as poly(d) + O(VC(H) log(1/α)) and sample complexity polynomial in 1/α (with an exponential-in-d factor), thereby resolving an open question on error-dependent (list-)replicability.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Theorem 2.1 gives a strikingly tight equivalence C_Glob ≤ C_Rep ≤ C_Glob + 1 and a principled amplification to ρ-replicability with an additive log(1/ρ) term, cleanly quantifying the “randomness budget” needed to strengthen deterministic stability into shared-coin replicability.

The DP results (Theorems 2.2 and 2.3) provide the first general, randomness-efficient two-way bridge between DP complexity and global stability, carefully controlling support size and leveraging distributional approximation to reduce randomness.

The agnostic PAC result connects randomness complexity to the Littlestone dimension, extending realizable-regime stability guarantees to the full agnostic setting with explicit dependence on α and identifying the right structural condition (finite Ldim) for bounded randomness complexity.
Experimental rigor and validation
Solid theoretical development with detailed proof roadmaps and careful parameter accounting, including discussions of sample/computation/randomness tradeoffs and where blowups occur.
Constructions are modular and build on known primitives (heavy-hitter extraction, DP selection, perfect generalization), with clear justifications for each reduction step.
Clarity of presentation
The paper is well-organized, motivating each definition (global stability variants, certificate complexity, DP complexity) and systematically comparing parameterized and parameter-free forms.
Technical overviews in Section 4 make the core ideas accessible, including helpful diagrams (e.g., the thresholding/rounding scheme for replicability).
Significance of contributions
Establishes a crisp foundational relationship between stability and randomness that unifies recent lines on replicability, DP complexity, and perfect generalization.
Resolves an open problem on agnostic error-dependent stability/replicability and frames a roadmap for designing randomness-efficient private/replicable learners.
Likely to influence both the theory of private/replicable learning and practical thinking about randomness budgets in privacy-preserving data analysis.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The DP-to-stability direction requires ε ≲ 1/√(T log T) and δ ≲ 1/T; while motivated via perfect generalization and often achievable, this excludes looser DP regimes and leaves open whether the dependence is inherent or an artifact of current reductions.

The agnostic PAC construction incurs exponential dependence on the Littlestone dimension in sample complexity (though improved in the heavy-hitter variant), limiting immediate practicality for high-d classes.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Some steps rely on perfect generalization as an intermediate notion; alternative pathways that bypass PG might yield cleaner or broader-parameter DP reductions and could improve constants.

Computational efficiency is not a focus; several procedures (e.g., enumerating labelings, list pruning) may be computationally heavy, and the paper does not analyze runtime or implementability in large-scale settings.
Clarity or presentation issues
The main text states the DP results informally (Theorems 2.2–2.3); given their centrality, including formal statements (with explicit parameter ranges) in the main body would aid readers.
Some notation toggles between collision-based and heavy-hitter global stability; although Appendix B proves equivalence, restating the key equivalence in the main text would reduce cognitive load.
Missing related work or comparisons

While the paper discusses related work broadly, a more explicit comparison of quantitative constants and randomness budgets with (Dixon et al., ICML’24) and (Canonne et al., ITCS’24) on canonical low-dimensional tasks would help situate the tightness of the new bounds.

The discussion of the independent concurrent work (Blonda et al., 2025) is helpful; a crisper side-by-side for the agnostic setting (assumptions, list vs heavy-hitter vs collision, dependence on VC(H) and α) would clarify the exact novelty frontier.
reviews.questions:
1. Theorem 2.1’s +1 additive gap: Do you have examples achieving C_Rep = C_Glob + 1 (i.e., showing the bound is tight up to constants), or can the +1 be removed with a refined construction?
2. Can the DP-to-stability reverse direction be proved without going through perfect generalization, potentially relaxing the ε ≲ 1/√(T log T) and δ ≲ 1/T requirements? Are there barriers (e.g., counterexamples) to such a direct route?
3. For the agnostic PAC learner, is the VC(H)·log(1/α) dependence in certificate complexity necessary? Can it be reduced to polylog(1/α) or made independent of VC(H) under additional assumptions (e.g., proper vs improper learning)?
4. What are the computational complexities (time/memory) of your constructions in Theorems 2.1–2.4? Are there polynomial-time instantiations for common classes (e.g., large-margin halfspaces, thresholds) with your stated randomness/sample bounds?
5. In Section 4.2 you rely on distributional approximation to reduce randomness (support-T distributions approximated within δ/2 using log T + log(2/δ) bits). Could you include a self-contained lemma or more details on this approximation step and how it composes with DP guarantees?
6. The discussion notes that subsampling-based DP amplification consumes Θ(T log(1/ε)) random bits. Do you see a plausible path to derandomize subsampling (e.g., via almost k-wise independence or PRGs) while preserving the statistical and privacy guarantees at O(log(T/ε)) randomness?
7. For the “heavy-hitter” improved sample complexity variant in the agnostic setting, could you include a formal theorem statement and proof sketch in the main text to highlight the improved dependence on d and β?
reviews.assessment:
This is a strong theoretical paper that makes clear, conceptually clean, and technically robust advances on a fundamental question: how much internal randomness is necessary for strong stability guarantees in learning? The tight equivalence between global stability and certificate complexity for replicability is especially elegant and will be a useful design and analysis tool. The two-way bridges to DP complexity, while parameter-laden, are carefully justified, and the user-level DP reformulation usefully distills the message into a parameter-free form. The agnostic PAC application fills a notable gap, tying bounded randomness complexity to finite Littlestone dimension with interpretable α-dependence and offering the first such bounds for important hypothesis classes.

The main limitations are quantitative rather than qualitative: reliance on PG in the DP reductions (hence relatively stringent ε, δ regimes), and exponential dependence on Ldim in agnostic learning sample complexity. Nonetheless, these are understandable given the current state of the art, the paper is transparent about them, and the results open concrete avenues for tightening. The writing is clear, the connections to related work are thoughtful, and the contributions should be of high interest to the ICML community working on stability, privacy, and reproducible learning. I recommend acceptance.

papers.title: Scaling Collapse Reveals Universal Dynamics in Compute-Optimally Trained Neural Networks

reviews.summary: This paper reports a striking empirical regularity in training dynamics: when models are trained under compute-optimal horizons, entire loss curves from different model sizes collapse onto a single universal curve after normalizing both compute and reducible loss by their final values. With learning-rate decay, this collapse becomes so tight that cross-scale variability falls below the per-model seed noise, a regime the authors call supercollapse. The paper explains (i) collapse under constant learning rate via a sum-of-power-laws scaling model and compute-optimal allocation, and (ii) collapse and supercollapse under decaying schedules via a simple stochastic-noise model that predicts schedule-dependent loss curves and a quantitative Δ ∝ √η(1 − τ̂) scaling for the collapse deviation.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Introduces the notion of supercollapse: a regime where normalized cross-scale variation of loss curves falls below the single-seed noise floor, and connects it to control-variate–like variance cancellation via final-loss normalization.
Provides a clean theoretical link between compute-optimal allocation and collapse for sum-of-power-laws loss functions; the “balance of power laws” argument is elegant and compelling.

Proposes a simple, practically usable model of SGD noise under learning-rate schedules that, despite strong approximations, accurately predicts schedule-specific loss curves with a single shared scalar α across models, schedules, and horizons.
Experimental rigor and validation

Demonstrates collapse and supercollapse across two architectures (transformers and MLPs), two tasks (CIFAR-5M next-token prediction, Lichess chess), multiple widths (roughly 10–80M parameters), and several learning-rate schedules (linear/cosine with and without holdouts).
Quantifies collapse via a clear metric Δ and compares it to a per-model noise floor σ, carefully distinguishing seed-induced variability from cross-scale differences.

Provides falsification-style tests: collapse degrades under suboptimal scaling choices (e.g., no µP parameterization or mis-specified data exponent γ), making the phenomenon a potentially sensitive diagnostic.
Clarity of presentation
The normalization choices, definitions (Δ, σ), and the role of L0 as irreducible loss are well motivated, with visualizations that make the phenomena easy to grasp.
The theory sections are modular and transparent about assumptions (quadratic approximation, slowly varying Hessian/Σ, schedule defined in normalized compute).
Significance of contributions
Suggests a joint scaling limit (model size and training horizon growing together) that preserves dynamical similarity, complementing infinite-width/depth limits that typically fix time.
If robust, supercollapse could provide a low-cost, high-sensitivity scaling diagnostic to tune exponents and parameterizations without large sweeps or many seeds.
Offers a unifying lens for loss-curve prediction across schedules, potentially informing practical schedule design and hyperparameter transfer.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The stochastic-noise model relies on a quadratic-loss approximation, slowly varying curvature/noise, and a single global α; while surprisingly predictive, this limits theoretical guarantees and may hide schedule- or data-dependent failure modes.

The compute-optimal horizon t*(p) is estimated under constant learning rate and reused for decayed schedules; although the authors cite prior work suggesting near-optimality up to constants, empirical verification that t*(p) remains near-optimal per schedule is limited.

The comparison between Δ (normalized by final stochastic loss) and σ (per-model relative fluctuation of reducible loss) blends distinct normalizations; while the control-variate interpretation is insightful, the “below noise floor” claim would be stronger with a matched normalization baseline.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Scale is modest (≤ ~80M parameters) and on proxy tasks (CIFAR-5M, character-level chess). Claims of universality would benefit from larger, more realistic language modeling setups and co-scaling ladders (width, depth, batch size, weight decay).

Seed counts are sometimes small and heterogeneous across settings; for some plots, it is unclear whether σ and Δ are averaged over sufficient seeds to robustly separate collapse from noise, especially in the decay tail where curves converge.
Sensitivity to the fitted L0 is shown qualitatively; more systematic uncertainty quantification of L0 estimation and its effect on collapse metrics would strengthen the case.
Clarity or presentation issues
The mapping from discrete steps to gradient-flow time τ and normalized τ̂ could be specified more precisely to facilitate reproduction, including how η(τ) is computed with Adam/µP preconditioning.
The derivation and role of the schedule mapping y(x) (Eq. 21) are somewhat terse; more intuition/examples would help.
Missing related work or comparisons

While many scaling-law and theory papers are cited, a more explicit empirical comparison to alternative loss-curve predictors (e.g., Tissue et al., Luo et al.) in the same settings would contextualize the benefits/limitations of the proposed model beyond qualitative overlays.

The paper could better relate to dynamical mean-field accounts of joint time–size scaling (e.g., Bordelon et al. 2024 DMFT) by clarifying where predictions concur/diverge, especially regarding late-time finite-size effects.
reviews.questions:
1. How sensitive is supercollapse to the precise estimation of t*(p)? If you recompute schedule-specific compute-optimal horizons, do the normalized curves and Δ-vs-σ comparisons change materially?
2. Could you provide quantitative error metrics (e.g., MAE/RMSE) comparing your loss-curve predictor (Eq. 18 with one α) against Tissue et al. (2024) and Luo et al. (2025) on the same runs? This would clarify the practical predictive advantage.
3. The comparison of Δ to σ mixes different normalizations (final-loss-normalized vs instantaneous). Can you report a matched-baseline σ̃ that also uses control-variate normalization within each seed (e.g., variability of L(t)/L(t*) across seeds at fixed p) to more rigorously substantiate “below noise floor”?
4. How robust is the Tr(Σ)/L ≈ h(x) universality across optimizers (e.g., AdamW vs SGD+momentum) and parameterizations (µP vs standard)? Have you tested other datasets where irreducible loss is a large fraction of total (e.g., language with limited context)?
5. Can you probe collapse under co-scaling ladders (jointly scaling width, depth, batch size, and weight decay) and report whether the same normalization still yields supercollapse? If not, what modifications are needed?
6. When you perturb γ away from optimal, can you quantify how the collapse deviation grows (e.g., as a function of |γ − γ*|) and whether this can be used to estimate γ* with confidence intervals?
7. The α parameter is global across settings. Is α interpretable in terms of batch size, curvature scale, or optimizer statistics? Can it be predicted rather than fitted?
reviews.assessment: This paper identifies and explains a compelling and practically useful regularity in training dynamics: compute-optimal training induces a universal loss-curve shape across model sizes, and learning-rate decay drives a supercollapse where cross-scale differences drop below per-seed noise due to control-variate cancellation. The theoretical components are simple yet insightful (power-law balance; noise model leading to Δ ∝ √η(1 − τ̂)), and the empirical evidence—though at modest scales and on proxy datasets—is careful, quantitative, and includes informative ablations that demonstrate diagnostic value. The main reservations are the limited scale/scope of experiments, reliance on a fitted α and on constant-LR t*(p) across schedules, and the normalization choices in the Δ vs σ comparison. Nonetheless, the work is novel, thought-provoking, and likely to influence both practical scaling diagnostics and future theory on joint scaling limits. I lean positive and recommend acceptance after minor clarifications and, where feasible, small additional analyses to strengthen the statistical and comparative claims.

papers.title: Cross-environment Cooperation Enables Zero-shot Multi-agent Coordination

reviews.summary: This paper studies zero-shot coordination (ZSC) in cooperative multi-agent RL by proposing Cross-Environment Cooperation (CEC): training a single policy in self-play across a large distribution of procedurally generated environments, rather than against a population of diverse partners on a single task. The authors provide a fast JAX-based procedural generator for Overcooked (and a toy Dual Destination game) and show that CEC improves generalization to novel partners and novel environments, outperforming population-based training (FCP) and a recent strong SP baseline (E3T) in simulation and yielding better subjective human ratings, while achieving competitive human-AI performance without human data.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Reframes the ZSC axis from partner-diversity to environment-diversity, with a clear training objective and a principled isolation of factors via self-play.
Introduces scalable, high-throughput JAX implementations for procedural Overcooked and a toy benchmark expressly designed to disentangle partner vs. environment diversity effects.
Applies empirical game-theoretic analysis to cross-algorithm interaction, offering a richer view of equilibria and attractors in the ZSC meta-game.
Experimental rigor and validation

Extensive evaluation includes: toy gridworld (fully/partially observable and multi-task variants), Overcooked with 5 standard layouts and 100 procedurally generated held-out levels, cross-algorithm ad-hoc teamplay, and human studies with 80 participants.
Clear compute parity (3B steps) across methods and ablation on fine-tuning (CEC-FT) highlight the generalization-specialization trade-off.
Clarity of presentation
Core hypothesis is stated early and consistently tested across increasing complexity.
Figures effectively convey key results (e.g., failures of PBT to generalize beyond a single layout, CEC’s success on novel levels, human preference patterns).
Significance of contributions
Demonstrates that training on diverse environments can yield emergent cooperative norms that transfer across partners, including humans, without human data.
Provides tools and datasets (procedural generators) likely to be valuable for future ZSC research.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Potential inconsistency regarding whether the five original Overcooked layouts (their wall structures) are fully held out from CEC training: the main text claims holdout, while Appendix A.1 suggests sampling from those base predicates and only avoiding exact duplicates via object placement checks.

Limited exploration of how CEC performs with partners trained by substantially different algorithms beyond the provided baselines; ad-hoc teamplay is touched on but could be deeper (e.g., LLM-derived partners, rule-based policies).
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Human-subjects analysis uses multiple t-tests but does not report mixed-effects models or corrections for multiple comparisons despite repeated-measures and multiple metrics; order and learning effects may confound results.

Baseline failure (near-zero reward) on 100 held-out layouts for FCP/E3T seems stark; more diagnostic analysis (e.g., partial credit metrics, success breakdowns per layout type) would strengthen the claim that environment diversity—not other factors—drives the gap.

Combining partner and environment diversity is only tested with E3T-in-CEC and performs poorly; broader combinations (e.g., PBT over environment distributions, OP-style symmetry breaking with environment diversity) are not explored.
Clarity or presentation issues
XP reward scaling and normalization across tasks/layouts are not fully specified in the main text, making cross-task comparisons harder to interpret.

Some training and architectural details (e.g., observation encodings, reward shaping, hyperparameters, exact number of seeds per matrix entry) are deferred to the appendix; the main text would benefit from a concise summary.
Missing related work or comparisons

While “Other-Play” and UED are cited, more direct empirical comparisons to OP-like symmetry-breaking or population-based methods trained with environment randomization would help position CEC’s advantage.

Additional discussion of recent multi-agent open-ended training and diagnostics (e.g., MAESTRO variants, open-ended MARL evaluations) as potentially complementary would contextualize the findings further.
reviews.questions:
1. Please clarify the holdout protocol: were the five original Overcooked wall layouts entirely excluded from CEC training, or were those wall predicates used with randomized object placements and only exact duplicates held out? Appendix A.1 seems to conflict with statements in the main text.
2. How is XP reward normalized across tasks/layouts in Figures 6–7? Are scores directly comparable across different layouts and between the five originals and the 100 procedural tasks?
3. For human studies, did you use a within-subjects mixed-effects model or corrections for multiple comparisons across the seven subjective metrics? How were order and learning effects handled beyond randomization?
4. Can you provide diagnostics explaining why FCP and E3T achieve near-zero reward on the 100 procedural tasks (e.g., per-layout breakdowns, failure modes, qualitative examples)?
5. Have you tried PBT or OP-like symmetry-breaking combined with environment diversity (e.g., populations trained across a distribution of environments)? If so, how do they compare to CEC?
6. Beyond IPPO/E3T/FCP partners, did you evaluate ad-hoc teamplay against qualitatively different partner classes (e.g., scripted/heuristic or LLM-based policies)? If not, do you anticipate similar gains?
7. How sensitive is CEC to the breadth of environment diversity? Are there diminishing returns or thresholds (e.g., number of predicates, object multiplicity) for achieving robust ZSC?
reviews.assessment:
This paper presents a compelling and timely perspective: environment diversity can be more effective than partner diversity for achieving zero-shot coordination in cooperative MARL. The contribution is practically useful (fast procedural Overcooked generator), empirically thorough (toy to human studies), and conceptually clean (self-play with many tasks induces general norms). The human findings—lower collisions, higher subjective cooperation—even when reward lags a strong single-task baseline, are particularly meaningful for human compatibility.

I do have reservations about the precise holdout protocol for the five standard layouts, the limited exploration of combining partner and environment diversity, and the statistical treatment in the human study. Addressing these would strengthen confidence in the claims. Nonetheless, the core message is well supported by multiple experiments, the tools are likely to be valuable to the community, and the result challenges a prevalent assumption about the insufficiency of self-play for ZSC. I recommend acceptance, with revisions to clarify the holdout inconsistency, expand methodological details, and refine the human-subjects analysis.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models

reviews.summary: This paper investigates the quality of representations across layers of large language models (LLMs) and related architectures. It proposes a unified framework that connects information-theoretic (matrix-based entropy), geometric (curvature, effective rank), and augmentation-invariance (InfoNCE, LiDAR, DiME) metrics via the Gram matrix of hidden states, and uses these tools to analyze layer-wise behavior. Empirically, the authors report that intermediate layers often yield better embeddings than final layers on 32 MTEB tasks across multiple architectures (decoder-only transformers, encoder-only transformers, and state-space models), and provide analyses of architectural differences, training dynamics, finetuning (including CoT), extreme input conditions, and extension to vision models.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
The unifying lens around matrix-based entropy to connect compression, geometry (effective rank/anisotropy/curvature), and augmentation-invariance is conceptually appealing and practically useful.

The cross-architecture, cross-modality framing (transformers, SSMs, vision models) highlights objective-driven commonalities (e.g., autoregressive mid-layer bottleneck), which is a valuable synthesis.
The paper operationalizes the framework to produce actionable tools (e.g., unsupervised layer selection via DiME/InfoNCE/entropy) with demonstrated gains, which is practically impactful.
Experimental rigor and validation
Broad empirical sweep: multiple model families (decoder-only, encoder-only, SSM), sizes (from ~10M to ~1B for Pythia), and 32 MTEB tasks, plus vision models (ViT, CLIP, BEIT, DINOv2, MAE, AIM/AIMv2).
Multiple complementary metrics (entropy, curvature, InfoNCE/LiDAR/DiME) are correlated with downstream performance, and the correlations appear robust across measures (dCor, Spearman, Kendall).
Analyses beyond static snapshots: training progression, finetuning effects (LLM2Vec; CoT), sub-layer analyses of transformer blocks, and stress tests with extreme inputs.
Clarity of presentation

The narrative is coherent: it motivates the question, introduces a unified framework, and then uses it to interpret consistent empirical phenomena (intermediate layer “sweet spots,” autoregressive bottlenecks).
The figures (as described) are informative and support the main claims; key takeaways are highlighted at the start of sections for readability.
Significance of contributions

Clear relevance to the LLM community: if intermediate layers systematically outperform final layers for embeddings, this changes prevailing practice in representation extraction and diagnostic tooling.
The framework could guide model diagnostics, efficient inference (layer selection), and architecture/learning-objective design in both language and vision.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Some theoretical claims and proofs are either informal or appear flawed. For instance, the “Effective Rank ≤ exp(S1(Z))” proof normalizes σ and λ in a way that breaks the elementwise inequality used to argue majorization, casting doubt on the stated bound as written.

The connection “I(X;Z) ≤ H(Z)” where H is a matrix-based entropy on linear-kernel Gram matrices is asserted but not rigorously justified relative to Shannon/von Neumann entropy; this risks conflating surrogate quantities with information-theoretic ones without conditions.
The dataset-entropy scaling theorem is explicitly “informal,” with no proof sketch or assumptions, leaving unclear when/how it holds.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Insufficient detail on how sentence/prompt embeddings are constructed from layer-wise hidden states for different architectures (pooling strategy, normalization/whitening, token selection for decoder-only LMs), which can materially affect MTEB outcomes and reproducibility.

The augmentation choices (character-level perturbations) may interact unpredictably with subword tokenization; the semantic invariance assumptions underlying InfoNCE/LiDAR/DiME could thus be violated, potentially biasing invariance conclusions.
Claims of “consistency across architectures and tasks” would benefit from per-task/per-dataset breakdowns and significance testing; showing only averages can hide variation or outliers.
The vision section mentions “attention probing” on ImageNet-1k but does not define the protocol, metrics, or evaluation details; comparability to standard linear-probe setups is unclear.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some notational inconsistencies (K vs Kz, ZZ^T vs Z^T Z), occasional typographical slips, and mixing of theorem numbering reduce precision.
The sub-layer residual analysis is intriguing but under-specified (exact points of measurement; role of LayerNorm/residual scaling; controls).
Missing related work or comparisons

The empirical comparisons omit widely used embedding baselines and pooling strategies (e.g., SimCSE, E5/GTE, modern instruction-tuned encoders), and do not discuss whitening/postprocessing (common in MTEB pipelines).
While anisotropy/intrinsic dimension works are cited, a more direct empirical alignment or contrast with those metrics (beyond brief mention) would strengthen the “unified” claim.
reviews.questions:
1. How exactly are sentence/prompt embeddings constructed from layer-wise hidden states for each architecture (decoder-only, encoder-only, SSM)? Please specify pooling (CLS/mean/last-token), normalization/whitening, and any postprocessing used before MTEB evaluation.
2. Can you provide per-task (not just averaged) MTEB results and statistical significance analyses to substantiate “intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers,” and report how often the best intermediate layer beats the final layer across tasks?
3. For the augmentation metrics, how sensitive are findings to tokenization artifacts from character-level perturbations? Could you add word-level paraphrase/back-translation augmentations to better capture semantic invariance and report their correlations?
4. In Theorem 1, the majorization argument appears to rely on an elementwise inequality that does not hold after the normalization to unit sum. Can you provide a corrected proof or restate the claim with appropriate conditions?
5. For the bound “I(X;Z) ≤ H(Z)” with H as matrix-based entropy, what exact entropy notion is being used (Shannon, von Neumann, kernel entropy)? Under what assumptions does this inequality hold, and how does the linear kernel choice affect its validity?
6. In the vision experiments, what is the “attention probing” protocol on ImageNet-1k (feature extraction point, classifier, training/validation splits, hyperparameters), and how does it compare to a standard linear probe?
7. In the residual sub-layer analysis, where precisely is entropy measured within a block (pre/post-attention, pre/post-MLP, before/after residual merges, LayerNorm variants), and what controls were run to isolate residual connections from normalization/scaling effects?
reviews.assessment:
This paper offers a timely and practically relevant study of layer-wise representations, with a unifying perspective that ties together compression, geometry, and invariance via matrix-based entropy and the Gram matrix. Empirically, it delivers broad and consistent evidence that intermediate layers often yield stronger embeddings than final layers across architectures and even modalities, and it proposes a simple unsupervised layer selection heuristic with measurable gains. These contributions are valuable for the ICML community.

However, the theoretical parts contain issues that require correction or clearer conditions (notably the effective-rank bound and the MI/entropy relationships), and several experimental details are underspecified, limiting reproducibility and interpretability (pooling/postprocessing for embeddings, augmentation semantics under tokenization, per-task breakdowns, and exact vision probing protocols). The work’s novelty is more in synthesis and scope than in new theory; strengthening rigor and clarity would elevate the contribution.

On balance, I view this as a strong empirical synthesis with immediate practical utility and an appealing conceptual framework. With revisions addressing the theoretical gaps and methodological details, it would be a solid contribution. I lean toward a weak accept.

papers.title: The dark side of the forces: assessing non-conservative force models for atomistic machine learning

reviews.summary: This paper investigates the consequences of using non-conservative (directly predicted) force models in atomistic machine learning, contrasting them with conservative models whose forces are exact energy gradients. The authors provide theoretical analysis and extensive empirical evidence that non-conservative force fields can cause ill-defined geometry optimization, severe energy drifts and thermostat-dependent artifacts in molecular dynamics, thereby compromising both equilibrium and dynamical observables. They propose a practical hybrid strategy: pre-train on direct forces for efficiency, fine-tune an energy head to recover conservative forces, and use multiple time stepping to combine fast direct forces with occasional conservative corrections, achieving near-conservative accuracy at substantially reduced computational cost.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Introduces a clear diagnostic for non-conservativity via the antisymmetric component of the force Jacobian and analyzes its distance-resolved behavior (pairwise λ_ij), providing novel insights into how non-conservative errors grow with interaction range.

Offers a theoretically grounded critique of using direct force prediction in MD by connecting lack of a Hamiltonian to loss of symplectic structure and equipartition, and by discussing limitations of thermostatting.

Proposes and validates a pragmatic hybrid approach: pre-train with direct forces, conservative fine-tuning of an energy head, and multiple time stepping (MTS) with conservative corrections, which is both conceptually clean and easy to adopt.
Experimental rigor and validation

Systematic evaluation across NVE and NVT MD, including temperature drift, species-resolved kinetic temperatures, velocity–velocity spectra, and thermostat sensitivities (local vs global), with clear demonstrations of failure modes.
Includes geometry optimization tests (FIRE, L-BFGS) and reveals instability/flaky convergence induced by non-conservative forces.

Compares custom models (PET/PET-NC/PET-M) and reports accuracy trade-offs; touches on general-purpose models (e.g., ORB, Equiformer) with complementary appendix results and makes code/data available for reproducibility.
Clarity of presentation
The narrative effectively blends theory (integrability/Jacobian symmetry) with concrete MD pathologies and diagnostic procedures, offering actionable guidance.
Clear, interpretable figures (e.g., temperature drift, velocity spectra, training curves) that connect the theory to observed artifacts.
Significance of contributions
Addresses a pressing question in the MLIP community about the safety and practicality of non-conservative force models at scale.

Provides a credible path forward (hybrid/MTS plus conservative fine-tuning) that preserves most of the speed advantages while avoiding unphysical behavior, directly informing best practices for universal/foundation MLIPs.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The λ metric requires Jacobian evaluation, which can be computationally prohibitive; while the paper notes this, more scalable approximations (e.g., stochastic Jacobian–vector products, curl estimators) are not explored experimentally.

Stress predictions and constant-pressure dynamics are only discussed in appendices; the main text focuses heavily on forces and constant-T/V ensembles, leaving limited space for cell DOFs where non-conservativity in stress can be equally consequential.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

The primary in-depth case study is liquid water; while appendices broaden the scope, main-text generalization to diverse chemistries (metals, ionic solids, organics) is limited. Some head-to-head comparisons (e.g., ORB on water) are acknowledged as unfair due to dataset mismatch.

Quantitative wall-clock benchmarks of the proposed MTS hybrid vs pure direct vs pure conservative inference are discussed only qualitatively in the main text; precise throughput measurements and scaling on representative hardware would strengthen the practical claim.
Geometry optimization results emphasize molecular snapshots; a broader evaluation (e.g., crystal relaxations, NEB barrier finding) would underscore the generality of the stated failure modes.
Clarity or presentation issues

Certain key implementation details (thermostat parameters, integration time steps, model sizes) are dispersed across the text/appendices; a consolidated experimental setup table in the main text would aid reproducibility.

The interplay between direct-force architectural choices (cutoff, message-passing depth) and observed non-conservativity is insightful but could benefit from a more explicit ablation taxonomy in the main text.
Missing related work or comparisons

There is limited discussion of alternative integrability-promoting strategies (e.g., conservative regularizers; Helmholtz–Hodge projections to enforce curl-free fields; data-driven penalties using stochastic Jacobian approximations) and how they fare in cost/benefit terms.

Given emerging benchmarks on phonons and experimental MD stability (e.g., recent studies showing disconnects between stability, higher-order derivatives, and elastic/phonon properties), a tighter synthesis with those findings in the main text would further contextualize the conclusions.
reviews.questions:
1. How is λ (the Jacobian antisymmetry metric) computed in practice for larger systems—full Jacobians via AD, finite differences, or stochastic JVPs/VJPs? What is the wall-clock cost, and could you recommend a feasible protocol (frequency, subset of atoms) for production diagnostics?
2. Can you provide quantitative wall-clock throughput comparisons (atoms/second, memory) for direct, conservative, and MTS(M=8, M=16, etc.) runs across a few representative systems and hardware, to substantiate the claimed ≈20% overhead?
3. How robust is the hybrid MTS scheme across different timesteps, system sizes/densities, and materials classes (e.g., metals with electrons smeared in reference data, ionic solids)? Is there a principled way to choose M given a model’s measured λ or observed NVE drift?
4. Did you experiment with lightweight integrability-promoting regularizers (e.g., stochastic curl penalties, contrastive matching between conservative and direct heads, or Helmholtz projections over random loops) that avoid computing full Jacobians? If so, what was their efficacy/cost?
5. For geometry optimization, could you report results on crystalline relaxations and NEB saddle searches with non-conservative vs hybrid vs conservative models, including failure modes and stopping-criterion ambiguities?
6. Beyond water, which systems in the appendices most clearly illustrate the stress/enthalpy drift issues in NPT with direct-stress heads, and how well does MTS mitigate those in practice?
7. Given that direct-force models may require larger receptive fields, do you see a path where architectural changes (e.g., extended-range interactions, learned long-range terms) can reduce non-conservativity artifacts without resorting to conservative differentiation?
reviews.assessment: This manuscript makes a timely, careful, and practically important contribution by dissecting the “dark side” of non-conservative force prediction in MLIPs. The combination of rigorous theoretical framing, persuasive empirical demonstrations of MD/optimization failures, and a pragmatic hybrid remedy will be valuable to both researchers and practitioners deploying universal/foundation interatomic potentials. While the main text centers on a water case study and some practical details are deferred to appendices, the conclusions are consistent with emerging evidence across multiple recent benchmarks and papers. I recommend acceptance after minor revisions that strengthen generality and practical guidance: (i) include concise, quantitative throughput/memory numbers for direct vs conservative vs MTS; (ii) surface a broader-material summary from the appendices; and (iii) expand the discussion of alternative integrability-promoting strategies and cost-aware diagnostics. Overall, this work is well-positioned to influence community best practices on training targets, MD validation protocols, and deployment recipes for fast yet physically faithful simulations.

papers.title: Stochastic Smoothed Primal-Dual Algorithms for Nonconvex Optimization with Linear Inequality Constraints

reviews.summary: The paper proposes single-loop stochastic smoothed primal-dual algorithms for nonconvex optimization with linear inequality constraints (via a standard slack-variable reformulation), focusing on the linearly constrained, polyhedral-feasible-set setting. The core idea is to view a single projected SGD step on a linearized proximal augmented Lagrangian as an inexact gradient step on the Moreau envelope of the constrained objective; this allows one-sample stochastic gradients, constant penalty parameters, and non-negligible dual updates. The authors establish O(ε⁻⁴) sample and iteration complexity under standard bounded-variance stochastic gradients and improve to O(ε⁻³) with a STORM-style variance-reduction scheme under expected-smoothness assumptions; they also extend to stochastic linear constraints via a safeguarded dual update.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The analysis frames a linearized proximal ALM step as an inexact gradient step on the Moreau envelope of the constrained problem, enabling single-sample stochastic updates with constant penalty and substantive dual steps—departing from penalty-style analyses with negligible dual updates.

The potential function built from the Moreau envelope of the proximal AL and the constrained objective’s Moreau envelope is carefully constructed to handle the stochastic single-sample setting on polyhedral sets without bounded-domain assumptions (in the deterministic-constraints case).

The extension to stochastic constraints incorporates a safeguarding mechanism and constraint qualifications to control dual growth, which, while classical, is nontrivial to analyze within this framework.
Experimental rigor and validation

While primarily theoretical, the results include sharp complexity bounds: O(ε⁻⁴) with bounded-variance gradients and O(ε⁻³) with expected smoothness and STORM; both are optimal in their respective oracle models even for unconstrained problems.

The proof techniques combine recent stochastic proximal analysis (Davis–Drusvyatskiy) with global error bounds for polyhedral constraints and a refined handling of the proximal center update, showing good awareness of technical pitfalls (e.g., variance terms, z-updates).
Clarity of presentation
The problem setup, algorithms, and assumptions are clearly stated. The two interpretations (linearized proximal ALM vs. inexact GD on the Moreau envelope) aid intuition.
A detailed proof sketch is provided, isolating the main lemmas and their roles in the descent analysis; parameter orders are given in the main text, with explicit constants delegated to the appendix.
Significance of contributions
Advances the state of the art for stochastic ALM in nonconvex settings with polyhedral constraints, closing a gap left by prior work limited to X = Rⁿ.
Achieves optimal sample complexity under standard (weaker) stochastic assumptions without expected-smoothness, and matches best-known O(ε⁻³) rates under expected-smoothness with variance reduction.
The framework can serve as a building block for constrained training scenarios in ML where linear (in)equality constraints arise naturally.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The post-processing step to convert near-stationarity to ε-stationarity requires a one-shot large batch of size Θ(ε⁻²); while it does not change asymptotic complexity, it may be significant in practice and relies on knowledge of Lipschitz constants for stepsize choices.

The stochastic-constraints extension requires compactness of X, a Slater-type CQ, full row-rank, and explicit dual safeguarding with a threshold M_y that may be hard to set; resetting the dual to zero, while analyzable, can be algorithmically brittle.
Parameter choices depend on problem constants (L_f, ∥A∥, σ), which may be unknown; no adaptive or linesearch variants are given.

The inequality-constraint handling via slack variables increases dimensionality and may worsen conditioning; there is no discussion of practical preconditioning or alternative treatments (e.g., direct handling of inequalities via projections).
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
No empirical evaluation is provided to corroborate the predicted gains from non-negligible dual steps or to illustrate numerical stability versus penalty methods.
Practical performance relative to prior single-loop penalty methods or variance-reduced baselines is not demonstrated.
Clarity or presentation issues

Minor typographical artifacts (e.g., corrupted symbols in Table 1) and occasional notational overload (multiple Moreau envelopes and proximal points) could be streamlined; a high-level roadmap for the potential function would further aid readability.

The relationship between the bounds on Ax*(y,z)−b (proximal subproblem solution) and feasibility of the actually returned iterate x̂ could be emphasized earlier, with a succinct proposition in the main text.
Missing related work or comparisons

While the paper surveys ALM/penalty literature well, it would benefit from a brief discussion contrasting with recent single-loop stochastic constrained methods beyond ALM (e.g., projection-free or mirror-prox-based variants) and clarifying when projections onto polyhedral X remain efficient in high dimensions.
reviews.questions:
1. How sensitive is the algorithm to misspecification of L_f, ∥A∥, and σ in stepsize choices? Can you design or analyze adaptive variants (e.g., residual-based tuning, linesearch) that preserve rates?
2. In the post-processing step to obtain ε-stationarity, can the batch size be reduced via a multi-step small-batch scheme without worsening the total complexity, or via a variance-reduced estimator?
3. For the stochastic-constraints case, how robust is the dual reset to zero in practice? Could milder safeguarding (e.g., projection onto a ball, adaptive clipping) be analyzed without changing rates?
4. The feasibility guarantee in Lemma 3.6 involves Ax*(y_{t+1}, z_t) − b. Can you clarify, in the main text, how this translates to feasibility of the returned iterate x̂ and whether a bound on ∥Ax̂ − b∥ ≤ ε holds directly?
5. Do the constants in the complexity bounds depend unfavorably on the conditioning induced by the slack-variable reformulation for inequalities? Are there alternatives (e.g., handling t ≤ 0 via projections onto half-spaces) that avoid potential ill-conditioning?
6. Can the framework be extended to inequality constraints without slack variables by directly incorporating indicator functions and projections (e.g., via proximal steps for I_{t≤0}) while retaining single-sample updates and rates?
7. Would small-scale numerical experiments (e.g., QPs, constrained regression, or simple NN training with linear constraints) be feasible to illustrate stability and the advantage of non-negligible dual updates?
reviews.assessment: This paper makes a solid theoretical contribution to stochastic nonconvex optimization with linear constraints by delivering single-loop ALM-type methods that work with constant penalty parameters and substantive dual steps and achieve optimal sample complexities under standard oracle models. The integration of a Moreau envelope viewpoint with a linearized proximal AL step is insightful and technically well-executed, addressing an open gap for polyhedral feasible sets beyond prior work limited to unconstrained domains. The extension with variance reduction is natural and attains the known optimal O(ε⁻³) rate under expected smoothness. The main limitations are practical: parameter dependence on problem constants, reliance on a one-shot large-batch post-processing step, and stringent assumptions and safeguarding for stochastic constraints. The absence of empirical evidence is also a missed opportunity. Overall, the work is timely, rigorous, and of clear interest to the ICML community; I recommend acceptance.

papers.title: Temporal Difference Flows

reviews.summary: This paper introduces Temporal Difference Flows (TD-Flow), a family of methods for learning Geometric Horizon Models (GHMs) of the discounted successor measure using flow matching and diffusion. The core contribution is a Bellman equation over probability paths and a TD^2 learning objective that bootstraps both in sampling and in the regression target, yielding provable convergence and significantly reduced gradient variance. Extensive experiments across 22 DeepMind Control tasks show that TD^2 variants achieve accurate long-horizon predictions (up to 5x longer than prior methods), improve value estimation, and enable stronger planning via Generalized Policy Improvement when combined with policy-conditioned GHMs.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces a Bellman-style operator on probability paths B_t^π and proves it is a γ-contraction in W_1, implying convergence of the learned path to the Monte Carlo conditional path fixed point.
Proposes TD^2-CFM (and TD^2-DD) that bootstrap from the previous model in both sampling and regression targets, rigorously analyzed to reduce gradient variance relative to TD-CFM and Coupled TD-CFM.
Extends the framework from flows to diffusion, including a mixture-of-diffusions result, providing a unifying view across iterative generative models for GHMs.
Clear identification and analysis of “computational variance” as distinct from data-induced variance, with precise dependence on γ.
Experimental rigor and validation
Broad empirical study on 22 tasks from 4 domains with multiple metrics: Earth Mover’s Distance, (normalized) NLL for models with tractable likelihood, and value-function MSE.
Horizon scaling study up to effective horizon 100 (γ=0.99) supports the variance theory: TD^2 methods remain stable while alternatives deteriorate sharply.
Ablations on conditional path geometry (straight vs curved) validate theoretical predictions: TD^2 is robust, while Coupled TD-CFM degrades with curved paths.
Downstream utility demonstrated via policy-conditioned GHMs and GPI, showing consistent 25–35% improvements over FB policies across sampling strategies.
Clarity of presentation
Method variants (TD-CFM, Coupled TD-CFM, TD^2-CFM) are well-motivated and visually summarized, helping the reader understand the coupling and bootstrapping differences.
Theoretical statements are clearly separated and assumptions are stated, with proofs deferred appropriately to the appendix.
Significance of contributions
Addresses a central obstacle in long-horizon generative modeling—training instability and compounding errors—via a principled TD-based framework that scales GHM horizons well beyond prior practice.
Demonstrates practical gains in value estimation and planning when composed with behavior foundation models, making the work impactful for model-based RL and offline RL.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns
Convergence guarantees rely on exact minimization of the (conditional) flow/diffusion loss each iteration; no finite-sample or function-approximation error analysis is provided.
The contraction analysis targets the path operator B_t^π and shows convergence to the MC-CFM path; the implications for the induced likelihood or finite-time bias are not quantified.
Computational cost is nontrivial: training with 3M–8M steps and bootstrapped ODE/DDIM sampling (albeit with few steps) may limit practicality in larger-scale or real-time settings.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Baselines omit recent off-policy GHM methods that use n-step mixtures (e.g., Wiltzer et al. 2024b) or other stabilized TD-style successors; a direct empirical comparison would strengthen claims.
Architectural parity: flows/diffusions use UNet-style architectures, while GAN/VAE use MLPs; although capacity matching is stated, this still leaves potential confounds in representational power.
Computational resource reporting (GPU hours, memory footprint) and ablations on solver steps (e.g., ODE steps, DDIM steps) are missing; these would clarify efficiency/accuracy trade-offs.
Evaluation focuses on continuous-control DMC; the generality to discrete or visually rich domains is not explored.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some notation is overloaded or inconsistently rendered (e.g., occasional hats/tilde on v and m; time indexing in diffusion section; occasional equation number mismatches).
“Normalized NLL” is not defined in the main text; negative values appear in tables, which may be confusing without a clear normalization convention.
Missing related work or comparisons

While related work is generally thorough, a more explicit empirical/analytic comparison to n-step bootstrapping GHMs and recent “Bellman diffusion” approaches (beyond acknowledging Schramm & Boularias, 2024) would further contextualize novelty and practical gains.
No comparison to rollout-based world models for value estimation (e.g., Dreamer variants) to show benefits/tradeoffs of GHMs for long-horizon evaluation, even if only as a reference point.
reviews.questions:
1. What is the precise definition and normalization used for “normalized NLL,” and why do some entries become negative? Could you include a short derivation or reference in the main text?
2. Can you report training and inference compute (GPU hours, memory), and ablate ODE steps and DDIM steps to quantify accuracy/efficiency trade-offs for TD^2-CFM and TD^2-DD?
3. How sensitive are the results to the choice of p0 and to the path schedule (e.g., different α_t, β_t beyond the two explored)? Is there a principled way to select a curved path that consistently benefits TD^2-CFM?
4. To what extent does off-policy dataset coverage affect the learned successor measure and downstream value estimation? Did you explore importance weighting or conservative objectives when coverage is poor?
5. Do you observe practical differences between TD^2-CFM and Coupled TD-CFM in finite-sample regimes beyond straight vs curved paths (e.g., stability, speed of convergence, robustness to network capacity)?
6. Could you compare against the n-step mixture approach for GHMs (Wiltzer et al., 2024b) empirically, and discuss relative pros/cons (e.g., bias-variance, off-policy applicability)?
7. Have you tested TD^2 methods on discrete or high-dimensional observation spaces (e.g., pixel-based control), and do the conclusions about variance and stability persist?
8. For planning with GPI, did you examine calibration of Q estimates induced by GHMs (e.g., via reliability diagrams), and how does calibration relate to the observed improvements over FB?
reviews.assessment: This work makes a compelling and well-substantiated contribution to long-horizon generative modeling in RL. The TD^2 formulation, grounded in a Bellman operator on probability paths and accompanied by a clear variance reduction analysis, is both elegant and practically consequential. The empirical evaluation is broad and supports the core claims: TD^2 methods deliver accurate GHMs at substantially longer horizons, improve value estimation, and enable effective planning when composed with policy-conditioned representations. While some experimental comparisons and computational reporting could be strengthened, and finite-sample theory is absent, the overall package is strong. I recommend acceptance at ICML; the ideas are novel, the analysis insightful, and the practical gains are significant for the community interested in model-based RL, off-policy evaluation, and planning.

papers.title: Masked Autoencoders Are Effective Tokenizers for Diffusion Models

reviews.summary: This paper studies what makes an effective latent space for latent diffusion models and argues that “structured” latent spaces with fewer effective mixture modes and more discriminative features ease diffusion training and improve image quality. It proposes MAE-Tok, a plain autoencoder trained with masked modeling and auxiliary shallow decoders to predict multi-level targets (pixels, HOG, DINOv2, CLIP, optional text BPE), followed by decoder-only fine-tuning to recover reconstruction fidelity. Empirically, MAE-Tok enables strong ImageNet 256×256 and 512×512 conditional generation with only 128 latent tokens, achieving competitive or SOTA gFID/IS and large speedups in training and inference; theoretically, the paper connects latent-mode complexity to diffusion sample complexity via existing results on GMMs.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Introduces a simple yet effective recipe to train continuous tokenizers: masked AE training with auxiliary decoders for multi-target reconstruction plus decoder-only fine-tuning, clearly decoupling “discriminative latent space” learning from “pixel fidelity.”

Provides a unifying perspective that connects latent mode structure to diffusion training difficulty; the use of GMM-fitting diagnostics and LP-vs-gFID correlation offers a practical lens to analyze tokenizers.
