Uses 1D latent token design with learnable tokens for aggressive compression (128 tokens) at both 256 and 512 resolutions, simplifying the generative backbone’s workload.
Experimental rigor and validation

Comprehensive ablations on masking, auxiliary target choice, mask ratio, and auxiliary decoder depth; includes linear probing, GMM-fitting NLL trends, UMAP visualizations, convergence comparisons, and unconditional generation metrics.
Strong system-level comparisons at both 256×256 and 512×512 ImageNet, with and without CFG, against a wide set of autoregressive and diffusion baselines.
Clear measurements of efficiency (e.g., FLOPs, throughput) and training-speed gains attributable to reduced token counts.
Clarity of presentation
The motivation, method, and training schedule (mask modeling + decoder FT) are explained cleanly with a helpful architecture diagram and consistent notation.
Results are presented in a reproducible manner, with code release promised and many training details relegated to appendices.
Significance of contributions
Demonstrates that well-structured continuous latents can match or surpass RA-VAE/VAE-based pipelines for conditional ImageNet, using dramatically fewer tokens.
If broadly validated, the insight that latent structure (vs. variational constraints) is the key driver for diffusion performance may influence tokenizer design across modalities and tasks.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The theoretical link from “fewer GMM modes” to improved diffusion performance relies on composing prior theorems under restrictive assumptions (equally weighted, spherical GMMs with separation). The bridge from real-tokenizer latents to this setting is suggestive but not rigorous.

GMM “mode counting” is inferred indirectly via NLL vs. number of components; it can be sensitive to covariance assumptions, dimensionality, and sample size. There is no principled model selection (e.g., BIC/AIC, cross-validated likelihood) to estimate K.

The approach injects semantics via DINOv2/CLIP targets, which amounts to a form of representation alignment; the claim that “variational constraints are not necessary” may conflate “no KL” with “strong external semantic supervision,” and thus should be framed carefully.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Fairness of comparisons: many baselines (e.g., VAEs) are trained without access to the same external teacher features (DINOv2/CLIP). A fully matched baseline (VAE/RA-VAE with identical auxiliary targets and training budget) would strengthen claims.
The compute overhead of extracting DINO/CLIP features during tokenizer training is not reported in wall-clock terms; the net training-time benefits vs. teacher-free pipelines remain unclear.
The theory’s sample-complexity prediction could be stress-tested by varying dataset size for different tokenizers to see whether performance degrades as suggested (O(K^4))—this is currently missing.
Generalization beyond ImageNet class-conditional generation (e.g., class-agnostic datasets, text-to-image) is not demonstrated, despite optional text-BPE targets being proposed.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some mathematical expressions suffer from minor formatting artifacts; more importantly, assumptions and their applicability to realistic latent distributions could be discussed more explicitly in the main text (not only appendices).
The exact training data used per tokenizer (ImageNet-only vs. LAION-COCO † variants) and their influence on subsequent diffusion results could be highlighted more prominently to avoid confusion.
Missing related work or comparisons

While many tokenizers and alignment approaches are cited, a more explicit, apples-to-apples comparison to recent representation-aligned VAEs/continuous tokenizers using the same external teachers would contextualize the contribution.
Discussion of model selection for latent complexity (other than GMMs) and related diagnostics (e.g., DP-GMM, spectral clustering, information-theoretic metrics) is limited.
reviews.questions:
1. How much wall-clock overhead (time, GPU-hours, energy) does teacher feature extraction (DINOv2/CLIP, BPE) add to tokenizer training, and how does this affect the claimed end-to-end efficiency gains?
2. Can you provide a matched baseline where a VAE or RA-VAE is trained with exactly the same auxiliary targets and training schedule (including decoder FT) to isolate the effect of “no KL” vs. “semantic alignment”?
3. How sensitive are the GMM-fitting conclusions to covariance modeling (full vs. spherical), dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA), or selection criteria (BIC/AIC) for estimating the effective number of modes?
4. Can you validate the theoretical sample-complexity prediction by training diffusion models on downsampled ImageNet (e.g., 10%, 25%, 50%) with different tokenizers and tracking gFID vs. data size?
5. Do the conclusions extend to text-to-image or other datasets beyond ImageNet? If not, what failure modes have you observed when scaling to open-domain prompts?
6. What is the effect of removing CLIP/DINOv2 targets at 512×512 on final gFID/IS? Could a teacher-free variant still beat VAE baselines given the masking and decoder FT alone?
7. How does the number of learnable latent tokens (L) trade off with reconstruction and generation quality at 512×512? Any scaling trends to guide practitioners?
reviews.assessment: This is a timely and practically impactful paper that challenges the prevailing reliance on VAEs/quantization for latent diffusion tokenization, showing that a masked AE with auxiliary semantic targets can deliver highly structured latents, markedly faster convergence, and state-of-the-art ImageNet performance with just 128 tokens. The empirical story is compelling and well-substantiated by ablations and diagnostics, and the training recipe is simple and likely to be adopted. The main caveats are (i) the theoretical argument is more illustrative than definitive for real-world latents, and (ii) fairness concerns around external semantic supervision (DINO/CLIP) versus classical VAE baselines need more controlled comparisons and explicit reporting of compute overhead. Addressing these would further solidify the central claim that latent structure, not variational regularization, is the key driver for diffusion quality. Overall, I view this as a strong contribution suitable for ICML, with high potential value to the community.

papers.title: Mitigating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models via Image-Grounded Guidance

reviews.summary: The paper proposes MARINE, a training-free and API-free framework to mitigate object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) at inference time. MARINE extracts object-level, image-grounded signals from open-source vision models (e.g., DETR, RAM++) and injects them as textual guidance, combining conditional and unconditional LVLM logits via a classifier-free guidance style interpolation controlled by a scalar γ. Across five popular LVLMs and multiple benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, GPT-4V-aided evaluation), MARINE reduces hallucinations while largely preserving or improving overall text quality, and it achieves a favorable latency–accuracy trade-off.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
The paper adapts classifier-free guidance ideas to LVLM decoding by conditioning on auxiliary image-grounded prompts and linearly combining conditional and unconditional logits per token.
The design to ensemble multiple open-source vision models and aggregate their outputs (with an intersection strategy) is simple yet effective for robust image-grounded guidance.
The method is training-free and API-free, making it broadly applicable and easy to deploy across LVLMs without architectural changes.
Experimental rigor and validation

Extensive evaluations on five LVLMs (LLaVA, LLaVA-v1.5, MiniGPT-v2, mPLUG-Owl2, InstructBLIP) and multiple datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) using standard hallucination metrics (CHAIR, POPE) and a GPT-4V-aided judge.
Useful ablations: single vs multi guidance models; intersection vs union aggregation; and sensitivity to guidance strength γ.
Inclusion of a “MARINE-Truth” oracle variant provides an informative upper bound on potential performance.
Clarity of presentation
The overall framework is well-motivated with a clear pipeline description and algorithmic pseudocode.
The role of γ and the conditional/unconditional branches is explained with intuition, and ablation curves aid understanding.
Prompts and implementation choices are documented in the appendix to assist reproducibility.
Significance of contributions
Addresses a widely recognized and practically important issue—object hallucination—without retraining.
Demonstrates consistent hallucination reductions with minimal overhead relative to competing decoding-time approaches.
The approach is model-agnostic and flexibly integrates improving external detectors/tags, suggesting lasting utility.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The theoretical grounding is light: while the analogy to classifier-free guidance is sensible, the derivation for autoregressive LVLMs remains heuristic, and some equations appear to contain typographical inconsistencies.

Reliance on external detectors/tags can lead to under-detection; the conservative intersection heuristic may bias toward omission, potentially impairing recall or instruction-following in some settings.
The guidance only targets object nouns; other hallucination types (attributes, spatial relations, counting) are not explicitly addressed.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Some recent, relevant, training-free or logit-steering baselines (e.g., Contrastive Region Guidance; recent “paying more attention to image” or latent-space steering methods) are cited but not compared experimentally.
The POPE “yes” ratio becomes notably conservative for some models (e.g., down to ~39%), suggesting possible overcorrection and residual bias toward “no.”
Limited sensitivity analysis of detection thresholds and aggregator behavior; the fixed high DETR threshold (0.95) may systematically suppress valid objects, and threshold sweeps are not reported.
The GPT-4V-aided evaluation shows relatively modest gains (with overlapping error bars in some cases), and statistical significance is not systematically analyzed across CHAIR/POPE.
Clarity or presentation issues
Minor formula inconsistencies (e.g., product expansions and conditionals) can confuse the guidance interpretation; a tighter, error-free derivation would help.
Details of the aggregation module (LLM-based vs rule-based) are not fully specified in the main text; which option was used in core experiments and any cost/latency implications should be clearer.
Missing related work or comparisons
Empirical comparisons against HALC (2024), Contrastive Region Guidance (2024), and other recent training-free steering methods are missing, limiting placement versus current state of the art.
Additional faithfulness metrics (e.g., TIFA, NOPE, ALOHa) would strengthen the claim of broader generalization beyond CHAIR/POPE.
reviews.questions:
1. What specific aggregation strategy was used in the main experiments (rule-based vs small LLM), and what was its computational cost relative to LVLM decoding? Could you share examples where aggregation changed the guidance set materially?
2. How sensitive are the results to the detector thresholds (DETR 0.95, RAM++ 0.68)? Can you provide a threshold sweep to show precision/recall trade-offs in guidance and downstream CHAIR/POPE impacts?
3. Have you tried dynamic γ schedules (e.g., higher at noun tokens or early tokens, lower otherwise) or confidence-weighted logit mixing based on guidance confidence? Could this reduce the “safe-no” bias observed in POPE for some models?
4. How does MARINE perform in domains where detector taxonomies are mismatched (e.g., medical, diagrams) or on tasks emphasizing attributes/relations (e.g., counting, spatial reasoning)? Any preliminary analyses or failure cases?
5. Could you compare against HALC and Contrastive Region Guidance, and possibly “pay more attention to image” or latent-steering methods, to more thoroughly situate MARINE among recent training-free techniques?
6. In the GPT-4V-aided evaluation, several improvements appear small and with overlapping standard deviations. Did you run multiple randomized trials and conduct statistical significance tests for CHAIR/POPE as well?
reviews.assessment: This paper addresses an important and active problem—object hallucination in LVLMs—with a practical, training-free, and API-free solution that is simple to implement and broadly applicable. The key insight—leveraging reliable image-grounded object signals and integrating them via classifier-free-style logit interpolation—achieves consistent gains across five LVLMs on CHAIR and POPE, while maintaining overall caption/VQA quality and keeping inference overhead near 2×. The ablations are thoughtful and reinforce design choices (multi-model intersection, γ control). The main weaknesses are incomplete comparisons with several recent, closely related training-free methods, limited analysis of sensitivity to detector thresholds, occasional over-conservatism (low “yes” ratios), and minor clarity issues in derivations. Overall, the contributions are solid and practically relevant; with stronger baselines and additional analyses, this work would be a compelling addition to ICML. I lean toward acceptance, contingent on addressing missing comparisons and clarifying sensitivity/aggregation details.

papers.title: Roll the dice & look before you leap: Going beyond the creative limits of next-token prediction

reviews.summary: This paper introduces a suite of minimal, controllable algorithmic tasks designed to abstract two forms of creativity—combinational and exploratory—and to measure “algorithmic creativity,” defined as the fraction of coherent, unique, and non-memorized generations. The authors empirically show that next-token prediction (NTP) is relatively myopic on these tasks, whereas multi-token approaches (teacherless training and discrete diffusion) yield substantially higher diversity and originality, and that input-level noise via seed-conditioning can elicit diversity comparable to or better than output-level temperature sampling. The work posits a conceptual account for why NTP underperforms in such “leap-of-thought” settings and presents evidence across multiple model sizes and objectives.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Introduces a clean, minimal testbed that isolates two cognitive-science–inspired facets of creativity (combinational and exploratory), with objective coherence checks and principled uniqueness/memorization handling.

Proposes and studies seed-conditioning (random input prefixes) as a simple, architecture-free way to elicit diversity that competes with or surpasses temperature sampling, an observation with practical implications.
Articulates a compelling conceptual critique of NTP for “leap-of-thought” tasks that require advanced planning of latent decisions, complementing prior impossibility/data-inefficiency arguments.
Experimental rigor and validation
Evaluates both larger (Gemma v1 2B) and smaller models (GPT-2 86M) and includes both Transformer-based and diffusion-based models, with ablations on seeds, temperatures, and sampling.
Measures creativity alongside memorization and coherence, enabling diagnosis of where NTP fails (e.g., memorization vs. mode collapse).
Includes an initial real-world proxy (summarization) showing modest diversity gains at matched ROUGE, suggesting partial external validity.
Clarity of presentation
Clearly states the core hypothesis, defines the tasks and the algorithmic creativity metric, and connects the design to cognitive-science notions of creativity.
Presents intuitive visualizations for tasks (sibling/triangle discovery; circle/line construction) and explains the leap-of-thought mismatch with NTP.
Significance of contributions
Provides a much-needed controlled environment to reason about diversity/originality in generation, advancing discussion beyond accuracy-centric benchmarks.
Offers actionable guidance: multi-token objectives and input-level noise should be considered for open-ended, diversity-sensitive applications.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns
The tasks, while elegant, are synthetic and the mapping to “real” creativity remains only loosely grounded; claims about broader creative limits of NTP may be stronger than the evidence warrants.

The “no permutation helps” claim for some tasks is asserted but not rigorously established; more direct tests against permutation-based or partial-lookahead objectives (e.g., XLNet-like or σ-GPT variants) would strengthen the case.
Teacherless training details are under-specified; the hybrid objective and autoregressive inference could confound attribution of gains (are they due to objective, decoding, or both?).
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Some comparisons couple seed-conditioning with the training objective in ways that complicate attribution; clearer controlled studies isolating each factor would help.
The “data inefficiency” hypothesis for NTP is plausible but not demonstrated via systematic scaling of training set size with sample complexity plots.
Diffusion vs. Transformer comparisons are limited to small models; an apples-to-apples large-model diffusion comparison is missing.
The real-world summarization diversity gains are small and may not be practically significant; statistical significance and robustness analyses are limited.
Clarity or presentation issues
Several crucial results and ablations are deferred to appendices; explicit main-text summaries or tables of key ablations would improve readability.
The exact formulation and implementation of teacherless training (Eq. 2) are pivotal but only sketched; pseudocode or a concise schematic would aid clarity.
Missing related work or comparisons
The discussion of permutation or bidirectional/context-permutation training could engage more explicitly with XLNet and related permutation LM literature.
Additional connections to prompt-based control tokens, control codes, and structured noise-injection beyond soft prompts (e.g., prefix-tuning variants for diversity) could be covered more thoroughly.
reviews.questions:
1. Please describe the teacherless (multi-token) training objective precisely (with notation) and provide minimal pseudocode or a schematic. Are ground-truth tokens ever input, or is the sequence fully masked/noised?
2. Can you provide sample-complexity curves showing algorithmic creativity vs. training-set size for NTP and multi-token training to substantiate the “data-inefficiency” hypothesis?
3. For Sibling Discovery, does reversing the token order (Γ, γ, γ′) substantially close the NTP–multi-token gap, and does it raise memorization to a similar or different extent? Showing this would directly support the “adversarial ordering” claim.
4. For Circle/Line Construction, can you report results for permutation-based LMs (e.g., XLNet-style) or partial-lookahead methods to back the claim that “no permutation helps”?
5. Could you quantify how much of the seed-conditioning gain comes from diversity vs. coherence vs. reduced memorization across tasks, with per-component breakdowns? Additionally, are outputs calibrated with respect to the target distribution (e.g., estimated coverage or uniformity) when seeds are varied?
6. What is the exact relationship between seeds and outputs? Do unseen seeds at test induce unseen structural plans (measured via a latent proxy), and is there evidence that the model has learned a seed-to-plan mapping rather than surface perturbation?
7. Diffusion shows strong gains on several tasks but not all, and seed-conditioning appears less helpful for diffusion. Is this because diffusion already injects input-level noise/stochasticity? Can you analyze why Sibling Discovery is an outlier for diffusion?
8. The summarization diversity improvements are modest. Are they statistically significant, and do they hold across multiple datasets or random seeds? Can you share confidence intervals for the Self-BLEU and ROUGE trajectories?
9. Could you report sensitivity to top-k and nucleus parameters more prominently in the main text? In some figures seed+greedy outperforms temperature, but elsewhere sampling choices seem decisive.
10. What portions of the code and data will be released upon publication, and will they be sufficient for full reproduction of the main results, including all ablations?
reviews.assessment: This paper presents a timely and thoughtful study that moves beyond accuracy-centric evaluations and tackles diversity/originality in a controlled, measurable way. The task design is elegant and well-motivated by cognitive-science notions of creativity, the empirical results are generally consistent and informative, and the seed-conditioning finding is both surprising and practically relevant. While the work is necessarily synthetic and some claims (e.g., that no permutation helps) would benefit from stronger empirical or formal backing, the core contributions—establishing a minimal creativity testbed, demonstrating robust gains from multi-token objectives and diffusion, and introducing a simple, effective diversity mechanism via seed-conditioning—are valuable to the ICML community. I recommend acceptance, contingent on clarifying the multi-token objective/inference setup, surfacing more controlled ablations that isolate seed vs. objective effects, and tightening the comparative analysis to better support the generality of the conclusions.

papers.title: How Do Large Language Monkeys Get Their Power (Laws)?

reviews.summary: The paper investigates why, across diverse tasks, the negative log of the average success rate under repeated sampling (k attempts per item) follows a power law in k, despite the fact that for any single problem, the failure probability should drop exponentially with k. The authors resolve this apparent paradox by showing that aggregate power-law behavior arises when the distribution of single-attempt success probabilities across problems has a heavy left tail, specifically p(pass@1) ∝ p^{b−1} near zero, and they prove sufficiency and (under mild regularity) necessity results via Laplace/Tauberian-style arguments. Building on this distributional perspective, they propose a practical estimator that fits the single-attempt success distribution and simulates aggregate scaling, demonstrating improved sample efficiency over least-squares fits on synthetic and real datasets, and explaining deviations from power-law scaling in prior work.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Establishes a clear and rigorous link between per-problem exponential decay and aggregate power-law decay via the left tail of the across-problem single-attempt success distribution.
Provides both sufficiency and (conditional) necessity theorems, leveraging classical Laplace/Tauberian reasoning to characterize when power-law scaling must arise.

Introduces a practically useful “distributional estimator” that fits the single-attempt success distribution (accounting for limited resolution in the extreme left tail) and predicts scaling parameters with notably improved sample efficiency.
Experimental rigor and validation
Confirms the per-problem exponential scaling empirically on two domains: math problem solving (Pythia on MATH) and multimodal jailbreaking (frontier models on HarmBench).

Demonstrates that observed deviations from power-law behavior (e.g., Llama 3 8B IT in Best-of-N jailbreaking) correspond to an absence of the required heavy left tail in pass@1, aligning with the theory.
Provides backtesting with synthetic data to quantify the estimator’s relative-error advantages over least squares.
Clarity of presentation
Offers a compelling conceptual narrative that reconciles exponential per-item improvements with aggregate power-law behavior; figures reinforce the intuition.
Theorems are stated cleanly with clear claims about the behavior of p(pass@1) near zero and the resulting scaling.
Practical implications and forecasting procedures are well-motivated.
Significance of contributions
Unifies several empirical observations of “inference-time scaling” under repeated sampling, clarifying when and why power laws should emerge.
Provides a predictive, more compute-efficient methodology with immediate utility for evaluation design and compute planning.
Suggests broader connections to pretraining scaling via mixtures of decays, potentially informing how and when power laws emerge in other regimes.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Independence of attempts is assumed; in practice, repeated sampling can induce correlations (e.g., shared prompts, decoding heuristics, or adaptive strategies). The impact of correlations on the exponential per-problem decay and on the distributional estimator is not analyzed.

Necessity result likely relies on regular variation and Tauberian conditions; the paper references “mild regularity” but the precise conditions and their practical testability are not detailed in the main text.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Real-data studies use relatively small benchmarks (128 MATH problems; 159 HarmBench prompts), which may limit the reliability of inferred left-tail behavior and exponent estimates.

Goodness-of-fit for the proposed distribution families (e.g., scaled Kumaraswamy-/Beta-Binomial) is shown visually; quantitative tests (KS, Cramér–von Mises, likelihood ratios, information criteria) are not reported.

Claims of “2–4 orders-of-magnitude less inference compute” rest primarily on synthetic backtesting; a concrete operational definition of “inference compute” and a broader set of real-data backtests would strengthen the claim.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some inconsistencies/typos in naming fitted distributions (e.g., references to scaled Beta-Binomial vs. scaled Kumaraswamy; notational artifacts like “pass;@1”) make it harder to track exactly what is fit where.
The statistical estimation details (discretization procedure, parameter constraints, optimization) are only sketched; more precise description would help reproducibility.
Missing related work or comparisons

The mixture-of-exponentials-to-power-law connection is classical; citing additional standard sources from regular variation/Tauberian theory (e.g., Feller, Bingham–Goldie–Teugels) would contextualize the necessity/sufficiency claims.

Connections to randomized algorithm runtimes and restart strategies under heavy-tailed distributions (e.g., Luby et al.-style analyses) could further situate the findings relative to broader CS theory on “best-of-N”/amplification phenomena.
reviews.questions:
1. How sensitive are the main conclusions and the distributional estimator to correlations across attempts (e.g., shared prompts, reranking, or adaptive sampling)? Can you characterize conditions under which mild correlations preserve the effective exponential per-problem decay?
2. Could you provide quantitative goodness-of-fit metrics (e.g., KS statistics, AIC/BIC) for the fitted pass@1 distributions across models/benchmarks, and compare alternative families beyond scaled Kumaraswamy/Beta-Binomial?
3. What precise regularity assumptions are required for the necessity result, and can you reference or restate the applicable Tauberian theorem(s) to make the proof self-contained?
4. In real-data backtesting, how does the distributional estimator perform at reduced sampling budgets compared to least squares (e.g., halving the number of attempts or problems)? Can you report confidence intervals for the estimated exponent b?
5. How do decoding parameters (temperature, nucleus sampling p, presence/absence of chain-of-thought) influence the inferred pass@1 distribution and the resulting exponent? Is the tail exponent stable across these choices?
6. Can the method generalize to other domains with pass@k metrics (e.g., code generation/HumanEval, GSM8K variants, theorem proving)? Any preliminary results or negative cases?
7. In safety settings, can your framework help choose a budget k that bounds residual attack success at a desired confidence, given uncertainty about the left tail (e.g., via conservative tail modeling)?
reviews.assessment:
This paper offers a clear and conceptually satisfying resolution of an important empirical puzzle: why aggregate success under repeated sampling follows a power law even though each problem improves exponentially with attempts. The distributional mechanism and accompanying theorems are technically sound, leveraging established asymptotics, and the empirical analyses convincingly support the key claims across two application areas. The proposed distributional estimator is a practical contribution with demonstrated sample-efficiency benefits in backtesting and plausible utility for forecasting.

While some presentation details (distribution nomenclature, estimation procedure) could be sharpened and the empirical section would benefit from additional quantitative fits, robustness checks, and real-data backtesting at reduced budgets, these are addressable concerns. The work is timely, broadly relevant to inference-time scaling and evaluation methodology, and likely to be valuable to both practitioners and researchers. I recommend acceptance.

papers.title: Addressing Misspecification in Simulation-based Inference through Data-driven Calibration

reviews.summary: This paper proposes RoPE, a method for addressing model misspecification in simulation-based inference by combining neural posterior estimation with an optimal transport (OT) coupling learned between simulated and real observations. RoPE builds posteriors for real data as mixtures of posteriors trained on simulations, with mixture weights given by an OT plan computed in a learned feature space aligned using a small calibration set of labeled real data. The authors show theoretically grounded properties (self-calibration under balanced transport) and demonstrate strong empirical performance across four synthetic and two real benchmarks, often delivering calibrated and informative posteriors where prior SBI methods fail under misspecification.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces a principled, data-driven misspecification model via semi-balanced entropy-regularized OT between simulated and real observations in a learned representation space.
Proposes an elegant mixture-of-posteriors construction p(θ|x_o) ≈ Σ_j α_ij p(θ|x_s^j) that is simple, stable, and compatible with off-the-shelf NPE pipelines.
Provides meaningful interpretability/control via OT hyperparameters: γ to trade calibration vs informativeness and τ for robustness to prior misspecification.
States and discusses a “self-calibration” property under balanced OT that connects transport mass conservation with marginal prior recovery.
Experimental rigor and validation

Evaluates on six diverse tasks (including two real-world “Causal Chambers” benchmarks with ground-truth parameters), using sensible metrics: log posterior probability (LPP) and average coverage AUC (ACAUC).
Includes ablations (tuning-only vs OT-only), hyperparameter sweeps (γ, τ), and prior misspecification studies.
Compares against a comprehensive set of baselines (prior, NPE, J-NPE, MLP, NNPE, NPE-RS, HVAE), and reports multiple random seeds and uncertainty bands.
Clarity of presentation
Clearly states the modeling assumption x_o ⟂ θ | x_s and its implications, including limitations and regularization benefits.
Provides a transparent pipeline description (NPE training, feature fine-tuning on calibration set, OT on test set), and a thoughtful discussion of metrics and their scope.
Significance of contributions
Addresses a central obstacle for SBI adoption: reliability under misspecification when only limited real labels exist.
Introduces real-world benchmarks with labels for misspecified SBI, which is valuable for the community.
Offers a practical recipe (fixed γ works surprisingly well; τ for prior confidence) that seems robust and easy to apply.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The conditional independence assumption x_o ⟂ θ | x_s can be restrictive. While the authors argue it regularizes learning, more systematic characterization of failure modes when it is violated would strengthen the work.

The OT plan is computed transductively on the test set observations. While label-free, this test-time adaptation may complicate strict generalization claims and comparisons to strictly inductive methods.
Computational scalability of OT with large n_o and n_s can be challenging (quadratic memory), and practical limits are not fully quantified.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Joint calibration is not evaluated; ACAUC is a marginal metric. Some tasks have correlated parameters (e.g., Light Tunnel), and joint coverage or dependence-sensitive diagnostics would be informative.
Sensitivity to the number of simulations n_s and to feature-space choices (e.g., dimensionality of NSE, alternative costs) is not deeply explored.
HVAE and some other baselines are applicable only on subsets of tasks; while justified, it reduces cross-task comparability of certain claims.
Clarity or presentation issues
The semi-balanced OT parameterization via τ = ρ/(ρ+γ) could be explained more carefully, especially the limiting behaviors and how τ interacts with entropic regularization in practice.
Some readers may benefit from a more explicit discussion of the relationship between the learned representations h and g and approximate sufficiency in real vs simulated domains.
Missing related work or comparisons

There is a broader body of OT-based domain adaptation and alignment methods in representation space (e.g., OTDA variants, neural OT mappings) that could be more fully contextualized relative to the proposed approach.
Additional discussion of transductive domain adaptation vs inductive adaptation would help position RoPE’s test-time coupling strategy within sim2real literature.
reviews.questions:
1. Could you quantify the computational and memory cost of OT as a function of n_o, n_s, and feature dimension, and provide practical limits and wall-clock times for your largest experiments?
2. How sensitive is RoPE to the number of simulated samples n_s used to form the transport plan and mixture? Is there a diminishing returns regime, and do you have heuristics for selecting n_s?
3. Can you report joint calibration (e.g., 2D joint coverage, HPD region coverage, or simulation-based calibration diagnostics) on tasks with k≥2 to complement ACAUC?
4. How often does the independence assumption x_o ⟂ θ | x_s appear to be violated in your tasks (especially the real ones), and how does performance degrade as the violation increases (e.g., via controlled synthetic studies)?
5. In the RoPE* setting with prior misspecification (τ<1), the NPE is still trained with the simulator prior. Would retraining or importance-reweighting the NPE to reflect the effective “transported” prior further improve performance?
6. Have you tried alternative cost functions (e.g., learned Mahalanobis in feature space, contrastive losses, or OT in a shared encoder trained with domain-adversarial objectives) and how do they compare?
7. Could you clarify how γ and τ interact (since τ=ρ/(ρ+γ)) and provide guidance on tuning them jointly? Are there scenarios where high γ and low τ are beneficial or detrimental?
8. How would you deploy RoPE in streaming settings where test distributions drift over time? Can the OT plan be updated online (e.g., via Online Sinkhorn) without recomputing from scratch?
reviews.assessment: This is a timely and well-executed contribution to robust SBI under model misspecification. The central idea—model the sim-to-real gap via OT in a learned, approximately sufficient feature space and transfer posteriors by mixture—is both elegant and practical. The empirical evaluation is thorough, notably including real-world benchmarks with labeled parameters, and the ablations convincingly disentangle the roles of fine-tuning and OT. The method’s controls for calibration vs informativeness (γ) and prior robustness (τ) are intuitive and useful in practice. The main caveats are the reliance on the conditional independence assumption, the transductive nature of test-time OT, and limited assessment of joint calibration and scalability. Nonetheless, the paper presents a substantial step forward with clear value to the ICML community. I recommend acceptance, contingent on clarifying transductive evaluation, adding scalability details, and, if possible, complementing calibration metrics with joint coverage diagnostics.

papers.title: A Unified Framework for Entropy Search and Expected Improvement in Bayesian Optimization

reviews.summary: The paper proposes Variational Entropy Search (VES), a unifying framework that casts information-theoretic acquisition functions (specifically MES) and Expected Improvement (EI) within a single variational inference perspective via a Barber–Agakov lower bound on mutual information. A key theoretical result shows that EI arises as a special case of MES when approximating p(y* | Dt, yx) with an exponential distribution (VES-Exp). Building on this, the authors introduce VES-Gamma, which uses a Gamma variational family and automatically determines its parameters per location to balance EI-like exploitation with information-theoretic exploration, demonstrating competitive to superior performance across synthetic, GP-sampled, and high-dimensional real-world benchmarks.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The paper gives a clear, principled unification of EI and information-theoretic AFs by lower-bounding MES with a variational distribution over y*, and proves that EI is recovered when using an exponential family approximation (Theorem 3.2).

VES-Gamma is a nontrivial generalization that leverages the Gamma family (subsuming exponential at k=1), with an automatic, per-location parameter selection derived from maximizing the bound; the resulting fixed-point equations mirror Gamma MLE conditions, offering a principled procedure rather than heuristics.

The introduction of a mutual-information lower-bound view for directly approximating p(y* | Dt, yx) (as opposed to p(yx | Dt, y*)) complements prior work and broadens design space for information-theoretic AFs.
Experimental rigor and validation
Broad empirical coverage: classic synthetic functions, GP-prior samples across dimensions and length-scales, and several high-dimensional real-world tasks (up to 388D).
Public implementation in BoTorch and clear hyperparameter/implementation details (e.g., 128 posterior samples, inner iterations, stopping criteria).
Ablation-like checks on the claimed EI–VES-Exp equivalence via a KS test (despite limitations; see weaknesses).
Clarity of presentation
The theoretical development is well-structured: BA bound derivation, ESLBO definition, and connection to EM/ELBO laid out cleanly; proofs are provided in the appendix.
The role of the Gamma parameters and their estimation is explained with equations and intuition, including uniqueness arguments and regularization details.
Significance of contributions
Conceptually impactful: ties two prominent BO paradigms (improvement-based and information-theoretic) under a single umbrella, offering design principles for new AFs.
Practical potential: VES-Gamma often matches or beats strong baselines, especially on some high-dimensional tasks, indicating value beyond pure theory.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The framework and proofs rely on noiseless observations and the lower-bounded support of y*. Many BO applications are noisy; while acknowledged as future work, this is a substantial limitation for practical deployment.

The VES-Gamma objective requires joint sampling of (y*, yx); in continuous high-dimensional spaces, sampling y* via GP path maxima is nontrivial. The paper references pathwise conditioning but lacks concrete algorithmic details on how global maxima of sample paths are obtained or approximated in practice.

The auto-determination of Gamma parameters depends on MC estimates of E[z*] and E[log z*] with clamping of z* to avoid numerical issues. This introduces bias and breaks some independence assumptions; the net effect on optimization quality is not analyzed.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Baseline coverage is limited: PES, ES, Knowledge Gradient, Thompson Sampling, and more recent information-theoretic methods (e.g., JES variants) are not included. Given the paper’s positioning, comparisons to PES/JES seem essential.

The KS test for equivalence between VES-Exp and EI uses sequences of function values across runs; because acquisition optimization is nonconvex and early choices induce path dependence, these samples are not identically distributed in a controlled sense. The test provides weak evidence for equivalence relative to a direct comparison of selected x’s or acquisition surfaces.

Computational overhead is an order of magnitude larger than EI/MES; while often acceptable in expensive BO, several benchmarks used are relatively cheap. The proposed VarPro acceleration is not empirically validated.
Limited sensitivity analyses: no study of the effect of the number of posterior samples, number of inner iterations N, or clamping threshold on performance/stability.
Clarity or presentation issues
Occasional notation artifacts and minor typos (e.g., stray characters, support indicators, “non-closed-form” labels) distract in places.
The paper sometimes says it compares to “EI,” but elsewhere states it uses LogEI interchangeably; this is confusing and may affect conclusions—LogEI differs from EI in behavior.
Missing related work or comparisons

While Takeno et al. (2020, 2022) and JES (Hvarfner et al., 2022) are cited, empirical comparisons are absent; likewise for PES and KG. Given the paper’s thesis (unifying EI and information-theoretic AFs), a broader empirical context would strengthen claims.
Recent high-dimensional BO baselines designed for very large d (e.g., trust-region or subspace methods beyond UCB/EI) are not considered, which could be relevant for the 100–1000D settings.
reviews.questions:
1. How exactly do you sample y* from GP sample paths in high dimensions—over what candidate sets or optimization routines? Please specify the size of candidate sets, optimization budgets, and how you ensure approximate global maxima for the pathwise draws.
2. How sensitive are VES-Gamma’s results to the number of posterior samples (128), the number of inner iterations N, and the clamping threshold for z*? Can you provide ablations and variance vs. compute trade-offs?
3. Why are PES, JES, and KG not included in the empirical comparisons? Given your unifying thesis, these seem like important baselines. Can you comment on expected relative performance or any obstacles to including them?
4. In practice you sometimes use LogEI and state you use EI and LogEI interchangeably. Which one is actually used in each plot/table, and how might this choice affect the fairness of comparisons to VES-Gamma and MES?
5. Can VES-Gamma be adapted to noisy observations by modifying the support of q(y* | Dt, yx) and the ESLBO accordingly? If so, what are the main technical hurdles?
6. The Gamma parameters are determined by maximizing ESLBO for each x, akin to Gamma MLE on z*. Could you compare this to simple moment matching and discuss any advantages of the ESLBO-driven choice?
7. Have you attempted the proposed VarPro acceleration in practice? If so, what speedups and accuracy changes do you observe vs. Algorithm 2? If not, could you provide a rough complexity reduction estimate?
8. For the real-world SVM and Lasso problems, are the objectives deterministic (e.g., fixed splits/seeds) or noisy (e.g., CV with randomness)? If noisy, how do you reconcile this with the noiseless theoretical assumptions?
reviews.assessment:
This work offers a compelling, principled bridge between EI and information-theoretic BO via a variational lower bound on MES, with a clear theorem showing EI as the exponential-family special case. This unifying view is theoretically neat and, in my opinion, of genuine interest to the BO community. The proposed VES-Gamma is a simple yet effective instantiation that often performs competitively or better than EI and MES across a broad set of benchmarks, including challenging high-dimensional tasks, and the paper is generally clear and well-motivated.

However, the current scope has notable limitations. The reliance on a noiseless setting, limited baseline coverage (missing PES/JES/KG), the significant computational overhead without demonstrated mitigation, and some gaps in practical details (e.g., how y* is sampled in high d) detract from the overall strength. The empirical equivalence test between EI and VES-Exp is also not the most convincing methodology.

On balance, I view the conceptual contribution as sufficiently novel and valuable, with promising empirical results, to merit publication if the authors can address the most salient concerns—particularly clarifying y* sampling, disambiguating EI vs LogEI usage, adding at least one strong information-theoretic baseline (e.g., PES/JES), and including a brief sensitivity analysis or an initial VarPro speedup result. With these improvements, the paper would make a strong and impactful contribution. My current recommendation is a weak accept.

papers.title: Conformal Prediction as Bayesian Quadrature

reviews.summary: The paper proposes a Bayesian reinterpretation of conformal prediction by casting risk control as Bayesian quadrature over the quantile function of the loss distribution. It derives a distribution-free, prior-robust upper bound L+ on the posterior expected loss via a worst-case quantile construction and Dirichlet-distributed quantile spacings, showing that split conformal prediction and conformal risk control emerge as special cases from the posterior mean of L+. Building on this, the authors propose a data-conditional, high-probability decision rule that selects λ to ensure Pr(L+ ≤ α | calibration losses) ≥ β, and empirically demonstrate improved control of per-trial risk with competitive set sizes across synthetic and MS-COCO experiments.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Recasts conformal prediction and conformal risk control within a unified Bayesian decision-theoretic framework using quadrature over quantile functions, which is an original and elegant conceptual bridge.

Introduces a distribution-free, prior-agnostic stochastic upper bound L+ for the posterior expected loss using Dirichlet spacings of quantiles; this yields a full posterior-like distribution rather than just a point estimate and directly motivates high-probability, data-conditional procedures.
Recovers split conformal prediction and CRC as special cases (via the expectation of L+), neatly situating past work within the new framework.
Experimental rigor and validation
Evaluations on both synthetic and real tasks (MS-COCO FNR control) with many random splits (M = 10,000 in synthetic) and clear metrics (failure rate above α and set/interval size).
Includes RCPS with Hoeffding bounds as a strong high-probability baseline, illustrating the trade-off between tightness and conservatism.
Clarity of presentation
The decision-theoretic setup and the progression from Bayes risk to quadrature over quantiles are clearly laid out and intuitive.
Visuals (schematics, histograms) effectively convey the differences between marginal (CRC) and data-conditional (proposed) guarantees and the behavior of L+.
Significance of contributions

Addresses a timely and important gap: marginal (expectation) guarantees can be unsatisfactory per-trial in deployment; the proposed data-conditional, high-probability alternative is practically valuable.
The framework is flexible and could incorporate additional structure or priors when available, promising broader applicability.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The central stochastic dominance result (Theorem 4.3) is stated without a complete proof in the appendix; its validity hinges on how uncertainty over quantile levels is handled and how the Dirichlet spacings arise in a posterior (rather than unconditional) sense. This is critical to the main guarantee.

The treatment of discrete loss distributions (e.g., 0–1 miscoverage) is deferred; the paper states Dirichlet spacings “stochastically dominate” discrete spacings but does not provide a formal finite-sample result. Many practical CRC/CP losses are discrete.

The elimination of the prior via a supremum over quantile functions together with the use of Dirichlet spacings leaves some ambiguity about the precise inferential target and conditioning (posterior vs. unconditional law of spacings). Stronger formalization of p(t1:n | l1:n) under minimal assumptions would help.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

While RCPS is included, there are few baselines offering per-trial or high-probability control other than RCPS; e.g., recent risk-control variants (OCE/CVaR risk control) or asymptotic L-statistic-based UCBs could provide complementary comparisons in appropriate regimes.
Sensitivity analyses are limited: number of Dirichlet samples (1000) and robustness of the selected λ to Monte Carlo variance or to β are not deeply explored.
Clarity or presentation issues
The role and status of the Dirichlet spacing distribution as posterior vs. distribution-free input noise could be clarified; currently it reads as a hybrid of Bayesian and frequentist reasoning.
Minor inconsistencies (e.g., floor/ceiling indices in Prop. 3.1 vs. earlier equation) and small typographical artifacts may confuse readers.
Missing related work or comparisons

The connection to Bayesian nonparametric predictive inference (e.g., Dirichlet process posteriors over CDFs and quantiles) is cited (Hill, 1968; 1988) but not leveraged to justify the posterior over quantile spacings; bringing this thread into the main theoretical argument could strengthen the guarantees.
Recent extensions of CRC to non-expectation risks (e.g., OCE/CVaR) could be discussed as to whether the proposed L+-based approach can naturally extend to tail-risk functionals.
reviews.questions:
1. Could you provide a full proof of Theorem 4.3 (stochastic dominance of L+), explicitly stating the assumptions under which p(t1:n | l1:n) yields the Dirichlet spacing law or is lower-bounded by it in the sense required for the inequality?
2. How does your guarantee extend to discrete loss distributions (e.g., 0–1 losses)? Can you formalize the claimed stochastic dominance of Dirichlet-weighted sums over discrete spacings and provide a finite-sample bound?
3. What is the computational complexity of selecting λ with the HPD criterion as a function of n, grid size for λ, and number of Dirichlet samples? Are there variance-reduction or quasi-MC techniques that you recommend to stabilize the probability estimates Pr(L+ ≤ α)?
4. How sensitive are the results to β and to the choice of B? Do you recommend procedures for estimating or stress-testing B in practice when it is not a priori known with certainty?
5. Can the L+-based approach be adapted to control tail risks (e.g., VaR/CVaR or general distortion/OCE risks) by replacing the integral over t with weighted quantile integrals? If so, what modifications to the bounding argument are needed?
6. In the MS-COCO experiment, is the observed 5.43% failure rate statistically distinguishable from the 5% target? Please include confidence intervals and discuss any sources of deviation (e.g., Monte Carlo error, grid discretization).
7. Could you clarify whether the Dirichlet spacings assumption conditions only on the order of losses or also on their values? Is there a Bayesian nonparametric prior (e.g., Dirichlet process or neutral-to-the-right process) under which your posterior over t1:n coincides with the Dirichlet result?
reviews.assessment:
This paper presents an elegant and potentially impactful Bayesian reinterpretation of conformal prediction that yields a practical, data-conditional, high-probability risk-control method. The key insight—bounding the posterior expected loss by integrating a worst-case quantile function against Dirichlet spacings—both recovers existing conformal methods and enriches them by providing a distribution over plausible risks, enabling more conservative and informed deployment decisions. The empirical results compellingly illustrate the gap between marginal and data-conditional guarantees and the favorable tightness–safety trade-off relative to RCPS.

However, the central theoretical ingredient (Theorem 4.3) is not fully justified in the paper, and the transition from unconditional distribution-free properties of order-statistic spacings to a posterior bound uniform over priors needs a complete proof. The discrete-loss setting also deserves a formal treatment. These issues are addressable and, if resolved, would put the contribution on very solid ground. Given the novelty, clarity, and promising empirical evidence, I lean toward acceptance contingent on clarifying and strengthening the theoretical underpinnings.

papers.title: Policy-labeled Preference Learning: Is Preference Enough for RLHF?

reviews.summary: This paper introduces Policy-labeled Preference Learning (PPL), a preference-based RLHF framework that augments pairwise trajectory comparisons with behavior policy labels and models preferences via regret. Theoretically, the authors derive a structural characterization of reward/Q-function equivalence classes under MaxEnt RL and prove a “Policy Deviation Theorem” linking the Q-function gap to a sequential forward KL, yielding a regret decomposition that motivates a contrastive KL regularizer. Empirically, PPL is evaluated on MetaWorld in offline (homogeneous/heterogeneous) and online settings, where it generally improves upon CPL and SFT and is competitive with the reward-based P-IQL baseline.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces a clear formulation of “likelihood mismatch” in preference learning with heterogeneous behavior data, arguing for the importance of policy labels and regret modeling.

Derives a regret decomposition into an action-likelihood term and a sequential forward KL, yielding a conceptually appealing contrastive KL regularizer that connects DPO-style objectives with forward-KL-constrained RLHF.

Provides a structural “equivalence class” result (Lemma 3.2) that parameterizes optimal Q* as α log π* + β(s), presented as a bijection that sharpens prior surjective characterizations in DPO literature.
The “Policy Deviation Theorem” (Theorem 3.4) relating Q gaps to sequential forward KL appears broadly useful for MaxEnt RL beyond this application.
Experimental rigor and validation

Evaluates across six MetaWorld tasks with both homogeneous and heterogeneous offline datasets, and both dense and sparse preference regimes, which is more reflective of realistic data diversity than standard homogeneous setups.
Includes an online setting, demonstrating competitive learning dynamics with far fewer parameters than a reward-modeling baseline.
Ablation on deterministic pseudo-labels provides useful evidence about the role of policy labeling in heterogeneous datasets.
Clarity of presentation
The motivation for PPL and the “likelihood mismatch” failure mode is intuitively explained with a helpful schematic.
The connection from theory (regret/KL decomposition) to the practical algorithm (contrastive KL regularization with lookahead L) is conceptually coherent.
Significance of contributions

If correct and practical, the results provide a principled path to reconcile DPO-style policy learning with stochastic MDP dynamics and mixed-policy offline data, a setting highly relevant to RLHF in robotics and beyond.
The theoretical bridges among regret, policy likelihood, and sequential KL constraints could influence future algorithm design in preference-based RL and RLHF.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The theory is developed with respect to an unknown optimal policy π*, but the algorithm instantiates regret using the current learned policy πψ as a surrogate for π*. The paper does not formally justify this substitution or provide convergence guarantees for this bootstrapped procedure, creating a gap between theory and practice.

The sequential forward KL terms are intractable in general and are approximated using limited L-step “rollouts” that often reduce to using observed segment continuations. This can bias the estimator and, in the pseudo-labeled deterministic case, can collapse to multi-step behavior cloning rather than a true KL alignment with an actual behavior policy distribution.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Offline experiments frequently give PPL access to policy labels (or clean pseudo-labels) that baselines cannot exploit, confounding fairness. Since the central claim is that policy labels matter, a stronger study would (i) provide baselines augmented with the same label information where possible or (ii) compare against methods explicitly designed for heterogeneous behavior mixtures without policy IDs.

Preference labels are generated by an oracle SAC critic, not by humans. While standard in some prior work, the specific deviation from CPL’s label-generation procedure (no critic retraining step) and the use of an oracle may interact with methods differently; this is not disentangled. The claim that “all methods used the same labels” is true but not sufficient to show that observed gaps are not partially due to label noise interacting with algorithms differently.

Reporting “maximum average performance across a window” can inflate headline numbers. Mean ± std at fixed checkpoints and significance testing would provide a more robust picture. Some tasks in Table 2 show PPL underperforming P-IQL, making “consistently outperforms” too strong.

Limited sensitivity analyses: no ablations on L, normalization choices for the KL term, α (temperature), or the impact of the regularizer’s weight. The computational cost of contrastive KL with lookahead is acknowledged but not quantified.
Clarity or presentation issues

Notation around Q_*^π, Q_π^π, and r_* is dense and occasionally confusing; the relationship among these objects and the role of β(s) could benefit from a more careful, consistent exposition and assumptions (e.g., measurability, support, boundedness).
Some minor terminology inconsistencies (e.g., “Homogenous” vs “Homogeneous”) and typographic artifacts persist.
Missing related work or comparisons

There is discussion of forward-KL constrained RLHF (e.g., Wang et al., 2023; Shan et al., 2024), but empirical comparisons to methods that already exploit forward KL constraints would strengthen the case that PPL’s contrastive KL mechanism is a practical advance.
No experiments with real human preferences; the method’s robustness to realistic label noise and annotator inconsistency remains untested.
reviews.questions:
1. What exact information about the behavior policy do you assume is available in offline experiments? Is it only a policy ID per trajectory, or do you have access to the action distributions π±(·|s) at future steps used in the contrastive KL term? How are these distributions estimated in practice for stochastic π±?
2. In the offline heterogeneous setting, do baselines receive any benefit from policy labels (e.g., policy-ID conditioning or stratified training)? If not, can you provide a variant where CPL/P-IQL are augmented with this information to isolate the contribution of your modeling rather than the additional side information?
3. How sensitive is PPL to the lookahead horizon L and the normalization of the contrastive KL term? Please include ablations across L and regularizer weights, and quantify any compute overhead.
4. Your regret decomposition and Theorem 3.4 critically involve π*. In the algorithm, π* is replaced with the current πψ. Can you provide any theoretical justification or monotonicity properties for this substitution, or practical diagnostics (e.g., surrogate gap reduction) that correlate with policy improvement?
5. Could you report standard evaluation statistics (e.g., final-iteration mean ± std over seeds, AUC) in addition to the maximum moving-average, and provide statistical tests where appropriate?
6. How robust is PPL to realistic human preference noise or inconsistencies? Can you include experiments with synthetic annotator noise or, ideally, small-scale human studies?
7. Can you compare with a forward-KL preference optimization baseline (e.g., Wang et al., 2023; Shan et al., 2024) to better contextualize the practical benefit of your contrastive KL regularizer?
8. Please clarify assumptions in Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.4 (state/action measurability, boundedness, uniqueness of α-optimal solution, continuous-action integrability), and expand the proof sketch to reduce ambiguity around Q_*^π and β(s).
reviews.assessment:
This paper presents a thoughtful and timely contribution that (i) highlights a real failure mode—likelihood mismatch—when learning from preferences generated by heterogeneous behavior policies in stochastic MDPs, (ii) develops a regret-based modeling framework with a principled contrastive KL regularizer, and (iii) offers theoretical results that connect value gaps to sequential forward KL in the MaxEnt setting. The empirical results are promising, especially in heterogeneous and sparse regimes, and the online results suggest the approach can be competitive with reward-modeling pipelines at a fraction of the parameter count.

However, key concerns remain. The central theory depends on π*, whereas the algorithm replaces π* with πψ without formal guarantees, leaving a theory-practice gap. Offline experiments likely grant PPL extra side information (policy labels) not available to baselines, complicating fairness. The sequential KL approximation can degenerate toward multi-step behavior cloning when true behavior distributions are unknown, which needs further analysis and ablation. Reporting practices and limited sensitivity studies also weaken the empirical case. Despite these issues, the paper’s conceptual clarity, potential theoretical significance, and encouraging results argue for serious consideration. With additional clarification on assumptions, fairer comparisons under matched information, and stronger empirical diagnostics, this work could be impactful for RLHF in sequential, stochastic domains.

On balance, I lean toward a borderline acceptance if the above issues can be addressed; otherwise, it is a strong candidate for a revision cycle.

papers.title: Learning Time-Varying Multi-Region Brain Communications  via Scalable Markovian Gaussian Processes

reviews.summary: This paper proposes the Adaptive Delay Model (ADM), a Markovian Gaussian Process framework for learning time-varying, directed communication with temporal delays across multiple brain regions from large-scale neural recordings. The core idea is to connect temporally stationary multi-output GP kernels to finite-order state space models (SSMs) by deriving VAR coefficients directly from kernel-implied autocovariances, enabling scalable, parallel-scan Kalman EM inference and continuous, per-time-step delay estimation. Experiments on synthetic data, V1–V2 recordings, and a five-region mouse visual dataset show improved test likelihoods and qualitatively meaningful, dynamically evolving communication patterns relative to delay and non-delay baselines.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The paper presents a practical construction that maps arbitrary temporally stationary multi-output GP kernels to finite-order SSMs through a regression/Yule–Walker style moment-matching of block Toeplitz autocovariances, avoiding separability constraints common in prior GP→SSM conversions.

The model introduces continuously time-varying temporal delays (θij,t) within a multi-region latent GPFA setting without discrete switching states, addressing a key limitation of prior delay models (e.g., DLAG/mDLAG static delays; MRM-GP discretized phase changes).
The use of parallel-scan Kalman filtering/smoothing for the time-varying SSM yields an O(log T) time complexity in the number of time steps for inference on suitable hardware.
Experimental rigor and validation
Demonstrates delay recovery on synthetic data with explicit time-varying delays and ablations over SSM order P, including runtime comparisons between sequential and parallel EM.
Evaluates on established V1–V2 and Allen Neuropixels visual datasets and reports consistent improvements in test log-likelihood over relevant baselines (DLAG, MRM-GP; mDLAG for 5-region).

Provides an auxiliary GP-regression study (Appendix D) across multiple single- and multi-output kernels, showing the SSM approximation achieves MSE close to exact GP regression across diverse kernels.
Clarity of presentation
The model is presented step-by-step: GPFA setup, kernel-to-SSM derivation, Markovianization, and time-varying delay extension, with derivations for key covariance constructions (VVᵀ, WVᵀ).
Figures qualitatively illustrate recovered delays and communications, aiding interpretation of dynamic forward/feedback motifs in visual cortex.
Significance of contributions
Addresses a timely and important problem in systems neuroscience: inferring time-varying inter-areal communication speeds and directions at scale.
The kernel-to-SSM recipe and parallel-scan inference can be of interest beyond neuroscience, for any domain requiring scalable multi-output GP inference with temporal structure.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The “universal connection” is effectively a finite-order VAR approximation derived from GP autocovariances (a classical idea in stationary time series), so the universality claim feels overstated without approximation error guarantees or stability conditions as P varies.

Time-varying delays θij,t are introduced without an explicit smoothness prior or dynamical model; sharing a fixed length-scale l across t is a weak regularizer and may not prevent overfitting or identifiability issues across multiple communication subspaces.
The construction requires adding small diagonal terms to process noise (Q̂) for numerical stability, but the implications for matching the original GP covariance are not analyzed.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Comparisons on the five-region dataset omit non-delay multi-region baselines (e.g., mp-srSLDS, MR-SDS), and the mDLAG comparison may be confounded by ADM’s inclusion of within-region latents (parameter-count mismatch).

Claims of O(log T) complexity are not stress-tested on very long sequences or larger N; experiments top out at T ≤ 600 and N = 5, while memory scales as O(M N² P² T) and time as O(M N³ P³ log T), which could be prohibitive at scale.
Quantitative delay recovery metrics (e.g., RMSE of θt) are not reported on synthetic data; evaluation focuses mainly on test likelihood and qualitative plots.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some notation and proportionality (use of “∝” in the covariance block expressions) are informal; scaling constants and finite-sample effects are not carefully treated.
Minor inconsistencies (e.g., monkey vs mouse in V1–V2 description), and limited discussion of identifiability constraints (e.g., enforcing θij,t = −θji,t, rotation/scale ambiguities between C and x).
Missing related work or comparisons

The link between stationary processes and finite-order/infinite-order AR (Yule–Walker/Whittle/Hannan–Deistler) is not fully contextualized; prior state-space representations for GPs via SDEs and spectral approximations (e.g., Hartikainen–Särkkä, Solin–Särkkä, Wilson’s spectral mixture to oscillatory SSMs) deserve deeper discussion and differentiation.
Frequency-domain approximations and multi-output state space constructions (e.g., LMC in SSM form) could be more comprehensively compared, both conceptually and empirically.
reviews.questions:
1. How are the time-varying delays θij,t parameterized and regularized in practice? Do you enforce θij,t = −θji,t and any smoothness prior (e.g., GP/spline) across t to avoid overfitting?
2. Can you report quantitative delay recovery metrics (e.g., RMSE, correlation) on synthetic data under varying SNR, P, and mismatch between true/assumed ma, mw?
3. How sensitive are the results to the choice of P? Is there a data-driven way to choose P (e.g., via BIC/AIC/CV) and to ensure Ât stability?
4. In the five-region comparison to mDLAG, how do parameter counts compare? Can you provide an ADM ablation without within-region latents (or otherwise match parameters) to ensure fairness?
5. Could you include comparisons to non-delay multi-region baselines (mp-srSLDS, MR-SDS) on the five-region dataset to isolate the benefit of modeling delays?
6. What are the practical runtime and memory profiles on larger T (e.g., ≥10^4) and larger N (e.g., ≥10), and do the O(M N³ P³ log T) and O(M N² P² T) scalings become limiting? Any strategies to reduce the cubic dependence on N and P?
7. The “universal connection” relies on finite-order approximations. Can you provide theoretical or empirical error analyses as P increases, and discuss conditions for consistency and stability?
8. How robust are the inferred communications to alternative kernels (e.g., MOSM/CSM) and to sharing/not sharing l across time? Any ablations on kernel choice and hyperparameter tying?
reviews.assessment: This paper tackles an important and timely problem—learning time-varying directed communications with delays across multiple brain regions—and proposes a practical, scalable solution by approximating multi-output GP kernels with finite-order SSMs amenable to parallel-scan inference. The combination of continuous delay dynamics, multi-region latent structure, and efficient inference is appealing, and the presented results are promising both methodologically and neuroscientifically. However, several claims (especially the “universal connection”) feel stronger than warranted without error/stability analyses; the treatment of time-varying delays lacks explicit regularization and identifiability discussion; and the empirical evaluation, while supportive, would be stronger with more rigorous fairness controls, larger-scale stress tests, and additional baselines. With clarifications and additional experiments addressing these points, ADM could make a valuable contribution to ICML, both for neuroscience applications and broader time series modeling. As it stands, I view this as a borderline-strong submission; addressing the questions above would tip it clearly toward acceptance.

papers.title: Fully Dynamic Euclidean Bi-Chromatic Matching in Sublinear Update Time

reviews.summary: This paper introduces the first fully dynamic algorithm for Euclidean bi-chromatic matching in R^2 that achieves sublinear worst-case update time. The approach uses a bottom-up, p-ary quadtree (restricted p-tree) combined with “implicit” matchings solved on aggregated sub-instances (transportation between subcell centers) and on-demand conversion to explicit matchings. For any ε in (0,1], the data structure maintains an expected O(1/ε)-approximate matching with O(n^ε · ε^{-1}) update time, and experiments show dramatic speedups over static recomputation while providing accurate estimates of the 1-Wasserstein distance on both synthetic and real datasets.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces the first fully dynamic sublinear-update algorithm for Euclidean bi-chromatic matching, a core primitive for 1-Wasserstein distance estimation.
Proposes a bottom-up quadtree variant with implicit geometric transportation at cell centers that neatly decouples per-cell work from the total number of points.

The notion of maintaining implicit matches and converting to explicit ones when needed is elegant and practically relevant; the paper also sketches an explicit-maintenance variant via short augmenting paths.
Experimental rigor and validation
Provides an open-source C++ implementation and evaluates on large-scale synthetic and real data (NYC taxi), demonstrating millisecond-level updates at scale (up to 10^6 samples).
Empirical accuracy is close to exact and significantly better than the worst-case bound, and dynamic maintenance decisively outperforms periodic static recomputation.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level algorithmic ideas (p-tree organization, implicit/explicit matching, bottom-up maintenance) are clearly communicated, with intuitive figures and a structured pipeline.
The static algorithm is reworked bottom-up for clarity of subsequent dynamization.
Significance of contributions
Dynamic OT/EMD is a compelling and timely problem for ML applications such as drift monitoring; a sublinear-update solution can materially change what is feasible in practice.
The work bridges geometric approximation techniques and dynamic data-structural maintenance, with potential to inspire further dynamic geometric optimization results.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

There is a critical tension between the claimed O(n^ε) update time and the stated per-cell subroutine bounds: IMPLICIT-MATCHING runs in O(p^5 log p log n), and leaf recomputation via Hungarian is O(|Y_v|^3) with |Y_v| ≤ p^2. With p^2 chosen as Θ(n^ε) (as suggested in the overview), these yield per-node work as large as n^{2.5ε}–n^{3ε}, seemingly incompatible with O(n^ε) updates unless parameters are calibrated differently or faster subroutines are used; the paper does not reconcile this.
The approximation guarantee is only in expectation (via a single random shift) and the adversary model is not specified; expected guarantees can be fragile under adaptive updates.

The dynamic model oscillates between “pair insertions/deletions” (to maintain |A|=|B|) and single-point insertions (Section 4). It is unclear whether the structure supports arbitrary single updates while preserving a perfect matching or reverts to partial matching.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Baselines are limited to static recomputation variants; no comparison to popular approximate OT methods amenable to incremental updates (e.g., entropic Sinkhorn warm starts, quantization-based accelerations) is provided.
The experiments do not measure recourse (number of changed edges) or the overhead of explicit reporting, despite the importance for real-time applications.
The relation between p and the theoretical ε, and how this translates to observed approximation factors, is not quantified.
Clarity or presentation issues

Several key technical claims are deferred to appendices (e.g., “only two points change per cell after an update,” the low-edit implicit matching update), but the main text depends on them critically; readers cannot fully assess soundness from the body.
Minor inconsistencies/typos and formatting artifacts (e.g., random symbols, duplicated citations) distract, and the dependence on dimension d beyond 2 is asserted but not articulated.
Missing related work or comparisons
While dynamic optimal transport (Xu & Ding) is discussed, the paper could better position its geometric approach against incremental entropic OT or streaming/quantization EMD estimators.

The lower bound that (2−δ)-approximation with sublinear updates is impossible is only cited from an appendix (not included here); given its importance to contextualize the O(1/ε) factor, more visibility is warranted.
reviews.questions:
1. How do you reconcile the O(n^ε) per-update claim with Lemma 3.1’s O(p^5 log p log n) and the leaf Hungarian O(p^6) bounds when p^2 is stated to be Θ(n^ε)? What precise choice of p as a function of n and ε yields your final update bound, and how does this affect the “O(n^ε)-subcell” and “O(ε^{-1})-levels” statements?
2. Can you clarify the adversary model for the expected approximation guarantee? Does the bound hold against an adaptive adversary after a single random shift, or do you assume an oblivious adversary/update sequence?
3. Are updates restricted to paired insertions/deletions of one red and one blue point to maintain |A|=|B| at all times? If single-point updates are allowed (as in Section 4), what object is maintained (perfect vs. maximum-cardinality matching) and how does this affect time/approximation?
4. For the “improved dynamic algorithm” maintaining explicit matchings, could you summarize in the main text the key lemma that limits per-update changes to a short alternating path and provide its worst-case recourse bound?
5. Is there a faster specialized solver for the per-cell aggregated transportation instances that improves on O(p^5) by exploiting the grid or geometric structure (e.g., sparsity, Monge-like properties), thereby making the O(n^ε) bound straightforward?
6. In experiments, how do p and ε map numerically, and what is the empirical approximation factor vs. p (with error bars)? Could you also report memory usage and explicit recourse statistics?
7. Could you provide a brief outline of the (2−δ) lower bound construction in the main paper (assumptions, model, reduction target), given its centrality in motivating the approximation tradeoff?
reviews.assessment: This paper tackles an important and timely problem and proposes a novel and practically effective dynamic approach to Euclidean bi-chromatic matching with demonstrable benefits for dynamic Wasserstein estimation. Conceptually, the bottom-up implicit-matching framework is elegant, and the empirical results are compelling. However, there is a significant gap in the time-complexity exposition: as written, the per-cell subroutines and leaf recomputations appear too expensive to support the stated O(n^ε) worst-case update time under the parameter choices described. This mismatch, along with an unspecified adversary model for the expected guarantee and ambiguity about the update model (paired vs. single insertions), prevents me from fully endorsing the theoretical claims. I believe the paper can reach the bar with a careful re-calibration of parameters (or faster subroutines), a clarified adversary/update model, and a more thorough main-text presentation of critical lemmas that underpin the dynamic updates. Given the strong potential impact and promising empirical validation, I encourage a revision that addresses these concerns.

papers.title: Generalized Random Forests Using Fixed-Point Trees

reviews.summary: This paper proposes GRF-FPT, a modification to the Stage I splitting procedure of generalized random forests (GRFs) that replaces the gradient/Jacobian-based pseudo-outcomes with a single fixed-point step using only score evaluations. The key idea is to approximate child-node parameters via one Picard-like update from the parent estimate, thereby avoiding Jacobian estimation and inversion; this yields an efficient CART-ready pseudo-outcome. The authors prove asymptotic equivalence of their splitting criterion to a weighted oracle heterogeneity criterion and argue that, because Stage II is unchanged, the standard GRF consistency and asymptotic normality guarantees apply. Empirically, GRF-FPT attains up to 3.5× training speedup without loss of accuracy across simulated varying-coefficient and heterogeneous treatment effect models, and demonstrates scalability on a real California housing dataset.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces a simple yet effective fixed-point pseudo-outcome that removes the need for Jacobian estimation/inversion while preserving the spirit of GRF’s heterogeneity-driven splitting.
