The framing occasionally overstates optimization of the “original” (unregularized) value. The absence of even small-scale experiments and of an integrated environment-sample complexity further weakens the empirical credibility. Overall, I view this as a solid and interesting theoretical contribution with novel ideas that could stimulate further research, but I have reservations about the strength of assumptions and practical applicability at this stage. I lean toward a borderline recommendation; adding empirical illustrations and clarifying/pruning assumptions would significantly strengthen the case.

papers.title: Continuous machine learning on Euclidean graphs with unordered vertices

reviews.summary: This paper introduces the Nested Centered Distribution (NCD), a family of rigid-motion-invariant, permutation-invariant, and Lipschitz-continuous descriptors for Euclidean graphs with unordered vertices. The authors prove that NCD of order n (in R^n) is a complete invariant that uniquely identifies an embedded graph up to rigid motion and can be inverted in polynomial time; they further define a Nested Bottleneck Metric (NBM) that induces a Lipschitz-stable metric on the space of rigid equivalence classes. Empirically, the paper demonstrates a hierarchy of increasingly expressive invariants and reports fast, highly accurate element identification from local radial distances and separation of chemically different molecules in large molecular datasets.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The paper proposes NCD, a new invariant for Euclidean graphs that is complete up to rigid motion and computable in polynomial time for fixed n, addressing both unlabeled vertex permutation and geometric isometries jointly.
The construction is carefully nested (centered representations aggregated over anchors), enabling invertibility and obviating exponential enumeration over permutations or graphs.

The authors augment the invariant with a Lipschitz-stable metric (NBM) built from bottleneck matchings over max-metrics on centered representations, including a smoothing factor via triangle “strength” to handle orientation sign changes robustly.
The hierarchy SRD → SPD → PDD → NCD is well-motivated and practically useful as a cascade for efficiency vs expressivity.
Experimental rigor and validation
Large-scale screening on QM9 and GEOM_drugs indicates that simple radial summaries (SRD) already separate many structures, and the full NCD provides stronger separation when needed.
The element-prediction experiment shows that very short-range geometric cues (few nearest-neighbor distances) are highly informative; the pipeline is simple and reproducible.
Clarity of presentation
The problem statement is clearly formulated (Problem 1.1) with precise desiderata: completeness, Lipschitz continuity, invertibility, and computability.
Definitions are modular (SRD, SPD, PDD, CR, NCD, NBM) and the hierarchy is visually explained.
Significance of contributions
A complete, stable, computable invariant and metric for Euclidean graphs addresses foundational needs in geometric ML where permutation and symmetry pose persistent challenges.

The approach is broadly relevant beyond chemistry (e.g., pattern recognition for unlabeled Euclidean graphs) and provides theoretically grounded “coordinates” on the space of rigid equivalence classes.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Completeness for higher dimensions and degeneracies (e.g., all vertices confined to a lower-dimensional affine subspace) relies on appendices; the main text does not fully detail how uniqueness is ensured in measure-zero or fully degenerate cases without general-position assumptions.

The use of signed distances to encode edge presence is elegant but presupposes that graph edges are given and do not change under small perturbations; the behavior across bond-rearranging conformational changes or when edges are uncertain/noisy is not discussed.

The smoothing via triangle strength is key to Lipschitz continuity at orientation sign flips, but the geometric intuition and constants are largely delegated to prior work and appendices; sensitivity in nearly-degenerate anchors could be elaborated.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Empirical validation is mainly descriptive; there is no head-to-head comparison against widely used molecular descriptors (e.g., Coulomb matrices, SOAP/ACE/MBTR) on standard prediction tasks to contextualize benefits beyond uniqueness.

The very strong claim that chemically different molecules in QM9 and GD can be separated by a small number of farthest SRD entries is intriguing but under-documented: statistics, error rates, and robustness analyses (e.g., to coordinate noise, conformer variability) are missing.

The element-prediction baselines cited are drawn from different modalities/tasks (literature embeddings, composition-only models), so direct comparability is limited; a graph-geometry baseline with similar inputs would be more convincing.
Computation of NBM at higher orders can be expensive; scalability beyond screening subsets is not thoroughly analyzed, and wall-clock/resource details for the more complex stages are thin.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some notation and terminology (e.g., “pseudo-metric L∞ on SRD” vs metric after sorting) could be tightened; occasional typos and formatting artifacts distract.
The boundary between point clouds (no edges) and Euclidean graphs (with edges) is sometimes blurred in exposition; clearer statements about what parts require edge information would help.
Missing related work or comparisons
While the paper cites recent works on complete representations for point clouds, the empirical section does not compare to common invariant descriptors used in molecular ML in a controlled setting.

Additional discussion of invertible/factorizable graph representations and canonical forms (e.g., for 3D molecular graphs) would better situate the contribution relative to chemical informatics descriptors and canonicalization procedures.
reviews.questions:
1. Completeness under degeneracy: How does NCD handle cases where all points lie in a lower-dimensional affine subspace (e.g., planar molecules in R^3 or collinear point sets in R^2)? Can you provide a concise statement (and intuition) in the main text that covers these edge cases without appealing to general position?
2. Edges and stability: Since signed distances encode edge/non-edge status, what happens if the edge set can change across conformers or is inferred from geometry with thresholds? Is NBM stable with respect to small changes in edge sets, and is there a variant of NCD that degrades gracefully when edges are uncertain?
3. Complexity and constants: Could you report concrete wall-clock times and memory usage for NBM at orders h=2 and h=3 on representative subsets (e.g., m=30–100) and describe the practical breakpoints for using each level of the cascade?
4. Empirical evidence on “distinguishability”: The claim that a handful of farthest SRD entries separates all distinct compositions in QM9/GD is striking. Can you provide summary statistics (number of collisions, exact m and rounding precision required) and a small failure analysis if any?
5. Baselines and tasks: Can you include a controlled comparison against standard molecular geometry descriptors (e.g., Coulomb matrices, SOAP/ACE) on a simple recognition or retrieval task to quantify the practical advantage of NCD/ NBMs under noise and permutations?
6. 3D completeness in the main text: Since applications are primarily 3D, could you move a concise version of the n=3 completeness/invertibility/stability statements from the appendix into the main body, including the minimal anchor order and any special handling for mirror images?
7. Code and reproducibility: Will you release code and precomputed invariants/metrics for QM9 and GEOM_drugs to facilitate adoption and verification?
reviews.assessment:
This paper tackles a fundamental and under-served problem in geometric machine learning for Euclidean graphs with unordered vertices: constructing a complete, Lipschitz-stable, and computable invariant with an associated metric. The proposed Nested Centered Distribution and Nested Bottleneck Metric satisfy these desiderata (under the provided theorems), generalize earlier work beyond point clouds to graphs with edges, and are organized in a practical cascade that balances efficiency and expressivity. The theoretical contribution is strong and, if proofs hold as stated, of clear significance.

On the empirical side, the demonstrations are promising but limited. The striking claims about separability using very small subsets of SRD coordinates merit a deeper quantitative substantiation, and comparisons to standard geometric descriptors on benchmark tasks would strengthen the case for impact at ICML. Some treatment of degeneracies and edge uncertainty in the main text would also improve clarity and confidence.

Overall, I view this as a theoretically substantial contribution with high potential value to the ICML community, especially given the importance of invariant, stable representations for learning on geometric data. I recommend acceptance contingent on bolstering the empirical evaluation and clarifying edge/degeneracy handling, but I acknowledge that the current experimental section is lighter than typical ICML standards.

papers.title: Machine learning on rigid classes of Euclidean clouds of unordered points

reviews.summary: The paper tackles machine learning on unordered Euclidean point clouds under rigid motions by formulating a precise desiderata (Problem 1.1) that include completeness, Lipschitz bi-continuity with a true metric, realizability (invertibility with an explicit parameterization), point-matching guarantees, and polynomial-time algorithms. It proposes a new invariant, the Nested Distributed Projection (NDP), with an associated metric (NBM), and proves for n=2 that NDP is complete and bi-Lipschitz (with explicit constants), has an efficiently computable metric, and supports realizability via simple linear constraints; extensions to n>2 are discussed in the appendices. The paper further provides large-scale experiments on molecular datasets (QM9, GEOM_drugs), showing that geometric invariants (including simpler ones like SRV, SDV, PDD) separate molecules effectively and can predict atomic species from local distance signatures with high accuracy.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces a per-point, projection-based invariant (NDP) that is mathematically simple yet sufficiently rich to be complete for unordered planar point clouds.

Establishes a constructive realizability condition for the local point-based representation PR(A; p) via explicit linear constraints on [s, M] (sum rules ensuring centroid at the origin), giving an explicit parameterization of realizable values.

Defines a metric (NBM) on invariant values that satisfies the metric axioms, is Lipschitz in the input perturbation with explicit constants, and admits a polynomial-time algorithm for fixed dimension.
Provides an inverse Lipschitz-style point-matching guarantee (1.1(e)) in 2D with an explicit constant, going beyond prior work that focused only on forward Lipschitz continuity.
Experimental rigor and validation

Presents a hierarchical large-scale comparison pipeline on QM9, filtering with fast pseudo-metrics (SRV/SDV/PDD) and confirming hard cases with the complete NDP/NBM, illustrating practicality at scale.
Demonstrates robustness to noise for NBM (empirical linear dependence on perturbation magnitude, consistent with the theorem).
Includes case studies (e.g., the classical distance-based counterexamples) where NDP distinguishes non-isometric clouds that defeat SDV/PDD.
Clarity of presentation
Clearly states the global desiderata (Problem 1.1) and positions the contribution relative to each item.
Provides intuitive geometric interpretations (e.g., PR as coordinates in bases {p, p⊥}, mirror behavior) and supporting diagrams.
Complexity bounds are explicit, and the construction is modular (PR → NDP → NBM), aiding understanding.
Significance of contributions

A full solution of Problem 1.1 for n=2 (including realizability and inverse Lipschitz point matching) is a strong theoretical advance with practical ramifications for registration, similarity search, and ML on unlabelled clouds.
The explicit, efficiently-computable invariant/metric pair is of wide interest in geometric ML and computational geometry, and the empirical evidence suggests relevance for molecular modeling.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The inverse Lipschitz/point-matching guarantee (1.1(e)) is proved only for n=2; for n=3, only forward Lipschitz continuity and completeness claims are indicated, with inverse continuity suggested empirically but not proved.

The completeness claim for NDP is strong; while plausible, the main text gives only high-level intuition for Theorem 3.5. Given the subtlety of completeness results, more proof detail or precise dependencies/assumptions (e.g., handling degenerate configurations) would help evaluation.
The metric PRM combines several terms by a max; while this enforces the metric axiom, the choice and relative scaling merit discussion and ablation to confirm necessity and tightness of constants.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

The headline molecular result (predicting chemical element labels from k-NN distance profiles with ~98% accuracy) is compelling but orthogonal to NDP; it does not stress-test the proposed complete invariant relative to strong baselines on downstream ML tasks (e.g., conformation clustering, retrieval, geometry-based classification) where completeness/bi-Lipschitz properties could matter most.

The chemical claims sometimes appear overstated: the experiments show high but not perfect accuracy; asserting injectivity from “pure geometry” to full chemical identity needs careful qualification, controls (e.g., class imbalance, confounding by typical bond lengths), and calibration against known counterexamples (e.g., near‑isoelectronic substitutions).
Clarity or presentation issues

The paper occasionally over-claims scope (“full solution” versus the stated limitation for (e) in 3D) and could benefit from more explicit, consolidated statements delineating what is proved for n=2 versus what is conjectured or provided in appendices for n>2.
Some definitions in edge cases (e.g., PR when p=0) are briefly addressed; a concise lemma about their role in completeness would preempt confusion.
Missing related work or comparisons

Prior complete and continuous invariants for unordered point clouds (e.g., SCD/OSD and related simplexwise constructions by Widdowson & Kurlin, 2023/2026) are cited but the novelty boundary could be sharpened: which parts of Problem 1.1 are new here (notably realizability as explicit parameter ranges and inverse Lipschitz bounds in 2D), and how do complexity/metric properties compare directly?

Comparisons to recent Euclidean WL-based completeness results (2-SEWL/3-EWL) could be expanded to emphasize differences: theoretical guarantees (completeness vs Lipschitz/metrics), computational scaling, and practical invariance to degeneracies.
reviews.questions:
1. Can you provide a concise proof sketch (or key lemmas) for Theorem 3.5 (completeness of NDP) in the main text, particularly addressing how degenerate/symmetric configurations (e.g., multiple points at the centroid, collinear sets) are handled?
2. For n=3, which parts of Problem 1.1 are fully proved in the appendices, and which remain conjectural? In particular, what is the precise status of realizability (d) and point matching (e) in 3D?
3. How sensitive is NBM to the choice of PRM components and their aggregation (the max of |||p|-|q||, |R(A)−R(B)|, and BD of normalized M)? Do ablations (e.g., removing |R(A)−R(B)| or using a sum instead of max) materially affect Lipschitz constants or matching accuracy?
4. Could you outline an explicit reconstruction algorithm from NDP for n=2 (beyond the realizability of individual PRs), with its computational complexity, and clarify whether a “small part” of the invariant (the stated R^{n(m−(n+1)/2)} vector) suffices deterministically for all configurations?
5. In the molecular experiments, did you control for class imbalance and potential confounders (e.g., typical bond-length priors differing across elements)? Can you share confusion matrices and results under rebalancing or stratified splits? How do results transfer between QM9 and GEOM_drugs?
6. How does NBM compare empirically to the earlier SCD/OSD metrics on hard synthetic cases and on molecular pairs, both in accuracy (mirror separation, near-duplicates) and runtime?
7. For large m, the O(m^{3.5} log m) matching may still be costly. Are there sampling or multiscale strategies (e.g., subset selection of PRs or columns) that preserve guarantees while reducing computation?
reviews.assessment:
This is a strong theoretical paper that advances the foundations of invariant, metric-based learning on unordered point clouds. The proposed NDP/NBM framework offers a clean, efficient construction with completeness, a genuine Lipschitz metric, an explicit realizability parameterization for local PRs, and an inverse matching guarantee in 2D—collectively meeting the discriminative and (partly) generative desiderata in Problem 1.1. These are substantial contributions beyond most existing learned or heuristic descriptors, and the implementation appears practical for moderate sizes with polynomial complexity. The empirical section confirms scalability via a hierarchical pipeline and provides interesting molecular findings, though the latter are only loosely connected to NDP.

The main reservations concern scope and positioning: the strongest inverse result is proved only in 2D, while for 3D the paper currently falls short of a full solution to Problem 1.1(e); comparisons to prior complete invariants (SCD/OSD) could be sharper in terms of novelty and practical trade-offs; and some chemical claims should be tempered or better controlled. With clarifications and modest revisions to better delineate the advances over prior work, I believe the paper would be a valuable contribution to ICML. I lean toward acceptance based on the theoretical significance and clear potential impact.

papers.title: TS-RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation based Time Series Foundation Models are Stronger Zero-Shot Forecaster

reviews.summary: This paper proposes TS-RAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework for time-series foundation models (TSFMs) aimed at improving zero-shot forecasting and interpretability. The approach retrieves top-k semantically similar context–future pairs from an external time-series knowledge base using a frozen TSFM encoder and fuses their projected representations with a frozen TSFM backbone via a learnable Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) augmentation module. The authors report consistent improvements over strong TSFM baselines (notably Chronos-Bolt) on seven benchmarks, modestly reducing MSE/MAE while offering qualitative interpretability through retrieved exemplars.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
The use of a dedicated MoE-based augmentation layer that attends over retrieved future horizons and the query representation is a thoughtful, model-agnostic design beyond simple concatenation.

Clean separation between frozen backbone and a lightweight trainable adapter aligns with current practice for parameter-efficient adaptation and facilitates plug-and-play integration with different TSFMs.
Experimental rigor and validation
Results span seven commonly used benchmarks (ETTh1/2, ETTm1/2, Weather, Electricity, Exchange), with gains over a strong baseline (Chronos-Bolt).

Ablations probe the effect of the number of retrieved sequences (k), retrieval databases (pretraining vs. in-domain historical), and retrieval lookback window lengths, plus extended horizons via rolling forecasts.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level pipeline—encoder-based retrieval, MoE fusion, and frozen TSFM output—is easy to follow, and equations provide a concrete instantiation.
Case studies visualize retrieval quality and its impact on forecast alignment, supporting the interpretability claim qualitatively.
Significance of contributions
Retrieval-augmented forecasting is an increasingly relevant direction for FMs, and the proposed adapter offers a practical, low-touch way to improve zero-shot performance.
The qualitative interpretability benefit (showing similar retrieved exemplars that underlie the forecast) is valuable in application settings.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The novelty is incremental relative to recent retrieval-augmented time-series works; the main algorithmic contribution is a particular MoE fusion of retrieved horizons and the backbone representation.

Some architectural details are ambiguous (e.g., whether the projection/output head is frozen or trained, consistency between text/figure, gating computed from E_concat vs. E_att), which affects replicability and interpretation of improvements.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Missing direct comparisons to closely related retrieval-augmented baselines (e.g., RAF/RAF-Advanced, TimerAG) and to recent retrieval-free parametric memory adapters (TS-Memory) weaken claims of state-of-the-art gains attributable to retrieval and fusion design.

No measurement of retrieval overhead, latency, or memory/storage costs for large knowledge bases (e.g., 2.8M pairs) and FAISS indexing; practical efficiency is central to RAG viability yet unreported.
Reported gains are modest on average (≈3.5% MSE, 1.4% MAE), and statistical significance is not assessed.

The “zero-shot” protocol relies on dataset-specific training splits as retrieval databases at inference; while common in RAF-style setups, stronger baselines leveraging in-domain non-parametric neighbors (e.g., kNN/DTW or simple retrieval-plus-linear fusion) are absent.
Clarity or presentation issues

Inconsistencies in the figure and text about which layers are frozen/trainable (projection head labeled both trainable and frozen in different places); the training objective for the MoE adapter is implied but not crisply specified.
Details on normalization, embedding dimensionality, and multi-variate handling (which channels are embedded/retrieved/used in fusion) are insufficiently described.
Missing related work or comparisons

Recent and highly relevant works are not compared empirically: Retrieval Augmented Forecasting (RAF; 2024), TS-Memory (parametric memory distillation; 2025), and RAID (metadata-driven retrieval for cold-start; 2024) from the provided summaries.
Discussion lacks an explicit positioning of TS-RAG’s MoE fusion relative to naive concatenation, learned gating without attention, or per-horizon fusion baselines.
reviews.questions:
1. Which layers are trainable vs. frozen in practice? The text and figure sometimes conflict (projection layer shown as both trainable and frozen). Please specify precisely which parameters are updated during adaptive pretraining.
2. How are embeddings normalized for retrieval (L2 normalization/cosine vs. raw ℓ2)? Are contexts and futures instance-normalized or aligned (endpoint/scale) before retrieval, as done in RAF?
3. Are the retrieved pairs multivariate (all channels) or univariate (target-only)? How are multivariate inputs handled in both retrieval and fusion?
4. What is the full architecture and size of the MoE adapter (MHA heads, hidden dims, gating MLP), and what is the training loss/objective used during adaptive pretraining?
5. What is the computational overhead at inference (latency per series, throughput) and the memory/storage footprint of the retrieval database for 2.8M pairs? Please report with and without FAISS, and include wall-clock comparisons to the frozen backbone without retrieval.
6. What hyperparameters were tuned per dataset (e.g., k, lookback length, retrieval database choice), and how was tuning performed without violating zero-shot protocol?
7. Can you include baselines for simple retrieval fusion (e.g., top-k normalized future averaging, linear blending with the TSFM output) and direct comparisons to RAF (naive and fine-tuned) and TS-Memory to isolate the benefit of your MoE design?
8. How sensitive are results to using only the Chronos pretraining database (no in-domain historical retrieval) at inference? Table 2 suggests in-domain helps; please quantify across all datasets and discuss deployment when in-domain history is limited or absent.
9. Do the retrieved examples sometimes come from the same series as the query (earlier periods)? If so, how do you prevent trivial near-duplicate retrieval from inflating performance, and do you enforce temporal or series-level exclusion constraints?
reviews.assessment: TS-RAG presents a reasonable and practically motivated retrieval-augmented adapter for frozen time-series foundation models, with a neat MoE fusion that consistently improves zero-shot performance and offers intuitive interpretability via retrieved analogs. The empirical gains, while consistent, are modest, and the work lacks key comparisons to very recent, closely related methods (RAF, TS-Memory) that directly target retrieval-augmented or retrieval-free adapters for TSFMs. Important details about which layers are trained, normalization/handling of multivariate signals, and inference overhead are missing or ambiguous, and statistical significance is not assessed. In its current form, the contribution feels incremental relative to the rapidly evolving literature and does not yet meet the bar for ICML. With clarified methodology, stronger baselines (including competing retrieval-augmented and adapter-based methods), and a thorough efficiency analysis, the work could be substantially strengthened and become a valuable resource for the community.

papers.title: An efficient implementation for solving the all pairs minimax path problem in an undirected dense graph

reviews.summary: The paper proposes and implements an O(n^2) algorithm for computing the all-pairs minimax (a.k.a. widest/bottleneck) path distance matrix on undirected dense graphs by leveraging the classical fact that the path between two nodes in a minimum spanning tree (MST) minimizes the maximum edge along any path in the original graph. The method constructs an MST, processes its edges in descending order, removes each edge to form two components, and fills all cross-component pairwise distances with the edge’s weight, arguing each pair is written exactly once. Experiments in Python (with some C++ baselines for O(n^3) methods) report substantial runtime improvements vs. Floyd–Warshall and a recursive O(n^3) baseline, scaling to 10k nodes.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The paper gives a simple, implementable procedure that exploits the MST minimax property to fill the full pairwise minimax matrix. The divide-by-largest-edge-and-copy idea is intuitive and can be parallelized.
The emphasis on turning theoretical O(n^2) statements into a concrete implementation is practically motivated.
Experimental rigor and validation
The study reports wall-clock timings over datasets up to 10k nodes and compares against O(n^3) variants, showing large speedups.
Using both Python and C++ implementations for O(n^3) variants partially contextualizes language effects.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level algorithmic idea is easy to follow, and the Python snippet conveys the intended implementation structure.
The connection to the widest path (maximum capacity) variant and how to adapt the code is clearly stated.
Significance of contributions
Efficient computation of minimax/LLPD distances is useful to ML tasks (e.g., path-based clustering and robust similarity), and having a practically fast implementation is valuable.
The paper could, in principle, help bridge adoption barriers for path-based methods that rely on this distance.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The core idea is long known: minimax distances equal the maximum MST edge along the MST path; single-linkage dendrogram (SLINK) yields the same ultrametric. The claimed novelty (“first code implementation”) is incorrect; O(n^2) single-linkage implementations and routines that return cophenetic distances (which equal minimax distances under single linkage) exist (e.g., fastcluster, SciPy’s hierarchy + cophenet).

The correctness and O(n^2) complexity arguments are informal. The code repeatedly runs DFS after each edge removal; the total DFS cost needs a careful amortized argument. Sorting edges costs O(n log n), and common MST routines on dense graphs may be O(n^2) or O(n^2 log n) depending on implementation; the paper does not precisely specify the MST routine used to guarantee O(n^2).

The claim that using a bottleneck spanning tree may lead to inaccurate APPD while an MST is accurate is asserted without proof or counterexample; the standard property is that any MST preserves pairwise minimax values via paths in the MST.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Missing the most relevant baselines: single-linkage O(n^2) algorithms (SLINK/CLINK), computing the ultrametric/cophenetic matrix directly from a dendrogram, and MST-based union-find procedures that fill the matrix via recursive bisection. These are precisely the techniques the paper positions itself against.
No correctness validation is presented (e.g., comparing Algorithm 4 outputs to a verified O(n^3) method for small graphs and reporting zero-error rates).

The datasets and weight generation are not described in sufficient detail, and there is no breakdown by graph families (e.g., path-like vs. balanced-tree MSTs) that could affect amortized running time.
Clarity or presentation issues

The paper contains formatting artifacts, duplicated lines, and inconsistent complexity claims (e.g., MST_shortest_path appears as O(n log n) in a table but O(n^3 log n) in text; the provided implementation suggests at least quadratic-to-cubic behavior).
Several strong claims (e.g., “no code implementation exists,” “theoretical algorithms are impractical”) are not substantiated and are contradicted by widely used libraries and literature.
Missing related work or comparisons

The paper does not engage with standard single-linkage O(n^2) methods (Sibson’s SLINK and later practical implementations), nor with the common practice of extracting pairwise ultrametric (cophenetic) distances from dendrograms, which are equivalent to the minimax distances under single linkage.
Existing literature on LLPD and practical toolchains (e.g., JMLR’20, hierarchical clustering libraries) is not adequately compared against.
reviews.questions:
1. How do you ensure in your implementation that each pair (p, q) is written exactly once? The provided code does not guard against overwriting, and removing a later (smaller) edge along the u–v path could, in principle, revisit the pair; please clarify with a formal argument or code-level invariant.
2. Which exact MST algorithm and data structures do you use to guarantee O(n^2) on dense graphs? NetworkX’s default implementations may not achieve this; can you provide a self-contained implementation using Prim with an adjacency matrix and report timings?
3. Please include correctness validation: for small/medium graphs, compare Algorithm 4 outputs to those from the O(n^3) Floyd–Warshall variant and report exact match rates.
4. Why do you not compare against single-linkage O(n^2) implementations (e.g., SLINK/fastcluster/SciPy) and report the time to compute the full cophenetic (ultrametric) matrix, which equals the minimax APPD? This seems to be the most relevant baseline.
5. Can you quantify the cumulative cost of the repeated DFS calls used to extract components after each edge removal, and bound it formally for worst-case MST shapes (e.g., a path/tree with high diameter)?
6. The paper claims that using a minimum bottleneck spanning tree (MBST) may yield inaccurate APPD values, whereas an MST is correct. Can you provide a formal proof or a counterexample to support this distinction?
7. The table lists conflicting complexities for MST_shortest_path (O(n log n) vs. O(n^3 log n) in text). Please correct and clarify the true complexity of that baseline and its implementation details.
8. Please release the code and data generation details, including how weights are defined for the datasets, so that results can be reproduced and compared.
reviews.assessment: The paper tackles an important and practical task—efficient computation of all-pairs minimax (widest) path distances on dense undirected graphs—and offers a straightforward implementation based on a well-known MST property. As an engineering note, this could be useful. However, the submission substantially overstates novelty (there are established O(n^2) single-linkage implementations that can produce the same matrix), omits the most relevant O(n^2) baselines, and lacks rigorous correctness and complexity analysis. Presentation quality is also below ICML standards, with formatting artifacts, inconsistencies, and unsubstantiated claims about the absence of code in prior work. With substantial revision—adding formal analysis, thorough correctness tests, strong baselines (SLINK/fastcluster/SciPy cophenetic), precise MST implementation details achieving O(n^2), and improved writing—the work could become a valuable practical reference. In its current form, I do not recommend acceptance at ICML.

papers.title: Consistent Multigroup Low-rank Approximation

reviews.summary: The paper proposes a new formulation and algorithmic framework for multigroup low-rank approximation that enforces a consistency (containment) property analogous to SVD: the rank-d solution is nested within the rank-(d+1) solution. The core idea is to select components one at a time by solving a rank-1 min–max problem that minimizes the worst-group “deficit” in captured variance relative to each group’s best rank-1 approximation, and to deflate the data by projecting to the orthogonal complement before selecting the next component. The authors derive a convex dual for the rank-1 problem, provide a Frank–Wolfe solver and an SDP relaxation, and prove strong duality and an exact, efficient algorithm for the two-group case; empirically, the method compares favorably to prior fair PCA approaches while ensuring consistency.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces a per-component, min–max “deficit” objective that composes additively under orthogonal deflation, enabling a consistent sequence of multigroup components analogous to SVD.
Derives a clean convex dual g(μ) = μ^T s − λ_max(A(μ)) over the simplex with an interpretable structure: the primal direction is the top eigenvector of a convex combination of group covariances.
Establishes strong duality and an exact, efficient solver in the two-group setting, including a one-dimensional root-finding characterization.
Provides an SDP relaxation and discusses tightness for two groups.
Experimental rigor and validation
Evaluates on several real datasets, reporting multiple metrics (marginal loss, incremental loss, reconstruction error) and runtime, and demonstrates clear consistency benefits.
Shows systematic runtime advantages over SDP-based fair PCA while achieving competitive accuracy.
Clarity of presentation
The overall framework, deflation procedure, and the role of the dual are well motivated and presented with helpful intuition.
Clear separation of the general k-group setting from the two-group special case with stronger guarantees.
Significance of contributions

Addresses a recognized limitation of prior fair PCA methods (lack of containment/consistency across ranks), which is both conceptually important and practically useful for scalable exploration of multiple target ranks.
The two-group optimality and equal-loss properties are of substantial theoretical and practical interest for common binary protected attributes.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns
For more than two groups, there is no optimality guarantee and the approach is fundamentally heuristic; this is acknowledged but remains a central limitation.

The Frank–Wolfe derivation includes a likely sign error in the gradient expression in the pseudocode (see Detailed Comments), and several minor algebraic inconsistencies (e.g., projection formula, SDP trace term notation) that should be corrected.

The method optimizes a particular “deficit” notion (relative to each group’s best rank-1) that, while natural for the proposed consistency property, is one of several plausible worst-case criteria; implications for other fairness/worst-case formulations (e.g., regret-normalized objectives) are not fully explored.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Comparisons are limited primarily to FAIR-PCA-SDP and one bicriteria baseline; strong recent alternatives (e.g., worst-case PCA formulations, MM-based FPCA, and recent two-group eigensolvers) are not included.
In the multi-group setting, some plots suggest that the incremental loss can be larger than baselines even if more balanced across groups; the paper does not analyze this trade-off in depth.
Clarity or presentation issues
A few mathematical typos and notational slips can impede careful readers (e.g., projection x onto span(V) should be V V^T x; Algorithm 2 line 6 sign; in SDP, Tr(A^i X) should be Tr((A^i)^T A^i X)).

The optimization status of the Frank–Wolfe procedure (maximizing a concave dual objective) should be described more precisely to avoid confusion with the minimization form often associated with Frank–Wolfe.
Missing related work or comparisons

There appears to be substantial overlap with “Fair PCA, One Component at a Time” (Matakos et al., arXiv 2025), which presents the same per-component deficit objective, the same dual g(μ), the Frank–Wolfe solver, an SDP relaxation, and the two-group strong duality and root-finding characterization. The submission does not position itself relative to this work, raising novelty concerns.

The paper does not compare or connect to worst-case PCA formulations with robustness guarantees over convex hulls of covariances (wcPCA) nor to recent efficient two-group FPCA algorithms via joint numerical ranges. These are important references for context and empirical comparison.
reviews.questions:
1. Please clarify the novelty relative to “Fair PCA, One Component at a Time” (Matakos et al., arXiv 2025), which appears to present the same objective, dual, Frank–Wolfe approach, and two-group strong duality/root-finding solution. What new theory, algorithms, or empirical insights does this paper add beyond that work?
2. In Algorithm 2, line 6 sets (∇g)_i ← s_i + v^T (A^i)^T A^i v, but Eq. (6) states (∇g)_i = s_i − v^T (A^i)^T A^i v. Which is correct? Please fix the sign and any implications for the update (line 7).
3. In the SDP relaxation (Algorithm 3), should the constraint be σ_1^2(A^i) − Tr((A^i)^T A^i X) ≤ z with X ≽ 0 and Tr(X) ≤ 1 (and X intended to be v v^T)? Please correct the notation and state the solver and tolerances used.
4. For |G|>2, can you characterize when the greedy per-component construction provably approximates the global d-dimensional optimum (e.g., under spectral gap or near-commutativity assumptions)? Are there counterexamples (as in wcPCA) where the greedy approach fails badly?
5. Several multi-group plots (e.g., compas-3 incremental loss) suggest your method can have higher incremental loss than baselines even if more balanced. Can you quantify and discuss the trade-off between balance and absolute performance? How does the empirical duality gap correlate with these outcomes?
6. How sensitive are results to group scaling/normalization (e.g., using s_i normalized by Tr((A^i)^T A^i) or by group size)? Have you considered regret-normalized variants or connections to wcPCA’s normalized objectives?
7. Could you add comparisons to (i) MM-based FPCA (Babu & Stoica, 2023), (ii) worst-case PCA (wcPCA, 2024), and (iii) two-group EigOpt (2025) to more fully position the empirical performance?
reviews.assessment:
The paper tackles an important and timely problem—socially fair dimensionality reduction—through a principled reformulation that restores the SVD’s consistency property, which prior fair PCA methods lack. The technical development is elegant: the per-component min–max “deficit” objective composes additively under deflation, the dual is clean and interpretable, and the two-group case is theoretically tight with an efficient solver. Empirically, the method convincingly equalizes incremental losses for two groups with strong runtime advantages over SDP-based baselines and remains a promising heuristic for more than two groups.

However, there are two substantial concerns. First, the core ideas, dual formulation, solvers (Frank–Wolfe and SDP), and the two-group analysis appear to substantially overlap with prior work (“Fair PCA, One Component at a Time,” Matakos et al., 2025), which is not cited or discussed. Without a clear articulation of what is new, the contribution risks being incremental. Second, the experimental comparison set omits several closely related and recent methods (wcPCA, MM-based FPCA, two-group EigOpt), and the multi-group empirical trade-offs (balance vs. absolute loss) are not deeply analyzed. There are also a few correctness/notation issues to fix.

Overall, I find the consistency angle compelling and the two-group theory strong. If the authors can (i) clarify and substantiate novelty relative to the overlapping prior work, (ii) expand comparisons and analysis to position the method among recent alternatives, and (iii) correct the technical slips, this would make a solid contribution. As it stands, due to the unresolved novelty/context issues, I lean toward rejection, but I would be positive about a revised version that addresses these points.

papers.title: Graph Transformers Get the GIST: Graph Invariant Structural Trait for Refined Graph Encoding

reviews.summary: The paper proposes GIST, a pairwise structural encoding for Graph Transformers that summarizes the common k-hop neighborhoods between node pairs as a k×k grid of exact-distance intersection cardinalities, augmented with fringe terms. To make this feasible, the authors estimate pairwise neighborhood intersections using MinHash for Jaccard similarities and HyperLogLog for union cardinalities, reducing complexity from O(k^2 n^4) to O(k^2 n^2). GIST is integrated as an attention bias and feature in a transformer-style block, and the method is evaluated on LRGB, ZINC/ZINC-full, and MoleculeNet, showing strong performance, including new SOTA on several ZINC benchmarks.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Introducing a k×k “substructure vector” that captures counts of nodes at exact k-hop distances from both endpoints is a clean, permutation-invariant way to encode pairwise higher-order structure beyond shortest-path distances or simple random-walk statistics.
Leveraging MinHash and HyperLogLog to build scalable, pairwise structural features extends sketching-based ideas from link prediction to global, pairwise features usable in Transformers.
Integrating GIST as a learnable bias in attention is a principled way to inject structural context at the core of the model rather than as purely positional encodings.
Experimental rigor and validation
Broad set of datasets (LRGB peptides, ZINC and ZINC-full, and MoleculeNet) indicates generality across graph sizes and tasks (classification and regression).
Consistent improvements on ZINC and ZINC-full, with results surpassing strong baselines such as GRIT and Subgraphormer, support the practical value of the approach.
Ablation on k shows robustness and an interpretable trade-off.
Clarity of presentation
The intuition behind GIST is well motivated with clear figures demonstrating how intersection patterns can disambiguate substructures.
High-level algorithmic flow is understandable, and the role of each component (MinHash, HLL, integration into attention) is explained.
Significance of contributions

Addressing structural encoding in Graph Transformers is an important and active research area; GIST offers a complementary route to SPD/LapPE/RWPE by focusing on pairwise intersection patterns of k-hop shells.
The empirical gains on popular molecular datasets suggest immediate utility for the community working on graph transformers for chemistry and biology.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The product of two unbiased estimators (MinHash-based Jaccard and HLL-based union) is not necessarily unbiased without independence and/or additional assumptions; the paper asserts unbiasedness without a careful justification of independence or bias correction.

The theorem and associated proof use “invariance” language where “permutation equivariance” is expected for node-wise mappings; the presentation suggests ψ(x_u) is invariant under isomorphism, which, if taken literally, would make the node mapping constant. This needs to be fixed precisely.
The definition of T terms and some recurrences have notational inconsistencies (e.g., T_{k_u-1,k}(u) vs T_{k_u-1,k}(u,v)) and require more careful derivation to ensure correctness.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Lack of runtime/memory profiling and scalability discussion. GIST stores an n×n×(k^2+2k) tensor per graph; for larger graphs this can be prohibitive. There is no empirical analysis of compute/memory overhead vs. baselines or a study of sketch sizes (m, p) vs. accuracy/time.

The attention mechanism deviates from standard softmax normalization (using a sigmoid on a dot with e_{u,v}) without justification or ablation vs. standard multi-head scaled dot-product attention with bias; this complicates attribution of gains to GIST vs. architectural choices.

MoleculeNet evaluation details are insufficient: missing clarity on splits (scaffold vs. random), input features/preprocessing, and tuning budget parity across baselines; this affects fairness and comparability.
No controlled comparison where GIST replaces an existing structural bias in a matched Graphormer/GPS/GRIT implementation to isolate the effect of the proposed encoding.
Clarity or presentation issues
Several notational slips and typos in definitions and proofs; some equations are ambiguous enough to impede precise reimplementation (especially for T terms).
The proof sketch in Appendix A is informal and contains problematic equalities of sets under isomorphism; it should present a rigorous permutation-equivariance argument for the model outputs.
Missing related work or comparisons

Prior pairwise structural encodings relevant to subgraph-level discrimination are under-discussed, e.g., DRNL/SEAL-style labels, distance encodings, and other pairwise encodings used in link prediction and subgraph GNNs.
A deeper comparison to Graphormer’s edge/shortest-path/centrality encodings and to GPS/GRIT’s structural biases would help position GIST more precisely.
reviews.questions:
1. Is the product estimator of intersection size truly unbiased in your implementation? Are the MinHash and HLL estimators independent (using independent hash families), and do you apply bias correction for HLL? Please provide a derivation or an empirical calibration (exact vs. estimated) with bias/variance plots.
2. Why depart from standard softmax attention? Could you report ablations comparing (a) standard softmax attention with additive GIST bias vs. (b) your sigmoid gating vs. (c) bias-only integration? This would help isolate the benefit of GIST vs. architectural choices.
3. Please clarify the exact definition and computation of the T terms and fix the notational inconsistencies (e.g., T_{k_u-1,k}(u) vs. T_{k_u-1,k}(u,v)). A step-by-step pseudo-code for constructing S_k(u,v) from C_{k_u,k_v} would aid reproducibility.
4. What are the MoleculeNet split protocols (scaffold vs. random), and what input features are used? How do you ensure comparable hyperparameter tuning and training budgets vs. baselines?
5. Can you provide runtime and peak memory comparisons against GRIT/Graphormer/GPS on LRGB/ZINC, as well as sensitivity to sketch sizes (m, p)? How does training time scale with n and k in practice?
6. Does GIST preserve performance under sparse attention (e.g., top-K or locality-restricted) to reduce O(n^2) costs? Any preliminary results?
7. Could you formalize the model’s permutation equivariance property with a proper statement and proof (and correct Theorem A.1)? Also, can you characterize the expressivity of GIST: are there graph pairs or substructures that GIST can distinguish but SPD/RWPE cannot?
reviews.assessment: This paper addresses an important open question—how to inject rich, general-purpose structural bias into Graph Transformers—and proposes a compelling pairwise encoding based on exact-distance intersection cardinalities, along with practical sketching to make it computationally feasible. The idea is intuitive, well-motivated, and empirically promising, with notable gains on ZINC/ZINC-full and competitive results elsewhere. That said, there are several issues that should be addressed for ICML: the estimator unbiasedness claim needs justification or correction; the theoretical section should be reframed around permutation equivariance with a rigorous proof; clarity issues in definitions (especially T terms) should be fixed; and more thorough experimental analyses (runtime/memory, attention formulation ablations, fairness on MoleculeNet) are necessary. With these improvements, the contribution would be significantly strengthened. In its current form, I view the paper as promising and of interest to the graph learning community, but recommend revisions to solidify technical correctness and empirical rigor.

papers.title: GraphFLEx: Structure Learning $\underline{\text{F}}$ramework for $\underline{\text{L}}$arge $\underline{\text{Ex}}$panding $\underline{\text{Graph}}$s

reviews.summary: This paper proposes GraphFLEx, a modular framework for unsupervised graph structure learning tailored to large and expanding graphs. The key idea is to constrain candidate neighbors for new or existing nodes via a two-stage reduction—community detection followed by graph coarsening—and then run any standard unsupervised structure learning method on the reduced subgraph, with a final projection back to the original node space. The paper claims scalability benefits (near-linear or substantially reduced runtimes), flexible instantiations (48 combinations of clustering/coarsening/learning modules), and probabilistic neighborhood-preservation guarantees, and provides empirical results on a mixture of real and synthetic datasets.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The decomposition of structure learning into clustering → coarsening → local structure learning is conceptually appealing and simple, making known methods more scalable without requiring new core estimators.
The framework is flexible and unifies several families of algorithms (clustering, coarsening, unsupervised GSL), enabling practitioners to tailor methods to their constraints.
A probabilistic neighborhood-preservation argument based on LSH-style hashing provides some theoretical intuition for why candidate neighborhoods can be preserved after coarsening.
Experimental rigor and validation
The empirical study is broad, spanning 20+ datasets of different types and sizes, including expanding-graph scenarios.
The paper demonstrates meaningful wall-clock savings for large graphs and reports downstream node-classification accuracy across several GNN architectures.
Qualitative visualizations on small graphs and embeddings support interpretability claims.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level pipeline and the role of each module are clearly articulated and intuitive.
The problem setting (large graphs with missing structure and expanding graphs) is well-motivated and practically relevant.
Significance of contributions

The problem of scalable and incremental graph structure learning is important for many applications where explicit graphs are either missing or too costly to reconstruct repeatedly (e.g., citation networks, single-cell, recommender-style contexts).
A modular framework that can mix-and-match best-of-breed components is potentially valuable for the community.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The theoretical claims do not match the strength of the stated contribution. The paper claims “strong theoretical guarantees that the structure learned from a small subset of nodes is equivalent to that learned from the full set,” but the formal result provided is a probabilistic subset coverage of k-neighborhoods under coarsening and certain assumptions; no equivalence of learned structures is established.

The neighborhood-preservation theorem hinges on LSH-style bounds and implicitly assumes independence when taking products over distances; this seems too strong and is not justified. Moreover, it does not quantify false positives introduced by the coarsening step.

The reliance on DC-SBM for community detection consistency is restrictive and may not reflect many real-world graphs (esp. heterophily), and the paper does not analyze performance degradation under substantial inter-community connectivity.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

The “vanilla” baselines and GraphFLEx are not clearly matched in the incremental setting. It appears vanilla methods may be recomputed on the full graph or per-timestamp without analogous reduction, which could bias runtime comparisons. A fair incremental/streaming baseline (e.g., dynamic/online kNN graph construction such as NN-Descent variants, HNSW with insertions, incremental A-NN graph construction) is missing.

Several results look unusually strong (e.g., large boosts in accuracy compared to typical reported numbers on citation benchmarks), and standard train/val/test split protocols are not detailed. It’s unclear whether splits follow standard practice and whether hyperparameters are tuned comparably across methods.

The mechanism to infer cluster assignments for incoming nodes is under-specified. GNN-based clustering (e.g., DMoN) depends on graph connectivity; it is not clear how new nodes without edges are embedded and assigned (feature-only inference? auxiliary edges?). This is crucial for reproducibility.

There is no ablation on the sensitivity to clustering quality, bin width r, number of communities K, or coarsening parameters. Nor is there a study of the trade-off between recall of true neighbors and computational savings.
Clarity or presentation issues
Inconsistencies and typos (e.g., “12-model” vs l2, GraphFLEx vs GraphFLEX) and several formula artifacts hamper precision. Some equations are only sketched or informally justified.

Important implementation details are missing (e.g., parameter choices for each module, how many methods among the 48 were actually evaluated, how the final node selection within supernodes is thresholded/tuned).
The code link is “unknown,” limiting reproducibility.
Missing related work or comparisons

The paper does not sufficiently connect to scalable/incremental kNN graph construction methods (e.g., NN-Descent, HNSW/FAISS with dynamic insertions), dynamic neighborhood graphs, or streaming approximate neighbor graph builders common in large-scale settings.
Comparisons to scalable GSP-based or sparse-precision-graph learning that use sketching, pruning, or divide-and-conquer strategies are limited.
Related work on dynamic and incremental clustering and coarsening methods (beyond UGC) is only partially covered.
reviews.questions:
1. How exactly are incoming nodes embedded and assigned to communities when using GNN-based clustering (DMoN)? Do you connect them to G0 temporarily, use feature-only encoders, or re-embed using a learned MLP? Please detail the inference pipeline, including any required edges and computational costs.
2. What are the precise training/evaluation protocols for node classification (splits, transductive vs inductive setting, hyperparameter search ranges, early stopping criteria)? Many reported accuracies exceed canonical baselines—please clarify to ensure apples-to-apples comparisons.
3. For runtime comparisons, are “vanilla” baselines re-run from scratch at each timestamp while GraphFLEx updates incrementally? If so, please also include incremental/streaming neighbor-graph baselines (e.g., NN-Descent updates, HNSW/FAISS insertions) to make the comparison fair.
4. Theorem 1 assumes a product over p(c) for all relevant pairs. What independence assumptions underlie this product? Can you justify or empirically validate them (e.g., via synthetic experiments) and discuss the impact on the bound tightness?
5. The paper claims “equivalence” of learned structures from subsets vs full graphs, yet the theorem provides probabilistic subset coverage. Can you restate the main theoretical claim more precisely and align it with the actual proven results? Is there any guarantee on false positive rates?
6. How sensitive is performance to the bin width r, the number of communities K, and the choice of coarsener? Please provide ablations showing accuracy/runtime trade-offs and neighbor recall/precision under different settings.
7. Do you have results on heterophilous graphs (beyond small synthetic) or datasets with significant inter-community edges? How does GraphFLEx degrade as inter-community connectivity increases?
8. Of the “48 configurations,” which combinations were evaluated in Tables 3–5? Please enumerate the actual choices used per dataset to enable reproduction.
9. Can you report structure recovery metrics (precision/recall of edges, spectral distances) relative to the known original graphs to corroborate the “preservation” claim beyond downstream accuracy?
reviews.assessment: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem—scalable, incremental unsupervised graph structure learning—and proposes a simple, modular, and potentially useful framework. The idea of restricting candidate neighborhoods via clustering and coarsening is sensible and likely effective. The empirical section is broad and suggests meaningful computational savings and competitive downstream performance. However, there are substantial concerns around the strength and correctness of the theoretical guarantees, missing or unclear details of the incremental clustering inference mechanism, and fairness/rigor of the experimental comparisons (notably against incremental neighbor-graph baselines and with standard evaluation protocols). Several implementation and methodological details are under-specified, and some reported numbers are surprisingly high relative to established baselines. The contribution, while useful, feels more like a well-engineered composition of existing techniques than a fundamentally novel algorithmic or theoretical advance; for ICML, stronger theoretical grounding and more rigorous, fair empirical evaluation would be necessary. I recommend rejection in the current form, with encouragement to (i) tighten the theory to match claims (or restate claims), (ii) include fair incremental baselines and standard evaluation protocols, and (iii) provide thorough ablations and clarity on the inference pathway for incoming nodes. With these improvements and a public code release, this could become a strong systems-paper contribution.

papers.title: How Classifiers Extract General Features for Downstream Tasks: An Asymptotic Analysis in Two-Layer Models

reviews.summary: The paper studies when and how features learned by a classifier transfer to unseen classes for clustering tasks. In a two-layer network trained with one gradient step under the proportional regime, the authors decompose the learned feature into a random initialization term and a “spike” term aligned with pairwise class decision directions. They derive population-level cohesion and separability expressions that depend on train–unseen similarity (via β^Tμ), show that separability improves only when unseen classes are effectively assigned to different training classes, and provide synthetic and image-retrieval-style empirical evidence supporting the trends.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Extends one-step feature-learning analyses (e.g., spiked CK perspective) from in-distribution generalization to out-of-distribution feature transfer and clustering, articulating conditions in terms of train–unseen similarity.

Provides an intuitive “spike” view in multiclass settings: unseen inputs are mapped via a linear combination of classifier heads weighted by β_ij^T x, highlighting the role of non-orthogonal spikes in feature expressiveness.
Experimental rigor and validation
Synthetic experiments are carefully designed to manipulate β^Tμ through controlled translations/rotations, and multiple data types (non-centered sub-Gaussian families) are tested.
Trends in cohesion/separability and recall@1 across settings generally align with the theory’s qualitative predictions.
Clarity of presentation
Clear high-level narrative linking the decomposition to clustering risks and the role of assignment signs in separability.
Visualizations (e.g., heatmaps, slope summaries) help convey the main monotonicity patterns and the effect of spike alignment.
Significance of contributions
Addresses an important question: when do classifier-trained features transfer to unseen classes for clustering, and how does similarity to training classes matter?
Offers practical implications for metric learning: adding semantically related classes helps; unrelated classes do not necessarily improve clustering.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns
Core analysis relies on a single gradient step, MSE loss, and a two-layer architecture, which limits direct applicability to modern training (multi-epoch, cross-entropy, deep networks).

The general sub-Gaussian assumption is narrowed to isotropic Gaussians with identity covariance for the closed-form cohesion/separability derivations (Condition 4.4), reducing the generality promised by Assumption 2.2.

Several key monotonicity and sign claims are “numerical-analytical”; explicit closed-form characterizations of ρ-terms and rigorous proofs of positivity (e.g., ρ^(4) > 0) are deferred or not fully established in the main text.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Practical experiments (ResNet18/50) are not aligned with the theory’s training regime; the mismatch complicates causal interpretation of observed trends.

Adding “whole ImageNet” vs “domain-only” classes is not tightly controlled for number of samples, class balance, or domain mismatch; possible confounders (data volume/imbalance) are not exhaustively ruled out.
Lack of ablations on number of gradient steps, loss type (cross-entropy), and regularization leaves open whether conclusions persist under standard training.
Clarity or presentation issues
Notational/formatting artifacts (e.g., equation references, Hadamard powers and indices, repeated “Submission and Formatting…” inserts) impair readability and precise parsing of formulas.
Some definitions (e.g., spike_L with Hadamard powers, exact shapes of ρ-coefficients) are opaque in the main text and rely heavily on appendices.
Missing related work or comparisons
Discussion of connections and contrasts to NTK/CK transfer analyses and to recent findings on transferability of layer features in deep nets could be expanded.
Empirical comparisons to alternative theoretical explanations (e.g., neural collapse transfer predictions, ULPM-based insights) are qualitative; more direct tests would strengthen positioning.
reviews.questions:
1. Can you provide explicit closed-form expressions or tighter sign/monotonicity conditions for the ρ^(4) terms in Propositions 4.5–4.6, and formalize when they dominate the sums, beyond numerical evidence?
2. How sensitive are the main conclusions to moving from one gradient step to multiple steps? Do you observe the same spike structure and β^Tμ-dependence after several training epochs in the two-layer model?
3. What changes if you use cross-entropy instead of MSE in the two-layer analysis? Are there theoretical obstacles, or do you expect qualitatively similar β^Tμ effects?
4. In the real-data experiments, can you control for total number of training images and classes when adding “related” vs “unrelated” classes, to isolate domain relatedness as the driver of improvements?
5. Can you quantify orthogonality effects in multiclass more precisely (e.g., bounds showing the contribution of a spike decays with angle between β_ij and x), and validate them empirically?
6. For Expr VII, how exactly are “duplicatively assigned” unseen classes detected and removed? Could you report domain-wise results and whether the improvements are consistent across model capacities?
reviews.assessment: The paper tackles an important and timely question—feature transfer from classifier training to unseen classes for clustering—and offers a conceptually appealing “spike” perspective with tractable two-layer analysis. The extensions from prior one-step feature-learning work to transfer and clustering risks are interesting, and the synthetic experiments substantiate the qualitative claims. However, the theoretical results rely on restrictive settings (one step, MSE, isotropic Gaussians for key derivations), and several central monotonicity/sign claims are supported primarily via numerical observation rather than complete analytic proofs. The practical experiments indicate consistent trends but would benefit from stronger controls and alignment with the theoretical setting to draw firmer conclusions. Overall, I find the work promising and directionally insightful, but not yet at the level of rigor and empirical conclusiveness expected for ICML acceptance. Strengthening the formal results (clarifying the ρ-terms and their dominance), tightening experimental controls, and probing robustness to standard training regimes would significantly increase the paper’s impact.

papers.title: IO-LVM: Inverse Optimization Latent Variable Models with Graph-based Planning Applications

reviews.summary: The paper proposes IO-LVM, a latent-variable framework that learns low-dimensional representations of cost functions underlying constrained optimization problems (COPs) from observed solutions. Instead of decoding directly into the discrete feasible set, IO-LVM decodes latent variables into cost vectors and reconstructs solutions by invoking a black-box solver, using a Fenchel-Young loss with input perturbations to obtain gradients without differentiating through the solver. Experiments on synthetic path planning, real ship routing, and Hamiltonian cycles (TSP instances) suggest that the learned latent space is interpretable, can separate multiple agents with different implicit costs, and yields feasible reconstructions and reasonable distributional predictions.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Introduces a principled way to combine amortized latent-variable inference with inverse optimization via perturbed solvers and Fenchel-Young losses, enabling reconstruction through a non-differentiable COP solver.
Frames multi-agent or multi-context behavior as a low-dimensional latent distribution over costs, avoiding the single-cost assumption common in many IO/IRL setups.
Demonstrates a clean gradient estimator (x − x̂ε) for linear objectives, avoiding the need to differentiate through the solver and supporting black-box, combinatorial settings.
Experimental rigor and validation
Evaluations on three regimes: synthetic Waxman graphs (paths), real AIS ship trajectories (large graph), and Hamiltonian cycles (TSP) with two TSPLIB instances.
Qualitative analyses show interpretable latent clustering by agent or correlated, unobserved attributes (e.g., ship width).
Quantitative comparisons include reconstruction (edge recall on TSP) and distributional prediction (DJS, Spearman), ablations over β and latent dimensionality.
Clarity of presentation
Clear high-level pipeline with a two-stage decoder (latent-to-costs, costs-to-solution via solver) and an algorithm sketch describing training with stochastic gradients.
Intuitive visualizations of latent structure and reconstructed trajectories that help ground the method’s behavior.
Significance of contributions
Addresses the important challenge of structured decoding for combinatorial outputs while capturing multi-modality in underlying preferences.
Provides a practical recipe for learning from decision data when constraints are critical and solutions must be feasible by construction.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns
Assumes observed decisions are optimal for some underlying costs; ignores bounded rationality or suboptimality, which may be substantial in real data.
The formulation of the Fenchel-Young loss and “regularization” is nonstandard/potentially imprecise; theoretical grounding beyond citing prior work could be strengthened.
Identifiability and uniqueness of recovered costs are not discussed; many cost vectors can rationalize the same path, which impacts interpretability claims.
Scalability and computational cost are not rigorously analyzed; training relies on per-sample solver calls on CPU, but runtime and memory profiles are not reported.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Baselines are limited: no comparison to multi-intent/multi-task IRL, mixture models, or recent differentiable shortest path methods at scale; VAE baseline is weak since it cannot enforce feasibility.

For distributional prediction, the KDE-over-latents strategy and evaluation (especially on the ship dataset) are under-specified; metrics like per-sample DJS on edges may not reflect path-level quality.
Sensitivity to perturbation noise ε (distribution, variance) is not explored, though it is known to be crucial for perturbed optimizer methods.
The impact of the choice of prior (e.g., standard Gaussian) on multi-modality vs. posterior collapse is not deeply probed; no exploration of richer priors (mixtures/VampPrior).
Clarity or presentation issues
The “ELBO” terminology is used even though the reconstruction is a surrogate (Fenchel-Young) rather than a log-likelihood; the objective is not clearly a valid lower bound.
Some notation overload (ε for both reparameterization and perturbations), and occasional inconsistencies in the FY loss description could confuse readers.
Details of ship data preprocessing and the mapping to the grid graph are summarized but leave room for ambiguity (e.g., treatment of noise/outliers, path segmentation).
Missing related work or comparisons
Missing discussion of multi-intent IRL/mixture-of-costs approaches and latent-variable IRL variants that model heterogeneous agents.

Limited comparison to differentiable shortest path or soft dynamic programming approaches that can scale (e.g., entropic regularization/softmin path planning), and to recent decision-focused learning on graphs.
reviews.questions:
1. Please clarify the precise definition of your Fenchel-Young loss and its connection to the standard Ω/Ω* framework. Under which conditions does your loss correspond to a convex smoothing with gradient x − Eε[ω(y + ε)]?
2. What is the distribution and scale of the perturbation noise ε used during training and inference, and how sensitive are results to this choice?
3. The objective is described as a modified ELBO. Is it a proper lower bound on any log-likelihood? If not, how should we interpret the optimization (e.g., as a regularized autoencoding objective)?
4. How do you handle potentially non-unique optimal solutions (ties) in the solver, especially for TSP instances? Does tie-breaking affect the gradient estimator or stability?
5. Can you provide runtime and scalability statistics (e.g., solver calls per epoch, wall-clock time per epoch, memory) and how they scale with graph size and batch size?
6. For the ship dataset, how is KDE conditioned on start/target pairs at prediction time? Do you fit separate KDEs per (s, t), or condition via the encoder, or share a global KDE? How do you prevent train-test leakage?
7. Could you compare against at least one multi-intent/multi-task IRL baseline (e.g., mixture models) to substantiate the claim that IO-LVM handles heterogeneous agents better than traditional IRL?
8. How robust is IO-LVM to suboptimal or noisy trajectories that are not exact optimum of any cost vector? Can you incorporate slack/regularization in the solver or the loss to account for bounded rationality?
9. The latent prior is standard Gaussian. Did you try richer priors (mixtures, VampPrior) to better capture multi-modality without relying heavily on β tuning?
10. For distributional evaluation, can you report path-level metrics (e.g., top-k path recall, exact match rate, or route similarity indices) in addition to edge-level DJS?
reviews.assessment: This is a thoughtful and practically relevant contribution that bridges inverse optimization with latent-variable modeling to reconstruct and analyze structured solutions via black-box solvers. The main idea—decode to costs, reconstruct with a solver, and train with a perturbed-optimizer Fenchel-Young loss—is clean and well-motivated, and the empirical results are compelling in showing feasibility guarantees, interpretable latent structure, and reasonable performance on both synthetic and real data. However, the paper would benefit from stronger theoretical exposition of the loss, a more rigorous experimental comparison to multi-intent IRL and structured prediction baselines, clearer distributional evaluation protocols, and a discussion of scalability and robustness to suboptimality. I view the work as a solid step toward generative modeling of combinatorial structures with guaranteed feasibility and multi-modality, with a few key gaps that, if addressed, would strengthen it for ICML. I lean toward a weak accept, contingent on clarifications and bolstered empirical comparisons.

papers.title: Identifying key amino acid types that distinguish paralogous proteins using Shapley value based feature subset selection

reviews.summary: This paper presents a simple, data-lean pipeline for identifying amino acid types that distinguish pairs of paralogous protein families. The method uses amino acid composition (AAC) features, a Shapley value-based feature selection method (SVEA) with a linear-separability game value, and a linear SVM to partition the selected amino acids into family-specific subsets. The authors report small “amino acid feature subsets” (AFS; 5–10 amino acids) across 15 paralog pairs and provide qualitative validation using multiple sequence alignments, structural contact analyses for heteromeric complexes, and supporting literature evidence, along with basic test-set classification performance.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The framing of feature selection as a Shapley-attribution game directly on data separability (rather than on a trained black-box model) is a clean instantiation of cooperative-game-based feature selection, adapted here to protein AAC features.
The class-wise partition of AFS via SVM weight signs is a pragmatic device to assign family-specific prominence given nonnegative AAC features.
Experimental rigor and validation
The study spans 15 paralog pairs across diverse functional regimes (e.g., globins, GPCRs, tubulins), increasing external face validity.
Multiple, orthogonal sources of domain validation are provided (qualitative MSA conservation, structural contact enrichment at interfaces, literature support).
Code and data curation details are shared, improving reproducibility.
Clarity of presentation
The pipeline is clearly described with an intuitive flowchart; the AFS results are summarized neatly (Table 1), with supporting figures for Shapley spectra.
The narrative linking AFS findings to structural/functional roles (e.g., catalytic or binding residues, interface residues) is accessible to both ML and biology readers.
Significance of contributions
A low-resource, quickly deployable pipeline for hypothesis generation is valuable where labeled data and wet-lab resources are scarce.
The result that composition alone often suffices to separate paralogs is a provocative empirical observation that can stimulate further mechanistic inquiry.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The SVEA game value v(S) is defined via a class-balanced hinge-loss minimization without explicit margin regularization (no ||w|| term), which may yield degenerate solutions and unstable minima; implementation and solver details are not provided, and no sensitivity analysis is conducted.

AAC are compositional features (sum to 1), yet no compositional data analysis (e.g., log-ratio transforms) is used; raw linear weights/signs can be misleading due to negative correlations induced by the simplex constraint.

The φ_cutoff = v(N)/20 threshold is heuristic and not statistically calibrated; no uncertainty quantification on Shapley estimates is reported (sampling variance, confidence intervals, or stability across runs/bootstraps).
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Potential phylogenetic and taxonomy confounds are not controlled; family-wise amino acid usage can reflect organismal lineage rather than paralog-specific function. No species- or clade-controlled evaluation is presented.
There is no quantitative statistical validation for MSA or structural analyses (e.g., enrichment over background, permutation tests, p-values), making several validations anecdotal.

Test-set design may permit close homolog leakage (e.g., Swiss-Prot→TrEMBL split without strict identity thresholds except limited CD-HIT for one GPCR subset); this can inflate performance estimates and derived AFS credibility.

Baselines are limited: no comparison to simple and relevant alternatives such as L1-regularized logistic regression, mutual information, univariate enrichment tests, permutation importance, or wrapper methods; MCI is the only competitive alternative considered.
Clarity or presentation issues
Key implementation details are deferred to the appendix (e.g., SVEA optimization specifics, number of Shapley samples, stopping criteria), limiting assessment of computational cost and robustness.
Some validations rely on qualitative visual inspection of alignments/structures without standardized quantitative metrics.
Missing related work or comparisons
The paper contrasts SVEA with SHAP/SAGE conceptually but does not empirically compare against model-based attributions on a straightforward linear/logistic baseline trained on AAC features.

Broader literature on composition-based protein classification and statistical enrichment of amino acid content is not discussed; likewise, modern attribution frameworks (and recent advances in Shapley computation on structured data) are not leveraged or positioned beyond brief mentions.
reviews.questions:
1. How many Monte Carlo samples were used for Shapley estimation per dataset, and what is the observed variance across runs? Can you provide confidence intervals or stability (e.g., Jaccard overlap of AFS across seeds)?
2. Why is the separability objective unregularized (no ||w|| term)? Did you try adding a margin penalty, and if so, how did AFS change?
3. Did you explore compositional-data transforms (e.g., log-ratio) or constrained models for simplex data? If not, can you comment on how the simplex constraint might bias weight signs and thus the AFS(P)/AFS(Q) partition?
