However, the theoretical justification remains largely heuristic; the generalization bound relies on an unproven equivalence between loss sharpness and Sρ, and the relation to Johnson & Zhang’s inconsistency rests on restrictive assumptions. Experimentally, the scope is limited to CIFAR-scale setups; semi/self-supervised comparisons lack standard baselines that also exploit unlabeled data, and no computational cost analysis is provided. The method’s dependence on an L2 parameter ball leaves open invariance concerns already raised in the sharpness literature. Overall, while promising and potentially impactful, the work would benefit from stronger baselines in label-scarce settings, broader-scale experiments, runtime/memory profiling, and either more rigorous theory or empirical validation of key assumptions. I lean toward a borderline rejection in its current form, with the expectation that addressing these points could make it a strong candidate.

papers.title: Deep Active Inference Agents for Delayed and Long-Horizon Environments

reviews.summary: The paper proposes Deep Active Inference (DAIF), an active inference agent that integrates a differentiable policy into a world model and learns a multi-step latent transition that directly predicts observations H steps ahead. By conditioning the transition on an explicit representation of the policy and backpropagating expected free energy (EFE) gradients to the actor, the agent avoids exhaustive tree search and aims to act effectively in delayed, long-horizon environments. The method is evaluated on a high-fidelity industrial manufacturing simulator with long-horizon, delayed performance signals and is reported to outperform a DQN baseline on energy efficiency per unit.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Integrating the actor “as a function” into the latent dynamics and training a single-step, H-step overshooting transition P(s_{t+H} | s_t, π̂) to enable one-look-ahead planning is an interesting twist on world-model and AIF agents.

Using EFE gradients to update the actor within a replay-trained generative model is conceptually clean in the AIF framework, unifying perception (VFE) and control (EFE) within one end-to-end pipeline.
The approach explicitly targets delayed and long-horizon settings and proposes to eliminate per-step planning via a single gradient update every H steps at deployment.
Experimental rigor and validation

The industrial simulation domain is challenging, with delayed and stochastic feedback, mixed discrete/continuous observations, and continual non-episodic control—well aligned to the paper’s stated motivation.
The month-long evaluation protocol with 10 replications and reporting of mean ± error bars on key KPIs indicates an attempt at robustness.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level motivation and positioning vis-à-vis AIF and world-model RL are clearly articulated.
The training loop alternates model learning (VFE) and actor updates (EFE), which is conceptually straightforward and well tied to the formalism reviewed in Section 2.
Significance of contributions
Demonstrating AIF-based control on a realistic industrial benchmark is valuable for broadening the application footprint of AIF beyond robotics and perception-heavy tasks.
If the one-look-ahead, policy-conditioned transition generalizes, it could reduce planning overhead in active inference and related model-based methods.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The proposed “policy embedding” Π is under-specified and, as implemented, appears ad hoc (concatenation of the input with intermediate/output activations for a given input), which likely does not faithfully represent the entire policy function over the horizon; this raises concerns about identifiability and generalization when π changes during training.

The single-step H-overshoot model conflates action sequence effects with a fixed-parameter policy proxy; without constraints or auxiliary supervision, the transition could overfit to specific states/actions seen during training, limiting extrapolation to new conditions or updated actors.
The claim that the method “naturally scales to continuous actions” is not backed by experiments; the main environment seems to use discrete switching actions.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Baselines are limited: there is no comparison to strong world-model agents (e.g., Dreamer/Plan2Explore/EfficientZero-like variants) or prior AIF implementations (e.g., MCTS-based or hybrid-horizon AIF), despite positioning against these lines of work.

The month-long evaluation is performed on the “best-performing instance” selected from several random initializations, which introduces selection bias. Reporting results averaged across all instances/seeds is necessary.
No ablations: there is no study of the effect of H, the policy-embedding design, dropout-based epistemic estimates, replay usage, or removing/altering particular EFE terms.
Computational cost and sample efficiency are not quantified versus planning-heavy or rollout-based baselines; the overhead of Monte Carlo sampling for EFE estimation is not measured.
Clarity or presentation issues
Inconsistencies and typos in notation and algorithmic steps (e.g., repeated lines, unclear use of symbols φ vs Ψ for preference mapping, multiple μ/σ definitions) hinder reproducibility.
The figure caption and text disagree on the horizon (H = 100 vs H = 300); this should be reconciled.
The definition of the preference mapping Ψ and the exact components of the EFE terms used in practice are not sufficiently specified in the main text.
Missing related work or comparisons
No direct empirical comparisons to Dreamer-family agents or other model-based methods that also handle long horizons via latent rollouts and value gradients.

Work on action-sequence-conditioned models or “macro-dynamics” (e.g., sequence-to-one transitions or policy-conditioned models via hypernetworks) is not discussed; these could be highly relevant to the proposed H-step transition idea.
reviews.questions:
1. How exactly is the policy embedding Π(Q_{φ_a}) → π̂ constructed during training and deployment? Please specify the dimensionality, which activations are concatenated, how input-dependence is handled, and why this embedding is expected to represent the full policy function over the horizon rather than a local input-output snapshot.
2. Does the transition P_{θ_s}(s_{t+H} | s_t, π̂) generalize to unseen or updated policies (i.e., new φ_a) at test time? Please provide experiments where the actor is changed after model training to assess robustness of the policy-conditioned dynamics.
3. Can you report results averaged over all environment initializations/seeds for the month-long evaluation (not just the best instance), along with confidence intervals, to remove selection bias?
4. Please add comparisons to strong model-based baselines (e.g., Dreamer variants) and to prior AIF agents (MCTS/hybrid horizon). How does DAIF’s compute time and sample efficiency compare?
5. There is an inconsistency regarding the horizon (H = 100 vs H = 300 in text and figures). Which horizon(s) were used where, and how sensitive are results to H?
6. What is the precise form of the preference mapping Ψ used to compute the extrinsic term in the EFE? How sensitive are results to this choice, and is Ψ domain-specific?
7. The algorithmic pseudocode includes duplicated lines and ambiguous symbols (φ vs Ψ; multiple μ/σ definitions). Could you provide a clean, unambiguous algorithm and release code or pseudo-code that matches the implementation?
8. Please quantify the variance of EFE gradient estimates (with and without dropout) and any regularization/stabilization used to ensure reliable policy updates.
9. Can you show ablations removing policy-conditioning from the transition and/or replacing it with sequential latent rollouts to isolate the benefits of the proposed one-look-ahead design?
10. You claim natural scalability to continuous actions. Could you include a continuous-control experiment (or a mixed-action variant) to substantiate this claim?
reviews.assessment: This paper tackles an important problem—making AIF practical in delayed, long-horizon settings—by proposing an innovative policy-conditioned, one-look-ahead world model trained via VFE/EFE. The industrial control experiments are compelling in motivation and suggest potential benefits. However, the current empirical evidence is not yet sufficient for a top-tier venue: strong baselines are missing, the month-long evaluation has selection bias, and there are several clarity issues and algorithmic ambiguities (especially around the policy embedding and the EFE computation). The central idea is promising and could be impactful if validated more thoroughly. I encourage the authors to strengthen the experimental comparisons, remove evaluation biases, clarify and justify the policy-embedding mechanism (possibly with a more principled design, e.g., hypernetworks or learned function codes), and provide ablations and compute analyses. In its current form, I lean toward rejection, but I see a clear path to a stronger version with expanded evaluation and clarified methodology.

papers.title: When recalling in-context, Transformers are not SSMs

reviews.summary: This paper investigates why modern recurrent token mixers (e.g., SSMs such as Mamba and Hyena) often underperform transformers on the Multi-Query Associative Recall (MQAR) benchmark. The authors show that recurrent models are far more sensitive to learning rate selection than attention baselines, that depth vs. width scaling affects attention and recurrent models in opposite ways (attention needs depth; recurrent models benefit from width), and that 1-layer transformers display a loss “bump” reminiscent of induction head formation without corresponding accuracy gains, while 1-layer Mamba—when tuned—can solve MQAR. Through ablations, they argue that some inductive biases (e.g., added local convolutions) can close the single-layer gap for transformers, and they compare Mamba, Mamba2, and DeltaNet, with DeltaNet exhibiting notably improved optimization robustness.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
The paper offers a careful and timely empirical analysis disentangling optimization sensitivity from expressivity on MQAR, a benchmark that has influenced recent discourse on SSMs vs. attention.
The identification and demonstration of a sharply narrower “good LR window” for SSMs vs. attention baselines is useful and under-discussed in prior work.

The observation of an induction-like loss phase transition in 1-layer transformers is interesting and, if confirmed mechanistically, would extend prior interpretability accounts beyond two-layer settings.
Ablations that show 1-layer attention can solve MQAR with lightweight local convolutions on Q/K/V give constructive avenues to reduce the gap without abandoning attention.
Experimental rigor and validation
Extensive learning-rate sweeps with multiple seeds, and side-by-side replication and tuning vs. Zoology help clarify prior discrepancies and confounds.
Systematic comparisons across widths, depths, and several recurrent mixers (Mamba, Hyena/H3/RWKV) and attention baselines increase confidence in trends (e.g., opposite scaling behaviors).
The inclusion of DeltaNet and Mamba2 highlights the connection between architectural choices, gradient flow, and training stability.
Clarity of presentation
The motivation, setup, and benchmark are generally explained clearly; figures are informative and help isolate the key claims (LR sensitivity, width/depth scaling, training dynamics).
The paper is explicit about what is meant by a “layer” (mixer + MLP), aiding reproducibility and fair comparison within this work’s conventions.
Significance of contributions
The work cautions against under-tuned comparisons that have shaped the narrative about SSM inferiority on recall tasks; this alone is valuable for the community.

The width/depth scaling dichotomy and the single-layer dynamics offer concrete hypotheses for future mechanistic and algorithmic work, and practical tips for stabilizing and fairly evaluating recurrent models.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Some central claims verge on overreach. For example, asserting that “transformers are not SSMs mainly because of their optimization dynamics” conflates an important empirical observation (LR sensitivity differences) with broader expressivity and inductive-bias differences that are only partially probed here.

The interpretation of the single-layer loss bump as induction-like behavior lacks mechanistic evidence (e.g., attention pattern analysis, circuit tracing, weight-structure probes), making the claim largely speculative.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Hyperparameter studies focus primarily on the learning rate with AdamW; other stabilizers (gradient clipping, β1/β2/ε sweeps, weight decay variations, longer/shorter warmup, alternative optimizers, mimetic/orthogonal initializations) are not explored, which weakens the “optimization sensitivity” diagnosis.

The ablation results in Table 1 are summarized as solve vs. not solve without detailed metrics or robustness curves; it is hard to assess stability, sample-efficiency, or sensitivity across sequence lengths from this binary outcome.
Comparisons are confined to MQAR; broader claims about language modeling or general reasoning are not corroborated by additional tasks or datasets.

Parameter-matched comparisons are not always enforced; adding convolutions to attention changes inductive bias and receptive field in ways that complicate direct “expressivity” or “one-layer” conclusions.
Clarity or presentation issues

Some architectural and training details (e.g., positional encodings for attention, exact normalization placements, initialization schemes, use of gradient clipping, precision settings) are under-specified for exact replication of nuanced stability claims.
The definition of “layer” (mixer + MLP) is clear in this paper but differs from common practice; occasional reminders would help prevent confusion in cross-paper comparisons.
Missing related work or comparisons

Recent results on one-layer transformer limitations are cited (e.g., Sanford et al.), but mechanistic interpretability results that could validate the proposed “induction-like” dynamics are not leveraged.

Prior work on stabilizing SSM training (e.g., tailored initialization, spectral constraints, state expansion variants) could be more comprehensively connected to the observed LR sensitivity and to the DeltaNet findings.
reviews.questions:
1. Could you provide mechanistic evidence for the claimed induction-like phase transition in 1-layer attention (e.g., attention heatmaps over training, cosine-similarity probes, or circuit-level analyses akin to Olsson et al.)?
2. How sensitive are your conclusions to other optimization knobs beyond LR (β1/β2/ε, weight decay magnitude, gradient clipping, warmup length, cosine vs. linear schedule, optimizer choice)? Any preliminary results?
3. What positional embeddings were used for attention models (e.g., learned absolute, sinusoidal, RoPE)? Did alternative positional schemes affect the single-layer failure or the LR robustness window?
4. For the “attention + convolution” ablations, can you provide parameter-matched comparisons and LR robustness curves to quantify whether the improvement stems from capacity, inductive bias, or simply easier optimization?
5. How do your findings change if you vary the query-to-context ratio (e.g., keep L fixed while increasing the number of queries) or decrease/increase vocabulary size? Does the width-vs-depth asymmetry persist?
6. Did you try stabilization techniques specific to SSMs (e.g., mimetic initialization, orthogonal/Householder parameterizations, spectral normalization) on Mamba? If so, how did they compare to DeltaNet’s robustness?
7. Can you release code and the exact LR grids per model to facilitate replication of the delicate stability findings?
reviews.assessment:
This is a thoughtful empirical study addressing a live and practically important question: to what extent do optimization issues, rather than expressivity alone, explain the performance gap between modern recurrent mixers and transformers on associative recall? The paper convincingly shows that recurrent models are acutely sensitive to learning rate and that neglecting this can lead to misleading conclusions. It further documents opposite scaling preferences (depth for attention, width for recurrence) and presents intriguing single-layer dynamics. The ablation results, particularly that adding lightweight convolutions enables 1-layer attention to solve MQAR, are constructive.

However, the paper’s broader claims sometimes overreach the presented evidence. The interpretation of induction-like dynamics in 1-layer attention lacks mechanistic substantiation; optimization analysis is largely restricted to LR; and several ablations are summarized in a binary fashion without robustness curves or parameter-matched controls. The scope is limited to a single synthetic benchmark, making it hard to generalize conclusions about “expressivity” or training dynamics to real language modeling. Despite these reservations, the work provides useful insights and cautions that can shape fairer evaluations of SSMs and hybrids. I view it as a borderline submission: valuable for practitioners and for stimulating further careful, mechanistic, and optimization-focused studies, but it would benefit from deeper mechanistic validation and broader optimizer/initialization ablations to meet the bar for a top-tier venue.

papers.title: Curse of Slicing: Why Sliced Mutual Information is a Deceptive Measure of Statistical Dependence

reviews.summary: The paper critically examines Sliced Mutual Information (SMI) as a dependence measure and argues that, despite its scalability and nullification under independence, SMI is fundamentally biased and can be misleading. The authors provide theory and experiments showing: (i) SMI saturates quickly and becomes insensitive to increases in dependence; (ii) SMI has a strong redundancy bias that can invert expected trends and violate data processing intuitions; and (iii) in high dimensions SMI decays to zero, reflecting a different “curse of dimensionality.” They derive closed-form and integral expressions for SMI (and k-SMI) in Gaussian settings, connect them to the Jacobi ensemble, and corroborate the phenomena on synthetic benchmarks and InfoMax-style tasks.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Derivation of a closed-form expression for SMI in an isotropic jointly Gaussian model via generalized hypergeometric functions, including sharp limiting behavior as d→∞ and ρ²→1.
Integral representation for k-SMI based on the Jacobi ensemble of eigenvalues, illuminating how random projector misalignment drives decay and saturation.

Clear articulation and formalization of “redundancy bias,” including a counterexample where MI and even linear correlation increase while SMI decreases, and a result (Proposition 4.4) linking k-SMI to MI under overcomplete linear embeddings.
Thoughtful discussion of the relationship between average SMI and its “optimized” counterparts (max-sliced, optimal-sliced), showing how redundancy concentration persists.
Experimental rigor and validation
Systematic synthetic benchmarks across several non-Gaussian families with ground-truth MI, examining multiple dimensionalities and slice ranks k.
Empirical evidence of saturation and decay trends consistent with theory, and a carefully designed Gaussian channel study highlighting the practical implication of redundancy preferences.
Demonstration in a Deep InfoMax setting that SMI maximization can collapse representations, aligning with the proposed failure mode.
Clarity of presentation
The overall argument is well-structured: theory first (with proofs), then synthetic validation and practical implications.
Technical derivations are generally precise; the use of classical results (e.g., Beta distributions of inner products, Jacobi ensembles) is apt and well-motivated.
Significance of contributions
Given the growing use of SMI as a proxy for MI in DNN analysis, generalization bounds, feature selection, and privacy auditing, identifying systematic pitfalls is timely and important.
The paper reframes how the community should interpret SMI measurements and when they can be misleading, which is highly valuable for practice.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Many of the strongest theoretical results are for the Gaussian case or settings with strong symmetry; generalization beyond Gaussian or linear settings is argued intuitively and empirically but not proven.

Proposition 4.4 relies on MI invariance to injective linear maps on the support; the proof sketch is brief and could benefit from a more rigorous measure-theoretic justification (e.g., conditions ensuring absolute continuity on submanifolds and MI invariance under such embeddings).

The claim that SMI can behave “worse than correlation” is stated strongly; beyond one constructed counterexample, a broader or more quantitative comparison to correlation (and other simple baselines) would solidify this point.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

The MI estimations on projections use KSG with k=1; while common, this is a very aggressive setting and could be sensitive. Ablations over k, sample size, and alternative estimators would help rule out estimator-induced artifacts.
The number of slices (128) is fixed; sensitivity analysis on the number of random projections and their sampling strategy (e.g., joint vs independent θ, φ) is not fully explored.

Limited comparison with alternative scalable dependence measures (e.g., HSIC, distance correlation, MICe, copula-based measures). Given the normative stance, it would be informative to position SMI against these in the same setups.

The InfoMax experiment is compelling but minimalistic (MNIST, 2-D embeddings). Ablations (e.g., different noise levels, embedding sizes, numbers of negatives, batch sizes) and inclusion of mSMI/oSMI variants would strengthen claims about collapse.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some formula rendering artifacts and minor typos are present (likely due to PDF extraction), occasionally impeding readability of equations.
The rhetoric (“deceptive measure”) is strong; toning down language or adding more constructive guidance would improve balance.
Missing related work or comparisons

Notable dependence measures (HSIC, distance correlation, Hoeffding’s D, MICe) are not discussed in depth, nor empirically compared. This context would better position SMI’s pros/cons in the broader landscape.
Copula-based dependence measures are mentioned in a figure but not adequately cited or contrasted.
reviews.questions:
1. Proposition 4.4 relies on MI invariance under injective linear maps into higher-dimensional spaces. Can you state the precise conditions (e.g., absolute continuity on submanifolds, invertibility on support) under which MI is preserved, and provide a more detailed proof or reference?
2. How sensitive are your synthetic results to the KSG hyperparameters (k, sample size) and the number of slices? Could estimator bias/variance or slice Monte Carlo error contribute to the observed saturation in some regimes?
3. Have you evaluated HSIC, distance correlation, MICe, or copula-based dependence measures on the same benchmarks to clarify whether the observed issues are unique to slicing or pervasive across scalable proxies?
4. In the InfoMax experiments, do mSMI or oSMI (with diversity regularization) also collapse, or do they mitigate redundancy-driven failures? Similarly, what happens if you enforce φ=θ (co-slicing) to remove projector misalignment?
5. Your theory and experiments indicate a strong effect of redundancy. Would a “whitened SMI” (pre-whitening X and Y before slicing) or a normalization by the aligned-slice MI (e.g., canonical correlations) alleviate saturation and the redundancy bias?
6. Can you provide additional empirical evidence for the claim that SMI can be “worse than correlation,” e.g., a broader sweep across families of transformations where correlation tracks dependence while SMI inversely trends?
reviews.assessment: This paper offers a timely and well-argued critique of sliced mutual information, a measure that has seen growing adoption as a scalable proxy for MI. The Gaussian analysis is technically strong and novel, making the mechanisms behind SMI’s decay and saturation transparent through random projection geometry and the Jacobi ensemble. The synthetic and task-based experiments, while not exhaustive, consistently reinforce the theoretical insights: SMI’s rapid saturation, high-dimensional decay, and strong bias toward redundancy can invert expected trends and undermine its use both as an analysis tool and as a training objective. The main reservations are scope and positioning: several key results are Gaussian, some claims are stated strongly without exhaustive cross-method comparisons, and parts of the experimental methodology would benefit from ablations and additional controls. Nevertheless, the core message is important for the NeurIPS community. I recommend acceptance after addressing the requested clarifications, adding comparisons with other dependence measures, and providing modest robustness checks. The work would recalibrate community expectations around SMI and catalyze the development of better-calibrated, scalable dependence measures.

papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into Grokking from the Embedding Layer

reviews.summary: This paper studies the role of embedding layers in the grokking phenomenon on modular arithmetic tasks using MLPs. The authors argue that two mechanisms—frequency-imbalanced embedding updates and bilinear coupling between embeddings and the first linear layer—are key drivers of delayed generalization. They propose two interventions: frequency-aware sampling of tokens and an embedding-specific learning rate scaled relative to downstream weights (ηE/ηW ∝ σmax(E)/σmax(W) · fW/fE), showing empirical speedups in grokking across several algorithmic datasets.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Positions embeddings as a primary driver of grokking and analyzes their bilinear coupling with downstream weights in a simplified MLP setting.
Proposes a coupling-aware learning rate ratio for embeddings based on singular values and update frequencies, connecting to optimizer–curvature heterogeneity arguments in Transformers.
Highlights the practical and under-discussed issue of token-frequency imbalance in embedding updates and ties it to grokking dynamics.
Experimental rigor and validation
Presents multiple algorithmic tasks (addition, multiplication, division, sum of squares mod p) and examines sampling schemes (uniform, skewed, random) across batch sizes.
Provides ablations on optimizer choice (Adam vs “Adam-LR”), sensitivity to learning-rate ratio c, and Hessian spectral diagnostics via HVP power iteration.
Clarity of presentation
Clear high-level narrative that connects embedding update dynamics to delayed generalization and positions bilinearity as a unifying lens.
Significance of contributions

If validated thoroughly, the work could influence how practitioners treat embeddings during training on discrete tasks and inform understanding of why adaptive methods and per-block treatment are effective in attention-based models.
The frequency-imbalance insight and the bilinear coupling perspective may help reconcile disparate observations about grokking, optimizer choice, and curvature heterogeneity.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The “proof” of the learning-rate ratio is heuristic; the derivation relies on proportional scaling of gradient norms by σmax and ignores nonlinearity, data-dependence, and coupling with activations. The paper at times overstates (“we prove”) what is essentially a plausibility argument.
The smoothness-based argument about p_i and loss decrease is quite generic and does not yield actionable or falsifiable predictions beyond “rare tokens update slowly.”
Mathematical inaccuracies and confusion in Section 3.2 (e.g., generator statements for additive and multiplicative groups) cast doubt on rigor.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
Results are largely single-run without error bars; robustness across seeds is not reported.
Comparisons with closely related accelerants (e.g., GrokFast, pruning/tickets, spectral or topology-based methods) are missing; AdamW vs Adam is not disentangled.

The proposed sampling intervention is emulated via dataset splits rather than explicit mini-batch rebalancing or reweighting; it is unclear whether observed effects are due to true per-step token-frequency control versus distribution shift between train/test.

The embedding-LR scaling is claimed to depend on σmax and update frequencies but is implemented as a fixed factor c=10; no adaptive online measurement or ablations tying performance to the predicted ratio terms are provided.
Clarity or presentation issues
Notation and equations have inconsistencies (e.g., continuous-time derivation retains η; some variables are undefined or garbled in the embedded-input description).

Several figure captions and references are ambiguous, and some textual descriptions are hard to reconcile with exact setups (e.g., tokenization “as sequences of digit representations” vs fixed token IDs).
Mixing Adam with weight decay without clarifying decoupling (Adam vs AdamW) is a source of ambiguity.
Missing related work or comparisons
Limited empirical positioning relative to recent, strong baselines that accelerate grokking (e.g., GrokFast; pruning/tickets; bounded-sphere/topology modifications). Some are cited but not compared.

The broader claim that the insights transfer to Transformers is not supported experimentally; relevant methods like per-parameter group LRs, Adafactor/LAMB/LARS, or embedding-specific LR practices in NLP are not discussed or compared.
reviews.questions:
1. Can you report results over multiple seeds with mean/variance for all main plots (sampling strategies, Adam vs Adam-LR, c-sensitivity), and indicate statistical significance?
2. How does your method compare to AdamW (decoupled weight decay) and to other per-block optimizers (e.g., Adafactor/LAMB/LARS)? Do your conclusions hold under these alternatives?
3. Your learning-rate ratio is motivated by σmax and update frequencies, yet you set c=10 fixed. Can you implement an online estimator of σmax(E), σmax(W), and fE/fW to adapt c during training and show that the predicted scaling correlates with optimal performance?
4. The sampling intervention appears to modify train/test splits. Can you perform controlled mini-batch rebalancing or per-token reweighting with the same train/test composition to isolate the effect of p_i on update dynamics?
5. The group-theoretic discussion in Section 3.2 seems inaccurate (e.g., generators of Zp−1 additive group and Zp*). Please clarify and correct; does any of this affect the empirical claims about addition vs multiplication tasks?
6. Can you provide an ablation that controls for model capacity when “adding embeddings” (e.g., matching parameter count between with-embedding and without-embedding setups) to ensure that grokking differences are not due simply to capacity and regularization interactions?
7. Have you tested the embedding-LR scaling on a small Transformer (even a single-layer encoder) to support the claim that the bilinear-coupling insight transfers beyond MLPs?
8. What is the precise tokenization used (direct token IDs vs digit sequences)? The text seems inconsistent; please detail inputs, vocabulary size, and how operation/equality tokens are handled.
reviews.assessment: This paper offers a plausible and practically relevant perspective that embeddings—and their bilinear coupling with downstream weights—can be primary contributors to grokking, particularly through frequency-imbalanced updates and curvature heterogeneity. The proposed remedy of increasing embedding learning rates is simple and, in the reported experiments, accelerates generalization. The spectral/Hessian diagnostics are directionally informative. However, the theoretical arguments are heuristic and sometimes overstated, the empirical evaluation lacks statistical rigor and broader baselines, several presentation issues (including mathematical inaccuracies) reduce confidence, and the leap from MLPs to Transformers remains speculative without experiments. With substantial revisions—adding multi-seed statistics, stronger and fairer baselines (including AdamW and state-of-the-art grokking accelerants), cleaner tests of p_i via batch rebalancing, capacity-matched ablations, and at least a minimal Transformer validation—this work could provide a valuable contribution. In its current form, I view it as promising but not yet ready for a top-tier venue.

papers.title: Can We Partially Rewrite Transformers in Natural Language?

reviews.summary: This paper proposes a rigorous, task-driven evaluation of whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and transcoders can enable “partial rewriting” of transformer layers into natural-language-defined, interpretable features without sacrificing performance. The authors generate automated natural language explanations of sparse coder latents, use an LLM to simulate latent activations from those explanations in context, and patch the decoded reconstructions back into the model’s forward pass. Across two models and both SAE and transcoder settings, the paper reports a largely negative result: replacing even a fraction of the encoder with LLM-simulated activations substantially degrades next-token prediction performance, performing no better (and often similarly) to mean ablation baselines. The authors argue this constitutes an informative and stringent benchmark of explanation faithfulness and feature specificity.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The paper introduces a clear and ambitious protocol for “partial rewriting” of transformer modules via natural-language-based simulation of sparse features, going beyond proxy interpretability scores to a behavioral standard.

The use of per-feature quantile normalization to calibrate LLM-generated activation predictions is thoughtful and grounded in optimal transport, addressing a key practical pitfall (miscalibrated simulator distributions).
Evaluating both transcoders and SAEs, with and without skip connections, in multiple models (Pythia-160M and SmolLM2-135M) strengthens the generality of findings.
Experimental rigor and validation

The evaluation is compute-heavy and systematic: millions of simulator queries, error bars, and comparisons across fractions of substituted latents, including random vs “top-scoring” selections and a strong mean-ablation baseline.
The paper ties simulation performance to established interpretability metrics (detection/fuzzing F1), showing how these relate to specificity/sensitivity and downstream degradation.
Clarity of presentation
The pipeline is clearly described end-to-end: sparse coder training, explanation generation and scoring, simulation setup, calibration, and patching.
Negative results are communicated transparently, with plausible causal analysis (specificity failures) supported by empirical histograms and diagnostic plots.
Significance of contributions
Provides an actionable, behavior-level benchmark to assess whether current explanation pipelines and sparse-coder features are sufficiently precise to substitute for parts of a network.
The negative findings are timely and important to the interpretability community, tempering expectations and pointing to concrete failure modes (false positives, lack of specificity).
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The substitution in the SAE setting discards the original residual stream output and replaces it entirely with the SAE reconstruction, a very aggressive intervention likely to overstate degradation; more conservative interventions (e.g., additive residual perturbations or partial routing) are not tested.
The simulator, scorer, and explainer rely on the same or very similar LLMs, raising concerns of correlated biases and limiting the ability to disentangle explanation quality from simulator behavior.

The discretized 0–9 scoring and scaling by maximum observed activation is coarse and potentially brittle across latents with long-tailed magnitudes; while quantile normalization alleviates marginal mismatch, the initial mapping could still distort per-feature calibration and ranking.
Enforcing a global TopK after normalization may inadvertently suppress truly active but subtle features and amplifies the consequences of rank errors in a sparse regime.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Limited baselines for the simulator: no comparison to simpler heuristic or lightweight learned simulators (e.g., token-level logistic regression trained on the same explanations, or binary trigger rules) to isolate whether the LLM itself is the primary bottleneck.

No oracle-style decompositions to separate sources of failure: e.g., replacing only a subset of ground-truth active latents with simulated ones, or vice versa, to quantify decoder/reconstruction vs simulator/explanation errors.

Calibration relies on per-latent quantile mapping estimated from 10% of the same distribution; it is unclear whether this is held out from evaluation (potential leakage), and no comparison to alternative monotonic calibrators (isotonic regression, splines) is provided.
The dataset filtering (excluding contexts with very low base loss) may bias results toward harder contexts without analyzing how this affects substitution sensitivity.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some choices (e.g., replacement vs addition for SAE interventions) and their rationale could be more explicitly justified given their outsized impact on loss.
It would help to present ablations on prompt window length, class-imbalance handling for the simulator, and how the final TopK threshold interacts with specificity/sensitivity.
Missing related work or comparisons

The paper would benefit from a more explicit positioning relative to model-editing and causal abstraction lines (e.g., ROME/MEMIT/SERAC, causal scrubbing/ACDC), which also “rewrite” or evaluate mechanistic equivalence in different ways.

Recent “output-centric” interpretability proposals are mentioned, but more direct experimental comparisons or a discussion of how output-centric labels might improve simulator specificity would strengthen the case.
reviews.questions:
1. For the SAE intervention, why choose full replacement of the residual stream output rather than an additive perturbation or gated blend with the original output? Can you report results for a milder intervention to separate reconstruction vs simulation errors?
2. Is the per-feature quantile calibration fit on a held-out split that does not overlap with evaluation contexts? If not, can you clarify potential leakage and report a strict held-out calibration variant?
3. Have you tried a two-stage simulator (binary detection for activity + conditional magnitude regression), potentially improving specificity before TopK is applied?
4. Can you provide oracle decompositions (e.g., replace only some of the truly active latents with simulated ones, or vice versa) to quantify upper bounds and identify whether decoder limitations or simulator errors dominate?
5. How sensitive are the results to the simulator prompt design (e.g., multiple sentences, contrastive positive/negative cues, chain-of-thought) and to the context window length beyond 32 tokens?
6. Did you evaluate alternative monotonic calibrators (isotonic regression, temperature scaling per-latent) or soft-sparsity activations rather than a hard TopK after normalization?
7. Could simpler simulators (keyword/regex or small linear classifiers) match or approximate the LLM simulator’s performance? This would help attribute the failure primarily to explanation specificity rather than simulator capacity.
reviews.assessment: This is a timely and carefully executed study that asks a hard and important question: can current sparse feature discovery and automated explanation pipelines support actual behavioral rewriting of transformer modules using natural language? The methodology is ambitious but well-motivated, and the negative results are presented with convincing diagnostics that highlight specificity as the central obstacle. While some intervention choices (especially for the SAE) may overstate degradation, and while more baselines and oracle ablations would strengthen the causal story, the core contribution—a rigorous, behavior-level benchmark revealing current limitations—is valuable to the NeurIPS community. I view this as a strong negative result that will inform future interpretability work toward faithful, specific, and deployable explanations. I recommend acceptance after addressing the main methodological questions (calibration split, intervention ablations, and minimal oracle analyses) to solidify the conclusions and broaden the paper’s impact.

papers.title: Stepwise Feature Learning in Self-Supervised Learning

reviews.summary: This paper studies shortcut learning in self-supervised learning (SSL) through the lens of stepwise feature learning governed by the eigenspectrum of the feature cross-correlation matrix. Building on the stepwise dynamics of Barlow Twins with small initialization, the authors introduce two notions—extent bias (features with larger spatial extent are learned earlier) and amplitude bias (features with larger amplitude are learned earlier)—and support these claims with analysis in linear toy settings, small synthetic experiments, a Colored-MNIST study, and brief nonlinear extensions.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The paper provides a simple, unified interpretation of shortcut phenomena in SSL via eigenvalues of the feature cross-correlation matrix, bridging prior observations about stepwise learning to concrete biases (extent and amplitude).

It offers a clean analytical characterization in controlled settings showing that feature learning order aligns with the eigenspectrum, giving an intuitive mechanism for why background-like features may dominate early training.
Experimental rigor and validation

The synthetic setups are carefully designed to isolate dimensional extent and amplitude, enabling direct comparison to the theoretical predictions (e.g., matching critical times and derivative magnitudes).
Quantitative checks (e.g., alignment metrics, singular value evolution, eigenvalue–loss coupling) mirror the theory closely in the linear regime.
Clarity of presentation
The theoretical development is generally easy to follow, with clear statements of assumptions and propositions and a consistent narrative from derivation to empirical validation on toy problems.
The visualizations of stepwise dynamics, eigenvalue trajectories, and feature alignments are helpful and align with the claims.
Significance of contributions

Understanding when and why SSL may favor shortcut-like features is important for robustness. The proposed extent/amplitude bias framing, tied to eigenvalue order, is a conceptually useful addition that may inform future algorithmic interventions.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The analysis relies critically on strong assumptions: linear networks, a toy Barlow Twins objective, very small/aligned initialization, and extremely simplified augmentations (primarily additive Gaussian noise). It is not clear how robustly these results transfer to realistic SSL pipelines (aug crops, color jitter, large-scale ViTs/CNNs, non-aligned initialization).

The assumption of right-singular vectors of W being aligned with top eigenvectors of Γ (or rapid early alignment) is asserted and shown only in toy settings; its validity in high-dimensional, nonconvex, convolutional SSL is not established.
Some notational inconsistencies and typos (e.g., C = W F W^T vs Γ, “biass”) raise concerns about technical polish.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Empirical validation beyond toy setups is limited: the only “real” dataset study (Colored-MNIST) appears to be a supervised training scenario (accuracy is discussed) rather than SSL pretraining with downstream evaluation, which weakens the claimed SSL scope.

No evaluation on standard spurious-correlation benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, Spurious CIFAR-10, IN-9, MetaShift) or on contemporary SSL methods (SimCLR, SimSiam, BYOL, DINO) under realistic augmentations.
The nonlinear experiments are relegated to the appendix and are not sufficiently detailed; it is unclear if they meaningfully go beyond the linear theory.
Clarity or presentation issues
Several equations have minor errors/typos and symbol mismatches (e.g., Γ vs F), and the paper occasionally switches between notation or omits definitions, which can impede precise understanding.
The Colored-MNIST experimental description lacks clarity about the exact SSL vs supervised protocol, pretraining/fine-tuning setup, and controls.
Missing related work or comparisons

Recent SSL-specific analyses on spurious correlations and representation bias are not discussed (e.g., LA-SSL [2311.16361], spurious connectivity under SSL augmentations [2406.18562], concept-balanced group-agnostic robustness [2402.13368]). These would contextualize the contribution and delimit its novelty relative to known SSL failure modes and mitigations.
reviews.questions:
1. Is the Colored-MNIST experiment conducted with SSL pretraining (e.g., Barlow Twins/SimCLR) followed by a linear probe, or with supervised training? Please clarify the exact protocol, loss, and evaluation pipeline.
2. How sensitive are the stepwise dynamics and the inferred extent/amplitude biases to the initialization scale and to misalignment at initialization? Do the phenomena persist with standard Kaiming initialization and in deeper CNNs/ViTs?
3. How do realistic augmentations (random crops, color jitter, cutout) affect Γ in your analysis, especially regarding spatial extent? Can you provide an analytical or empirical study showing that extent bias survives strong cropping?
4. Do your findings generalize across SSL objectives (SimCLR, SimSiam, BYOL, DINO)? Can you provide empirical evidence beyond the toy Barlow Twins setup?
5. Can you test the amplitude-bias prediction in a real image setting by manipulating contrast/brightness amplitudes of foreground vs background signals while controlling frequency content?
6. Could you compare against recent SSL spurious-robustness baselines (e.g., LA-SSL, LATETVG, CoBalT) on standard benchmarks (Waterbirds, CelebA, Spurious CIFAR-10) to validate practical relevance?
7. There are notational inconsistencies (e.g., C = W F W^T vs W Γ W^T) and typos. Can you fix these and provide a complete, self-contained derivation under consistent notation?
reviews.assessment: This paper offers a neat, conceptually appealing account of shortcut learning in SSL, arguing that the learning order is dictated by the eigenspectrum of the feature cross-correlation matrix and thus biases models toward large-extent and high-amplitude features. The theoretical development is solid for the linear, small-initialization regime and is well supported by synthetic experiments. However, the work remains largely in toy settings, and the single real-data experiment is not convincingly within an SSL framework. The reliance on strong assumptions and the absence of validation on standard spurious benchmarks or modern SSL pipelines make it difficult to assess the real-world significance of the proposed biases. I view this as an insightful, incremental step that refines our theoretical understanding, but it needs substantially stronger empirical grounding and clearer positioning relative to recent SSL robustness literature to meet the bar for NeurIPS.

papers.title: In-Context Learning under Distribution Shift: Optimal Attention Temperature for Transformers

reviews.summary: This paper studies how the attention temperature in Transformers affects in-context learning (ICL) robustness under distribution shift. The authors introduce a “linearized softmax” attention that preserves normalization and explicit temperature dependence while remaining tractable, derive a closed-form generalization error (Theorem 4.6) and an explicit expression for the optimal test-time temperature that minimizes this error (Theorem 4.7), and validate the theory with simulations on linear regression prompts and with LLaMA2-7B on question answering under label-noise shifts. The central finding is that tuning attention temperature is a principled and effective lever to mitigate distribution-shift degradation in ICL.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation
Introduces a linearized softmax attention model that retains temperature’s role and normalization, enabling closed-form analysis while remaining closer to softmax than standard linear attention.
Derives an explicit analytical expression for the ICL generalization error and a closed-form optimal temperature that minimizes it under broad Gaussian-task assumptions.
Provides a clear link between types of shift (covariance, task prior, noise) and the optimal temperature, including insightful special cases (e.g., isotropic covariance scaling).
Experimental rigor and validation
Synthetic linear-regression experiments align closely with the theory across multiple shift types, demonstrating the predictive value of the analysis.

LLM experiments (LLaMA2-7B on SCIQ with noisy in-context examples) corroborate the predicted trend that higher test-time noise favors larger attention temperature, and illustrate a practical performance benefit.
Clarity of presentation
Problem setup and assumptions are clearly stated; the role of reparameterized attention blocks in the prediction is well explained.
The decomposition of distribution-shift cases and their qualitative impact on ICL performance is easy to follow.
Significance of contributions
Addresses an important and practical question—robust ICL under shift—with a simple intervention (tuning τ) that practitioners can use immediately.
Complements and extends prior analyses of linear attention by bringing temperature (and softmax-like normalization) explicitly into the ICL robustness story.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The validity regime of the “linearized softmax” approximation is not fully characterized in the main text. Conditions under which the first-order expansion and normalization correction remain accurate (e.g., bounds on logit variance/scale) are not clearly stated.

The optimal-τ formula requires positivity conditions on trace terms; sufficient conditions ensuring these hold under realistic pretraining/test distributions are not provided, leaving ambiguity about failure modes (e.g., denominator near zero).

Pretraining lemma assumes access to or accurate estimation of σ2, μw, Σw and uses a closed-form parameter choice; applicability to practical pretraining (with stochastic optimizers, deep stacks, and non-Gaussian data) is discussed only qualitatively.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

LLM validation is limited in scope: one model family (LLaMA2-7B), one dataset (SCIQ), and a single type of shift (noisy labels). No comparison to alternative, simple robustness interventions (e.g., layer-wise scaling, attention mask reweighting, prompt selection or order strategies) is provided.
GPT-2 results are deferred to the appendix; the main text would benefit from at least one non-toy deep-model result beyond a single LLM/dataset to strengthen generality claims.
Clarity or presentation issues
Minor typesetting artifacts (e.g., stray prime in Eq. (15), formatting glitches) and placeholder characters in Related Work may distract.

The practical recipe to estimate or approximate τoptimal at inference in large models is not prominently documented in the main text (e.g., from observable statistics), though this is central for deployment.
Missing related work or comparisons

Limited discussion of distributionally robust ICL and robustness scaling (e.g., Wasserstein DRO perspectives on ICL robustness) and of recent analyses comparing softmax vs. linearized attention in retrieval/regression settings.
Connections to recent works that interpret softmax temperature as a bandwidth or preconditioning control in ICL could be discussed in more depth.
reviews.questions:
1. Linearized softmax approximation: Around which operating point is the softmax linearized, and under what quantitative conditions (e.g., bounds on the variance of QK⊤/τ) is the approximation accurate? Can you provide error bounds or empirical diagnostics indicating when Eq. (5) remains predictive?
2. Practical estimation of τoptimal: In large pretrained models, how do you estimate or approximate the traces in Theorem 4.7 without access to ground-truth A, B, and the trained M, V blocks? Do you recommend a concrete, model-internal statistic-based heuristic (beyond grid search), and how sensitive are results to that choice?
3. Positivity conditions: Can you provide sufficient conditions (on Σx, Σw, v21, v22, M11) that guarantee the numerator and denominator in Eq. (15) are positive, or propose a robust fallback when the denominator is small/negative (e.g., clipping, constrained search)?
4. Multi-head and deep stacks: Does your analysis extend in a straightforward way to multi-head attention (e.g., block-diagonal M11 per head) and multiple layers (compounding temperatures)? Is a single global τ per layer near-optimal, or do you observe benefits from per-head τ in practice?
5. Beyond Gaussian shifts: Have you tested the τ-tuning heuristic under non-Gaussian or heavy-tailed shifts (e.g., outliers, adversarial perturbations)? How robust are the qualitative predictions (e.g., τ increasing with noise) when the assumptions are violated?
6. LLM experiments: How was τ selected across layers and heads in LLaMA2-7B—uniformly or proportionally to layer statistics? Did you observe any optimization or stability issues (e.g., attention saturation, gradient anomalies in residual streams) when increasing τ at inference?
7. Baselines: Could you compare against other low-cost robustness adjustments (e.g., per-layer rescaling, calibrated attention masks, prompt-order optimization) to contextualize the magnitude of improvements from τ tuning?
reviews.assessment: This paper addresses an important and timely question—how to improve ICL robustness under distribution shift—through a theoretically grounded analysis of attention temperature. The linearized softmax construction is a thoughtful compromise that preserves temperature’s operational role and yields closed-form insights, including an explicit τoptimal. The synthetic experiments convincingly validate the theory, and the LLaMA2-7B results demonstrate practical relevance. The main limitations are the scope of the linearization (with limited discussion of validity regimes), relatively narrow LLM evaluation, and the absence of comparisons to alternative simple robustness interventions. Despite these, the contribution is sufficiently novel and useful: a principled treatment of attention temperature for ICL under shift, with actionable guidance and initial evidence of transfer to real models. I lean toward acceptance, recommending that the authors (i) clarify the approximation regime and positivity conditions, (ii) document a practical τ-selection heuristic in the main text, and (iii) broaden empirical validation or baselines if space permits.

papers.title: AH-UGC: $\underline{\text{A}}$daptive and $\underline{\text{H}}$eterogeneous-$\underline{\text{U}}$niversal $\underline{\text{G}}$raph $\underline{\text{C}}$oarsening

reviews.summary: The paper proposes AH-UGC, a graph coarsening framework that combines locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) with consistent hashing (CH) to enable adaptive (multi-resolution) coarsening without recomputing from scratch. It further introduces a type-isolated coarsening strategy to handle heterogeneous graphs by ensuring that supernodes contain only nodes of the same type and coarsening edge types accordingly. Experiments across 23 datasets indicate substantial runtime improvements over existing methods for multi-resolution generation, while preserving spectral properties and achieving competitive or superior node classification performance, including on heterogeneous graphs.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

The integration of LSH-based ordering with a CH-style clockwise merging scheme is a simple yet elegant way to make coarsening adaptive, enabling progressive refinement from a single sorted list of projection scores.
The paper provides a unified framework that explicitly supports both heterophilic and heterogeneous graphs, with a practical type-isolated coarsening strategy that preserves semantic constraints.
Theoretical components (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 1, Theorem 3.2) aim to justify locality preservation under projection and provide a probabilistic load-balance guarantee.
Experimental rigor and validation
Broad evaluation across 23 datasets spanning homophilic, heterophilic, heterogeneous, and large-scale settings, with multiple GNN backbones and spectral metrics, is commendable.
The adaptive setting is evaluated with multi-resolution runtime comparison showing large speedups, which directly supports the primary motivation.
Heterogeneous graph evaluation highlights supernode type purity and its effect on downstream accuracy.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level pipeline and motivation are clearly conveyed, especially via Figure 1 and the adaptive multi-resolution illustration.
The construction of the coarsening matrix and coarsened adjacency via C^T A C is standard and straightforward.
Significance of contributions

Addressing adaptive coarsening and heterogeneous semantics in a single, model-agnostic, scalable framework is timely and practically significant for large, evolving, or interactive graph analytics scenarios.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The heterophily-aware factor α is defined using ground-truth labels, which are typically unavailable prior to training in the coarsening stage; the paper does not explain how α is estimated in semi-supervised or unsupervised settings.

The projection/feature augmentation description alternates between concatenating Xi with the adjacency row Ai and projecting A via a random matrix first; the computational and memory implications (especially if d+N is large) and precise sparse implementation details are not made explicit.

The CH-based load-balance theorem (Theorem 3.2) appears to assume k random cuts of the circle (Dirichlet spacings), which is not obviously equivalent to the stated iterative “pick a node and merge with its immediate clockwise neighbor” process; the equivalence or approximation is not justified.
Locality guarantees (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 1) hinge on Gaussian projections, while the method text claims p-stable projections; the mismatch and any implications are not discussed.
Type-isolated coarsening ignores cross-type structural semantics (e.g., metapaths), which may limit optimality for heterogeneous graphs where cross-type context is essential.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues
No comparison to HGCond (heterogeneous graph condensation) in the heterogeneous setting, despite citing it; the absence weakens claims about SOTA on heterogeneous coarsening.

No ablations or sensitivity analyses for crucial choices: number of projections l, aggregation function (mean vs. max/median), α estimation, and the effect of random merge order on variance and stability across runs.
The streaming/evolving graph claim is not validated experimentally.

Some heterogeneous results look suspiciously uniform across several baselines, and multiple “OOT” entries reduce the strength of comparative conclusions; memory/time ceilings and fairness of resource limits are not discussed.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some orientation inconsistencies for X̃ and C (C vs. C^T), and minor notation/typographic artifacts, impede precision.
The code availability link is missing (“here” without URL).
Dataset count oscillates (23 vs. 24), and some table headings (e.g., “HE” in a classification table) may confuse readers.
Missing related work or comparisons

Beyond HGCond, the paper could better discuss recent scalable coarsening/sparsification efforts that support adaptivity or multi-resolution representations, and clarify differences with multilevel matching/partitioning heuristics under dynamic targets.
reviews.questions:
1. How is α computed when true labels are not available or only partially available prior to coarsening? Do you use label subsets, feature-based proxies, or structure-only estimates in practice?
2. Please reconcile the p-stable projection description with Theorem 3.1’s Gaussian assumption. Are you setting p=2 in all experiments? If not, what are the theoretical implications?
3. Theorem 3.2 appears to assume k random cuts (Dirichlet spacings), while your algorithm performs sequential random rightward merges. Can you justify the equivalence or provide a modified bound that matches the actual procedure?
4. How do you implement the “concatenate Ai” step efficiently for large, sparse graphs? Do you first project A via sparse random matrices (e.g., A Pk) and then concatenate with X? Please provide complexity and memory formulas in terms of N, E, d, and l.
5. Can you include comparisons to HGCond on the heterogeneous datasets and discuss trade-offs in runtime and accuracy?
6. What is the variance of accuracy and spectral metrics across different random seeds (LSH projections and merge order)? Can you report standard deviations and perhaps a stability analysis?
7. Could you add ablations on the number of projections l, the aggregation choice (mean/max/median), and the impact of the type-isolated constraint versus cross-type-aware coarsening?
8. Do you have empirical validation of the streaming claim (e.g., incremental cost for node/edge insertions) and adaptivity quality across successive ratios beyond runtimes (e.g., stability of spectral metrics across levels)?
reviews.assessment: The paper tackles an important and timely problem—adaptive, scalable coarsening that also respects heterogeneous semantics—with a simple, practical idea that reuses a single LSH-induced ordering and applies CH-style adjacent merges to support multi-resolution outputs. The empirical coverage is broad and shows compelling adaptive runtime advantages and competitive accuracy. However, several aspects require clarification or strengthening: the dependence on label-based α, the theoretical alignment between the stated algorithm and the load-balance analysis, the mismatch between p-stable and Gaussian assumptions, missing key heterogeneous baselines (HGCond), and a lack of ablations and variance analyses. Overall, I find the idea promising and practically valuable; with the requested clarifications and additional experiments, this work could make a useful contribution. As it stands, I lean toward a weak accept, contingent on addressing the stated concerns.

papers.title: From Steering Vectors to Conceptors: Compositional Affine Activation Steering for LLMs

reviews.summary: This paper introduces a principled activation-steering framework for large language models based on conceptor theory. The authors derive closed-form optimal linear and affine steering functions that act as soft projections (and optionally translations) onto concept-specific activation subspaces, and show how Boolean algebra over conceptors (AND/OR/NOT) can be used to construct compositional steering objectives. Empirically, conceptor-based steering consistently outperforms standard additive steering on in-context “function vector” tasks, shows advantages on composed functions via Boolean combination, and yields promising results on a complex alignment-relevant behavior benchmark; an additional residual application (I + C) is proposed and argued to better match transformer inductive biases.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Introduces a theoretically grounded derivation of optimal linear and affine steering operators from first principles, explicitly connecting activation steering to conceptor theory with closed-form solutions.

Extends steering beyond single-direction additive updates to full linear operators that encode rich covariance structure; proposes residual conceptor application (I + C) to better align with additive-residual architectures.
Leverages the Boolean algebra of conceptors (AND/OR/NOT) for principled multi-objective composition, going beyond heuristic vector arithmetic used in prior work.
Experimental rigor and validation
Evaluates across two families of models (transformers and an SSM) and multiple tasks: standard function-vector tasks, newly constructed composite functions, and an alignment-relevant behavioral task.
Includes ablations comparing linear vs affine conceptors and a head-to-head against a training-based LoRA baseline at similar intervention sites.
Clarity of presentation
The causal/steering setup and the contrast with additive methods are well-motivated and clearly explained with helpful geometric intuition.
The role of the aperture parameter and the nature of conceptors as soft projections are articulated clearly.
Significance of contributions
Steering and control of LLMs at inference-time are central and active problems; a closed-form, data-efficient, compositional method with strong empirical results is practically valuable.
The Boolean composition operators are a compelling and principled tool for multi-attribute/control scenarios where vector arithmetic is limited.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

The “optimality” objective for linear/affine conceptors minimizes distortion on concept-positive activations but does not include an explicit term that moves concept-negative activations toward the target; the steering effect on negatives is thus indirect and not part of the optimization criterion.

Notational inconsistencies and minor mathematical issues: e.g., mixing second moment vs covariance in derivations/implementations; a typo in the NOT operator line (¬C = I − C but printed as “-C = I − C”); unclear conditions under which Σ−1 is used (though later reduced to I − C).
Potential numerical/stability issues for large D: full D×D conceptor matrices may be ill-conditioned with small sample sizes; shrinkage/regularization beyond aperture are not thoroughly discussed.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

Missing comparisons to contemporary, stronger learned or nonlinear steering baselines (e.g., Steering Vector Fields, INNSTEER, FLAS, UNISTEER) that also address multi-attribute control and context dependence; LoRA is an odd comparator for inference-time steering and details are sparse (e.g., “full rank LoRA” phrasing).

Limited statistical reporting (error bars, significance) in main figures; some results rely on single best-layer selections and coarse hyperparameter search, notably in open-ended generation where conceptors underperform.

The composite-function dataset is synthetic (GPT-4o generated) with little characterization (noise, difficulty, linguistic diversity). Reported gains on the most difficult composition (English–French & antonyms) appear numerically small; practical significance is unclear.
Clarity or presentation issues
Some imprecision about where in the stack residual conceptors are applied vs standard conceptors in different experiments, and whether (I + C) or C was used for each result.
More specifics would help on computational overhead (per-layer costs, memory) and sample complexity vs additive steering.
Missing related work or comparisons

Recent steering frameworks that learn context-dependent, multi-layer, or flow-based operators (SVF, INNSTEER, FLAS, UNISTEER) are not compared against; discussion is limited relative to this growing literature.
Attention-level steering approaches aimed at mitigating KV-cache contamination (e.g., GCAD) are not considered; this matters for long-form or multi-turn stability.
reviews.questions:
1. Your “optimal” objective preserves concept-positive activations but does not explicitly pull negatives toward the concept. Can you clarify the intended steering mechanism for negatives and provide ablations (e.g., with held-out negatives) showing that residual application or Boolean combinations supply this attraction in practice?
2. Which estimator did you ultimately use in all experiments: centered covariance or uncentered second moment? Please provide an ablation (and a theoretical note) on how centering affects C and downstream performance.
3. Did you apply C or (I + C) in each experiment? Can you include an ablation quantifying the benefit of residual application and how it interacts with layernorm and stability in longer generations?
4. How robust are your results to the aperture α and sample size n? Do you use additional shrinkage (e.g., Ledoit–Wolf) or low-rank truncation to stabilize Σ estimates for high-dimensional layers with limited data?
5. For the composite functions, could you compare against stronger vector-composition baselines (e.g., the function-vector arithmetic from Todd et al., or sequential application) and report dataset quality metrics (noise rate, lexical diversity)?
6. Can you elaborate the LoRA baseline setup (rank, optimizer, training steps, data size)? Why is LoRA the right comparator for an inference-time method? Could you instead compare to recent learned steering baselines (SVF, INNSTEER, FLAS, UNISTEER)?
7. On the behavioral benchmark, can you add variance estimates and a broader layer/strength sweep for open-ended generation? Also, did you examine KV-cache effects in multi-turn settings (cf. GCAD)?
8. How costly is conceptor application at inference relative to vector addition (per token per layer)? Are there practical speed/memory strategies (e.g., low-rank SVD) that preserve most gains?
9. For the NOT/AND/OR operators, how do you choose α when composing conceptors trained with possibly different apertures and sample sizes? Any sensitivity analysis?
10. Can you share eigenvalue spectra or principal directions of learned conceptors to illustrate interpretability and the degree of subspace selectivity across tasks?
reviews.assessment: This paper offers a compelling and principled extension of activation steering from additive vectors to conceptor-based linear and affine operators, with a clear theoretical foundation, interpretable composition via Boolean algebra, and strong improvements on standard function-vector tasks. The residual formulation is a thoughtful architectural match, and the initial results on a complex behavioral task are promising. However, two issues temper the strength of the contribution at NeurIPS standards: (i) the “optimality” criterion focuses on preserving positives, leaving the mechanism for moving negatives toward the concept largely implicit rather than explicit in the learning objective; and (ii) the experimental evaluation omits comparisons to several recent, stronger learned/nonlinear steering baselines that specifically target multi-attribute control and context dependence. Clarity could be improved by standardizing the statistical reporting and disambiguating centered vs uncentered estimators, as well as detailing baseline setups (especially LoRA) and computational costs. Overall, I find the work novel enough and practically useful—particularly the compositional Boolean calculus and the closed-form, data-efficient operators—to be of interest to the community. With stronger baselines, clearer statistics, and explicit ablations addressing the concerns above, this paper would make a solid contribution.

papers.title: Query-Aware Subgraph Packing: A Knapsack Optimization Paradigm for Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation

reviews.summary: The paper proposes GraphPack, a query-aware GraphRAG framework that casts subgraph selection as a 0-1 knapsack optimization problem to jointly maximize semantic relevance and minimize structural redundancy under a size budget. It further introduces a query-aware graph encoder using FiLM-style conditioning on the query and an auxiliary graph-to-text reconstruction objective. Experiments on citation, social network, and knowledge-graph QA benchmarks suggest consistent gains over recent GraphRAG baselines in supervised, cross-domain, and zero-shot settings.
strengths: Technical novelty and innovation

Framing subgraph retrieval as a 0-1 knapsack packing problem is a clean and general abstraction that naturally enforces a trade-off between relevance and budget, and is different from commonly used path/subtree search (e.g., PCST) or pure similarity ranking.
The integration of a query-conditioned modulation (FiLM) within the graph encoder provides a simple, modular way to inject query signals into structural encoding.
The auxiliary graph-to-text reconstruction objective targets the known issue of long-context dilution of non-textual embeddings in LLMs.
Experimental rigor and validation

Evaluations span several regimes (supervised, zero-shot cross-domain, inference-time retrieval without SFT) and multiple datasets (citation, social networks, knowledge-graph QA), providing a reasonably broad perspective.
Comparisons include strong recent GraphRAG baselines (GRAG, G-Retriever) on WebQSP/CWQ, and an ablation on knapsack capacity that illuminates the quality/size trade-off.
Clarity of presentation
The high-level workflow (anchor retrieval → n-hop expansion → knapsack packing → query-aware encoding → LLM generation) is clearly conveyed, with an intuitive figure.
The intent behind each component (e.g., rank-based values, hop-based weights) is well-motivated.
Significance of contributions

Retrieval on graphs for LLM augmentation remains a timely and important problem; a practical packing formulation with query-aware encoding can be impactful for many downstream knowledge-intensive tasks.
The approach is conceptually compatible with many existing encoders/LLMs and thus potentially useful to the community.
weaknesses: Technical limitations or concerns

Additive knapsack cannot capture pairwise or higher-order redundancy/diversity; structural redundancy is only indirectly discouraged by hop-based weights, not by explicit diversity modeling (e.g., submodularity/DPPs/MMR-style objectives).

The selection over “elements” (nodes/edges) lacks explicit connectivity/closure constraints. It is unclear how invalid selections (e.g., isolated edges, disconnected sets) are handled beyond “linking to a query node,” which may undermine structural coherence.

The value definition value(e) = max_score − rank(e) is underspecified: what is max_score, and can values be negative? Ranking loses magnitude information from similarity; a calibrated scoring scheme may be preferable.
Experimental gaps or methodological issues

The evaluation on node-classification datasets (Cora, Citeseer, WikiCS, OGBN-Arxiv) is not clearly described in terms of how the generative setup, input serialization, and metrics (Acc/F1) align with standard graph learning practices. The relevance of LLM-based generation to these tasks needs clearer justification and standardized baselines.
Error bars or statistical significance are not shown in the main tables; several gains over strong baselines (e.g., GRAG/G-Retriever) are modest and could be within variance.
The claimed <0.25s retrieval on million-scale graphs lacks details (hardware, candidate subgraph size, indexing method, number of anchors, n-hop parameters).
Clarity or presentation issues
Inconsistent naming between GraphPack and GraphLLM appears multiple times and can confuse the reader about the exact method.
The Query-LM (FiLM) notation is ambiguous (e.g., γj(l), βj(l) vs per-node/per-channel vectors) and could better clarify dimensionalities and whether parameters are shared across nodes.
The auxiliary objective is under-specified (weighting, curriculum, masking of text, whether the LLM is frozen or tuned, and how h_g is fed).
Missing related work or comparisons

Limited discussion of diversity-aware or submodular selection for retrieval and graph subset selection (e.g., facility location, submodular maximization, DPPs, MMR) that more directly address redundancy.

Connections to optimization-based graph retrieval beyond PCST (e.g., minimum Steiner trees, constrained community detection) are only briefly mentioned; a more thorough comparison/discussion would help contextualize the knapsack choice.
reviews.questions:
1. How do you ensure the validity/closure of the selected subgraph (e.g., selecting an edge without endpoints, or a highly disconnected set)? Is there a connectivity constraint or post-processing step beyond attaching a “query node”?
2. What exactly is max_score in value(e) = max_score − rank(e)? Could values become negative? Why not use calibrated similarity scores or a learned value function?
3. Can you report error bars or multiple seeds for the main tables (especially WebQSP/CWQ) and clarify whether the observed gains are statistically significant?
4. For the node-classification datasets, please detail the problem casting to a generative LLM setting, the baselines’ adaptations, and why this evaluation is representative and fair.
5. What is the complexity of the overall retrieval (anchor search + n-hop expansion + DP packing), and what are the concrete hardware and hyperparameters behind the <0.25s claim on million-node graphs?
6. How sensitive is performance to the text encoder (e.g., SBERT choice) for anchor identification? Have you tried retrievable encoders fine-tuned on the specific domains?
7. Could you compare to or combine with a diversity-aware objective (e.g., submodular facility location/MMR) to more directly minimize redundancy?
reviews.assessment: This paper tackles an important and timely problem in GraphRAG with a conceptually simple and practical knapsack-based retrieval framework and a query-aware graph encoder. The formulation is appealing, and the empirical results on QA tasks are promising. However, the current method raises concerns about structural validity and redundancy modeling inherent to an additive knapsack objective without connectivity constraints, and some core implementation details (value calibration, auxiliary loss, runtime claims) need clarification. Parts of the evaluation (especially on node-classification datasets) are under-specified for a top-tier venue. With stronger theoretical/algorithmic treatment of structural constraints or diversity, clearer experimental protocols, and statistical reporting, this work could make a solid contribution. As it stands, I view it as borderline, leaning towards rejection, but potentially publishable after significant revision.

papers.title: Beyond Two-Stage Training: Integrating SFT and RL for Improved Reasoning in LLMs

reviews.summary: The paper proposes BRIDGE, a bilevel optimization framework that integrates supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve reasoning in LLMs. The key idea is to treat SFT as an upper-level problem over LoRA parameters and RL as a lower-level problem over base model parameters, using a penalty-based relaxation that explicitly maximizes the reward gap between joint SFT+RL updates and RL-only updates.
